docs.title: Major Project — Streaming machine learning : Drift detection and adaptation
docs.text:
Research-based project on machine learning from data streams, using River as the experimental framework.

Status: Phase 0 (research) complete, Phase 1 (experimentation) in progress — the first pilot (Exp-01) has been run.

docs.title: The one-paragraph version
docs.text: Almost all machine learning you've been taught assumes the dataset is a finished object: it sits on disk, you load it, you split it, you fit a model, you're done. Streaming machine learning drops that assumption. Data arrives one sample at a time, potentially forever, and is too large (or too fast) to store. The model must learn incrementally, in a single pass, using bounded memory. And because the world generating the data keeps changing, the model must also notice when it becomes wrong and adapt. That last part — concept drift, and specifically the cost of delayed labels (the "Delay Tax") — is the real research problem, and it's what makes this a project rather than a tutorial.

docs.title: The picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["Data stream<br/>x1, x2, x3, ... (never ends)"] --> P["predict_one(x)<br/>1. TEST"]
    P --> M["metric.update(y, y_pred)<br/>2. SCORE"]
    M --> L["learn_one(x, y)<br/>3. TRAIN"]
    L --> D{"Drift<br/>detector"}
    D -- "no drift" --> S
    D -- "DRIFT!" --> R["Adapt:<br/>reset / retrain / reweight"]
    R --> S

Each sample is used for testing before it is used for training, then thrown away. The model is never "finished" — it is permanently mid-training.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Experimentation
docs.text:
• Roadmap v2 — DF-H — the new ultimate goal: a label-free deep monitor plus supervised confirmation, targeting the KDD'26 detector benchmark and the delayed-label setting.
  • E01 — Metric v2 correction — the current headline: frozen recovered 0/11, DeepRiver's corrected damage_ref is 74.8 vs 515.0 samples·κ (≈6.9×), and the legacy 294× is retired as an upper bound.
  • E03 — Baseline ladder — at 11 seeds and 220 runs, every streaming adapter pays less drift damage than frozen and than every scheduled-retrain clock; the phase-noise test remains inconclusive because the refit buffer dominates the 1k/5k clocks.
  • E04 — Detector map — the synthetic map: eight detectors across four drift shapes and four generators; HDDM-A on the raw signal is the best default on the static host, recurring drift is the hard case, and smoothing raises false alarms.
  • E14 — Real-stream model check — ARF leads both real datasets and the deep model does not beat it: the evidence for using DriftFormer as a signal extractor, not the host. Provisional five-seed slice with acceptance rules.
  • E17 — Real-stream detector map — the same eight detectors on real Elec2 records; HDDM-A keeps its four-shape win on the static host, but ADWIN wins abrupt and recurring on the adaptive host, so the default is host-conditional.
  • E18 — Deep signal gate — the pre-registered AUC gate failed (best deep 0.616 vs error 0.598), but at 0.1/1k FAR the feature signals detect feature drift earlier than error and detect feature filtering where error is blind; the classical KS control is competitive.
  • E19 — DF-H v1 pilot — DF-H ranks 3rd overall (7.09) behind STEPD and SEED; FAR passes and it beats the no-feature control, but top-2 and the primary feature-cell test fail. The full E20 matrix is not run.
  • E21 — Delay Tax detector — the surviving headline: at L = 2,000, label-free Stage 1 warns in 70–513 samples while SEED/STEPD take 2,120–2,710 and ADWIN 2,472–3,269. The error-only panel pays the label tax; Stage 1 does not.
  • E22 — Detector shootout — the direct capability check on our data: DF-H is 3rd overall (7.34), ahead of HDDM-W, ADWIN, HDDM-A and PageHinkley; only SEED/STEPD lead. It owns feature permutation against the requested panel, with 0.04 FAR.
  • Exp-01: DeepRiver rolling vs frozen batch on SEA — the first atomic experiment (legacy metric; superseded by E01).
  • Exp-02: the 11-seed sweep — the sweep that made the claim statistical (legacy metric; corrected by E01).
  • Thesis: how streaming beats batch, and on what — the mechanism and the metric family where the win is structural.
  • Streaming vs Batch: real metrics where online learning wins (and where it doesn't) — evidence dossier + the Ch1 experimental protocol.

docs.title: DriftDeck — drift monitoring that keeps working when your labels are late
docs.text:
Product doc — turning the Delay Tax research into a product.

One line: DriftDeck is an ML observability platform that detects and prices model drift in production — and keeps doing so when the truth arrives late, partially, or selectively. Its engine is a hybrid detector (label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation), and its headline number is the drift cost in business terms, not an abstract accuracy drop.

(Working name — the file and title rename in one edit if you want a different one.)

docs.title: 1. TL;DR
docs.text: What ML drift monitoring for production models whose labels are delayed, partial, or selective Who MLOps / ML platform teams running fraud, lending, ads, intrusion, or content models The gap Every drift tool assumes labels arrive with the prediction. In production they don't (chargebacks take 30–90 days). The wedge DriftDeck is delayed-label-native — it models the delay, not papers over it The engine Hybrid detector = label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation The metric Damage area — skill lost × time wrong, converted to money The moat Four formal lemmas (the Delay Tax) that let the product state honest limits, not marketing promises The build order Validate the lemmas → MVP on fraud → hosted

docs.title: 2. The problem
docs.text:
A model is deployed. The world changes. The model silently gets worse. Two facts make this expensive, and they compound:

Fact 1 — drift is invisible to the people who own the model. You can't see accuracy in production without labels, and accuracy is exactly what's degrading. By the time a quarterly report catches it, the loss has already happened.

Fact 2 — the labels that would reveal drift arrive late, or never. This is the Delay Tax, and it is measured:

Cost of late labels Number Source Delayed labels raise user exposure +50% at 81 (DDM) / 61 (EDDM) epochs of delay Botacin & Gomes 2024 Delayed labels cut detection up to −75% Botacin & Gomes 2024 A 10,000-instance label delay shifts drift detection by ~10,000 instances (prequential accuracy pinned below 50%) Gomes et al. 2022 Batch retraining starves without labels tuned batch wins under delay+rare-class (AUCPR 23.41 vs 14.23) Amekoe et al. 2024

The production stories are concrete: a fraud model approves a transaction now and learns the truth when the chargeback lands in 30–90 days. An ad model serves now and learns the conversion next week. An intrusion model flags now and gets the analyst verdict later, or never. Labels arrive in overnight batches, out of order, and only for flagged cases — which makes the observed errors a biased sample of true errors.

Why this is a product and not a feature: the market's existing tools solve "detect drift when labels are here." The harder problem — "keep watching when labels are not here, and be honest about what you can and can't know yet" — is unsolved. That is the product.

docs.title: 3. The wedge: what everyone else assumes away
docs.text:
The research's gap analysis (26-page review, 38 papers, notes.pdf) established the wedge precisely. The delayed/partial-label literature is fragmented (five names for one thing: verification latency, delayed labelling, label latency, extreme verification latency, delayed partially labelled streams) and unbenchmarked: a standard benchmark now exists for immediate-label drift detection (Cerqueira et al., KDD'26), but none exists for delayed, partial, or selective labels.

Concretely, the competition falls into two camps:

Camp Examples What they assume The gap DriftDeck fills Data/target drift monitors Evidently, Arize, Fiddler, WhyLabs Labels eventually available, or ignore the delay Don't model when the truth arrives Label-free performance estimators NannyML (CBPE), Seldon Alibi Detect Estimate accuracy without labels Great — but they treat "no labels yet" as a state, not a costed, bounded timeline DriftDeck — Labels are a stochastic observation process with latency Models the delay, gives the earliest provable answer, prices the wait

The differentiation is narrow but real, and it is exactly what the four lemmas give.

docs.title: 4. From research to product — the mapping
docs.text:
Every piece of the research becomes a product feature. This table is the conversion.

Research artifact Product feature Lemma 1 — reaction floor (T ≥ τ + L_τ) "Earliest you can know" — the product tells the customer, honestly, the fastest possible confirmation given their median label latency, and shows the early warning meanwhile Lemma 2 — power loss (1/√p) Coverage dial — "you label 10% of traffic, so my confidence is ~3.2× noisier" — a per-model sensitivity/confidence number Lemma 3 — batch-arrival inflation (1+(b−1)ρ) False-alarm suppression on batch-reconciled labels (overnight jobs) — fewer spurious pages Lemma 4 — identifiability ceiling Honest limits — "this drift type is invisible without labels; here's what I can and can't see" Hybrid detector (Ch3) The core engine — early warning (fast, may be false) + delayed confirmation (slow, reliable) Damage area / recovery time / dip depth (Exp-01/02) The money metric — drift priced as Σ (baseline − actual) × cost-per-error Prequential harness (Ch1) The backtest/trust engine — prove the detector on your data before you deploy it The system chapter (Ch2) The deployment/scale story — replica divergence, backpressure, restart cost Exp-01/02 (measured) The proof-of-concept demo — a model that keeps learning heals itself; a frozen one doesn't

docs.title: 5. The engine — the hybrid detector
docs.text:
The product's core. It is justified by construction, not by tuning:

  • Stage 1 — label-free early warning (on P(X), live): KS / MMD / Jensen–Shannon two-sample tests over a sliding window. Fast, catches drift immediately, but also fires on harmless virtual drift.
  • Stage 2 — supervised confirmation (on the delayed error stream): join the late labels to the buffered predictions, form the error stream, run ADWIN / DDM / KSWIN. Reliable, but bounded below by the reaction floor (can't fire before labels land).
  • The hybrid logic: a warning inside a tolerance window, then a confirmation → alarm. A warning that never confirms → revoked, with its false-alarm cost recorded.

Why this is the information-maximal architecture: Lemma 4 proves Stage 1 cannot confirm (pure posterior drift is invisible to P(X)), and Lemma 1 proves Stage 2 cannot be early. So the hybrid is the only design that is both early and reliable given the available information. That is a defensible engineering claim, not a slogan.

Cheap to run: the detectors are O(1) per sample — literature puts monitoring at <150 ms and <50 KB of state per detector (Agu et al. 2026). DriftDeck can watch thousands of models on one node.

docs.title: 6. The money metric — damage area → drift cost
docs.text:
Recovery time tells you how long the model was wrong. Damage area tells you how much skill × time you lost:

damage = Σ (κ₀ − κ(t))   for t = drift → recovery      # in samples · Kappa
drift_cost = damage × cost_per_error(currency)        # the number the business sees

This is the product's "so what." A PM doesn't care about Cohen's Kappa. They care that "the model was 0.173 κ below baseline for 12,000 transactions, costing ~$X." DriftDeck reports the dollar number, with the Kappa behind it.

(Honest note from the research: the damage-area metric itself has a truncation defect — see ML.md §11.1 — that must be fixed before it ships. It is a known, bounded issue, not a mystery.)

docs.title: 7. Positioning vs competitors
docs.text:
Tool Drift detection Label delay handled Prices drift in money Honest limits Evidently ✔ ✖ (assumes labels) partial ✖ Arize / Fiddler / WhyLabs ✔ ✖ partial ✖ NannyML ✔ (CBPE, label-free) ✔ implicitly partial ✖ Seldon Alibi Detect ✔ ✖ ✖ ✖ DriftDeck ✔ hybrid ✔ native ✔ headline ✔ lemmas

The honest position: DriftDeck does not win "who has the most charts." It wins the one narrow, expensive case — "my labels are late and I need to know how wrong I am right now, and what it's costing me."

docs.title: 8. Who it's for — and the killer demo
docs.text:
Ideal customer profile: a team with production ML models where ground truth is intrinsically delayed or partial — fraud/payments (chargebacks 30–90 days), lending (defaults), ad conversion (weeks), cybersecurity (analyst triage), insurance (claims).

The killer demo is fraud, because it is the canonical Delay Tax story and it is visible: a fraud model approved a transaction; the chargeback lands 45 days later. A fraud team already understands the lag. Show them, on their own stream, that DriftDeck (a) warned within hours using input drift, (b) confirmed when the chargebacks landed, (c) priced the accumulated loss — and that their current monitoring said nothing for 45 days. That demo closes.

docs.title: 9. Architecture
docs.text:
The product is an observability sidecar/layer, not a serving framework — it attaches to any model (batch or streaming, yours or theirs). This is deliberately the Ch2 "systems" DNA: the hard part is not the math, it is the two-stream join and the operational reality.

                        ┌──────────────────────────────┐

                        │  emits (id, features, ŷ)     │
                        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                       │

                              │  event backbone   │   Kafka / Redpanda  (Redis Streams for single-node)
                              │  ── inference ──  │   topic 1: live, every sample
                              │  ── labels ─────  │   topic 2: late, partial, selective
                              └────────┬─────────┘
                                       │
              ┌────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
              │                        │                         │
        ┌─────▼─────┐           ┌──────▼──────┐           ┌──────▼──────┐
        │ stage-1    │           │ label-join   │           │ stage-2      │

        │ early-warn │           │ (retain ≥    │           │ confirmation │
        │ on P(X)    │           │  max delay)  │           │ ADWIN/DDM/…  │
