docs.title: The response half (optional, and where the research's adaptation side ships)
docs.text: Detection is the core. But the research also measured recovery (Exp-01/02: a model that keeps learning heals itself; a frozen one doesn't). So DriftDeck ships a "respond" tier: on a confirmed drift, trigger retrain / rollback / model-registry swap — or, for customers who want it, serve a continually-learning model that self-adapts within a bounded window. That second tier is what Exp-01/02 actually demonstrated.

docs.title: 10. Deployment model
docs.text:
Tier Shape When MVP docker-compose, single node, Redis Streams validate + first demo Scale k8s + Helm, Kafka/Redpanda, horizontal detector workers multi-model, high QPS On-prem / edge single binary or sidecar per model fraud/security customers with data-residency constraints

Detector cost is the enabler: O(1) per sample, <50 KB state per detector, so a small fleet of detector workers watches a large number of models. The expensive part is the label-join retention buffer — sized by the customer's max label delay, not by traffic.

docs.title: 11. The build order (roadmap)
docs.text:
Ordered so the product de-risks itself and the academic claims de-risk themselves — they are now the same thing.

Phase Build Exit criterion De-risks A — Validate Run the delayed-label experiments (the project's Exp-05): the four lemmas, on synthetic ground truth The 1/√p, reaction-floor, and batch-inflation curves hold empirically The core engine is true, not assumed — and Alencar 2026 is read B — MVP SDK + detector core + label-join + damage estimator + minimal UI, on one real dataset (CreditCard fraud) End-to-end: a live fraud stream, a late chargeback, a confirmed drift, a dollar figure The killer demo C — Harden Alerts, retrain trigger, model-registry integrations, auth/tenancy, multi-model A pilot customer runs it in shadow mode Product–market fit signal D — Distribute Hosted SaaS + on-prem enterprise, OSS the SDK + detectors Paying customer Business

The research's own roadmap (Exp-03 baseline ladder, Exp-04 real streams, Exp-05 delay tax) is Phase A–B of the product. There is no wasted work — the academic experiments become the product's proof and its backtest engine.

docs.title: 12. Business model (brief)
docs.text:
• OSS core — SDK + detectors + the hybrid logic. Builds trust and distribution in the MLOps community, and it is cheap to give away (the detectors are the research).
  • Paid — hosted (multi-model, retention, alerting, SSO, compliance, support) and on-prem. Per-model or per-event pricing, not per-seat — the value scales with drift cost, not headcount.
  • The wedge in pricing: the dollar "drift cost" the product reports is the ROI number that justifies the subscription. "You lost $X to drift last quarter; DriftDeck costs $Y."

docs.title: 13. Risks — honest
docs.text: Risk Severity Mitigation Crowded space (Evidently, NannyML, Arize, Fiddler, WhyLabs, Seldon) High Differentiation is narrow-but-real (delay); go deep on fraud/security, not wide NannyML already does label-free performance estimation Medium-High Differentiate on the timeline (earliest provable answer) + the dollar metric + honest limits, not on "we also estimate accuracy" Lemmas are unvalidated — the core claim is unproven until Exp-05 High Phase A runs first; the lemmas are cheap to test and can degrade to empirical claims if a proof resists Alencar 2026 (DSP) may scoop the measurement Medium-High Read it now; if it already has delay-vs-latency curves, the novelty shifts to the formal bounds + the hybrid protocol + the product Thin proof-of-concept (one synthetic stream, no detector actually run) Medium Position Exp-01/02 as the mechanism demo; the product's proof is Phase A–B, not the two experiments Buyer is MLOps, not infra Medium The author's infra background helps the build, not the sale — needs an MLOps-minded co-founder/early customer Data residency / compliance (fraud, security) Medium On-prem/edge tier first-class, not an afterthought

docs.title: 14. What the research already gives you
docs.text:
This is not starting from zero. The project hands the product:

  1. A pre-registered, reproducible proof of the mechanism — Exp-01/02: a model that keeps learning recovers from drift in bounded time; a frozen one never does (0/11 seeds). That is the "adaptation" half of the story, measured, with artifacts.
  2. The metric family — damage area, recovery time, dip depth — the product's money metric is already defined and (partially) measured.
  3. The four lemmas — a genuine, citable theory that becomes the "honest limits" feature and the marketing moat.
  4. The hybrid detector design — justified by construction, ready to build.
  5. The prequential harness — the future backtest/trust engine.
  6. The systems knowledge — replica divergence, backpressure, restart cost — the deployment/scale story no ML competitor has.

The honest gap: the lemmas and the hybrid are specified but not yet measured. The product's first move is to close that gap — and that move is the next experiment.

docs.title: 15. One-screen recap
docs.text:
Product. DriftDeck — ML observability that detects and prices model drift when labels are late, partial, or selective.

Why it exists. Existing drift tools assume labels arrive with predictions; in production they don't (chargebacks take 30–90 days), and the loss is invisible until it is large.

The wedge. Delayed-label-native monitoring — model the delay, give the earliest provable answer, price the wait.

The engine. Hybrid detector: label-free early warning (fast, may be false) + delayed supervised confirmation (reliable, floor-bounded).

The metric. Damage area → drift cost in dollars.

The moat. Four lemmas (reaction floor, 1/√p, batch inflation, identifiability) that let the product state honest limits instead of marketing promises.

The build order. Validate the lemmas (Exp-05) → MVP on fraud → harden → distribute.

The evidence. Exp-01/02 prove the adaptation mechanism; the harness is the future backtest engine; the research roadmap is the product's phase A–B.

docs.title: EverLearn — models that never stop learning
docs.text:
Product doc — turning the streaming-learning research into a product.

One line: EverLearn is a model-serving layer where the model is never stale, because it learns from every prediction it makes — one sample at a time, in bounded memory, with no retraining pipeline.

(Working name — rename in one edit if you want a different one.)

docs.title: 1. TL;DR
docs.text: What A self-learning serving layer: predict now, learn on the next label, forever Who Teams running high-velocity ML — fraud, ads, personalisation, recommendations, moderation The gap Every production model is frozen between retrains. The staleness window is where money leaks The wedge Real-time ML made the features real-time; the model never got there. EverLearn does The engine River / DeepRiver streaming learners — O(1) time and bounded memory per sample The metric Staleness saved = damage area avoided × cost-per-error, in dollars The moat A measured mechanism (Exp-01/02) plus governance that makes self-modifying models safe to deploy The build order Shadow mode on fraud → live on one stream → governance → platform

docs.title: 2. The idea
docs.text:
Almost every ML product runs the same ritual: train a model, freeze it, deploy it, watch it silently rot until someone reruns the pipeline. The model is a finished object that is periodically rebuilt.

Streaming learning inverts that. The model is never finished — it is permanently mid-training. Every sample that flows through it follows the same three steps: predict, score, learn, discard. The label arrives (now, or later), the model takes one bounded-memory update, and the world's most recent truth is already inside it. There is no retrain event because there is nothing to retrain: the model is always as current as the last sample it saw.

The product is that inversion, packaged. EverLearn wraps any model and makes it self-updating — the customer stops maintaining a retraining pipeline and instead owns a model that cannot go stale by construction.

This is deliberately not a drift-detection product. DriftDeck answers "is my model wrong?"; EverLearn answers "make it stop being wrong — automatically." Detection and adaptation are the two halves of the research; DriftDeck is the watch, EverLearn is the act.

docs.title: 3. The problem — the staleness window
docs.text:
Between one retrain and the next, the world moves and the model doesn't. The model is silently wrong for the whole window, and two costs compound inside it:

Cost 1 — the decay itself. Accuracy leaks continuously from the moment of deployment. A weekly retrain means the model is, on average, half a week stale — and that staleness is invisible to the team that owns it until someone measures it.

Cost 2 — the retrain machinery. The pipeline that rebuilds the model is itself a product-scale investment: feature stores, training jobs, validation, registry, rollout, rollback. MLOps teams spend a large share of their effort feeding a cycle that is, structurally, always behind the data.

The research already priced cost 1. On a drifting stream, the frozen model never recovered — its corrected damage_ref was 515.0 ± 97.1 samples·κ across 11 seeds, versus 74.8 ± 61.8 for the streaming model (≈6.9×), and a model that retrains on a schedule can only heal at the tick, staying wrong for up to a full interval by pure luck of phase. The staleness window is not an accident of bad ops; it is the defining property of batch-trained models.

Why this is a product and not a feature: every "retrain faster" fix reduces the window but keeps it — and keeps the machinery. Only a model that learns from the stream itself eliminates both at once. That is the offer.

docs.title: 4. The wedge — features are real-time, models are frozen
docs.text:
The real-time ML market already proved the demand for lower staleness. Tecton, Chalk, Fennel and friends made features real-time: sub-second freshness for the inputs to the model. But the model those features feed is still batch-trained — retrained nightly or weekly, deployed through a registry.

So the industry is currently real-time until the last mile, then frozen. A fraud model consumes a feature computed 100 ms ago, but its weights were decided three weeks ago. That last mile — the model's own knowledge — is the entire staleness that remains, and nobody sells it as a product.

Camp Examples What they made real-time What EverLearn changes Real-time feature platforms Tecton, Chalk, Fennel, Featureform Features (the inputs) Nothing — EverLearn sits downstream of them Serving + retrain platforms Seldon, Vertex, SageMaker Deployment, not learning The retrain job disappears Online-learning libraries Vowpal Wabbit, River The algorithm, as OSS The operational product around it EverLearn — The model itself The model's knowledge updates with every sample

The differentiation is one sentence: everyone else made the inputs fresh and left the model frozen. EverLearn makes the model fresh.

docs.title: 5. What the customer actually buys
docs.text:
Not "streaming ML" — nobody buys a mechanism. They buy the end of the staleness window, delivered as three things:

  1. The SDK. Wrap any model: EverLearn(model=your_model) preserves the .predict() contract; the learning happens invisibly when each label lands. Drop-in for sklearn / River / PyTorch serving paths.
  2. The engine. River / DeepRiver learners underneath — O(1) time and bounded memory per sample, so one node learns continuously at line rate instead of running batch jobs.
  3. The governance. The honest reason teams don't ship self-modifying models is fear. EverLearn's controls exist to make that fear manageable: shadow mode (learn silently, measure, deploy nothing), snapshots (the model is a sequence of versions, rollback to any of them), learning dials (per-model learning rate, sample cap, what-not-to-learn rules), and an audit log (what the model learned, when, from what).

The headline metric the product reports: staleness saved — the damage area the self-learning model avoided versus the customer's scheduled-retrain baseline, times their cost-per-error. The research's damage-area metric becomes the customer's dollar figure.

docs.title: 6. The evidence — the mechanism is already measured
docs.text:
The product's founding claim — a model that keeps learning recovers; a frozen one never does — is not a pitch, it is Exp-01/02 plus the E01 metric correction:

Fact Number Source Frozen batch model recovered after drift 0 / 11 seeds E01 Streaming model recovered (real excursion) 8 / 11 seeds; the other 3 never left the band E01 Damage paid while wrong, corrected damage_ref 74.8 ± 61.8 vs 515.0 ± 97.1 samples·κ — ≈ 6.9× E01 Damage over the rest of the stream (damage_full) 321.4 vs 3,472.9 samples·κ — ≈ 10.8× E01 Worst streaming seed vs best frozen seed 0.74×, not 24× E01 Streaming self-heal on the pilot stream back inside the pre-drift band 834 samples after drift on seed 42; frozen fell 0.75 → 0.59 κ and never returned Exp-01

The legacy 294× mean and 24× worst-vs-best figures were upper bounds from a truncated integral and are retired. The durable claim is the 0/11 frozen recovery and the corrected ≈6.9× mean damage gap.

The honest caveat, carried over from the research: this is one synthetic stream, two models, no delayed labels, no real data. It proves the mechanism, not the market. The product's first engineering phase exists to close exactly that gap — on the customer's own stream, in shadow mode, where the proof doubles as the sales demo.

docs.title: 7. The two killer use cases
docs.text:
Streaming learning wins in two different places, and it is worth keeping them distinct because they sell differently:

A. Self-healing serving — the drop-in upgrade. Fraud detection, ads, content moderation: the model consumes real-time features (already built), but its weights go stale. EverLearn sits behind the existing serving API; predictions are unchanged; the model simply keeps learning from each confirmed label (chargeback, conversion, verdict) as it arrives. The sale is "your current model, minus the decay between retrains." The killer demo: run the customer's own stream through a frozen model and the self-learning model side by side — the frozen one drifts off and stays off, the EverLearn model dips and heals itself live (this demo is Exp-01, rerun on their data).

B. Per-entity models — where streaming is the only option. One lightweight model per user, session, device, or seller, updated on every interaction, on-device or server-side. Batch systems cannot build per-user models at all — they fake it with embeddings and global retrains. Streaming learning makes per-entity models trivial: a few hundred bytes of state per entity, one update per event, personalisation that reacts to the user's last ten actions, not last month's global retrain. This use case has no batch competitor, which makes it the cleanest market entry.

docs.title: 8. How it works mechanically
docs.text:
The loop is the prequential harness from the research, productised:

   request ──► predict_one(x) ──► serve ŷ            (unchanged, fast path)
                                      │
                         (label arrives — now or days later)
                                      │
             join (prediction ↔ label) via the event backbone
                                      │
             learn_one(x, y)          (O(1), bounded memory)
             metric.update(y, ŷ)      (rolling κ, damage area, staleness saved)
             snapshot policy          (version the model when skill moves)

Every sample is scored before it is learned — that is what makes the reported skill honest — and nothing is stored. The infrastructure mirrors DriftDeck's: an SDK that emits (id, features, ŷ), an event backbone (Kafka at scale, Redis Streams for one node) with a predictions topic and a labels topic, and a join buffer sized by the customer's maximum label delay. The engineering hard part is the same two-stream join; the learning itself is the cheap part.

docs.title: 9. The hard problems — honest
docs.text:
The idea is strong; these are the things that kill it if ignored:

Problem Severity Honest status & mitigation The Delay Tax on the learner — labels arrive late, so the model learns yesterday's truth, and drift is exactly when it matters most High This is the project's open problem. The product's first experiment is a delayed-label learner; until then EverLearn can only promise bounded staleness, not zero lag Trust & governance — teams will not deploy a model that changes itself High Shadow mode first (measure, don't deploy), snapshots + rollback, audit log, per-model learning dials. Governance is the product, not an add-on Catastrophic forgetting — bounded-memory continual learning degrades on long streams Medium Hybrid design: streaming core + periodic offline consolidation. Known solutions; needs engineering, not research Poisoned labels — a model that learns from everything is exposed to bad labels Medium Learning dials (blocklists, confidence gates, anomaly fences) at the ingestion point Regulation — some industries require frozen, validated models Medium Target the ones that don't (fraud, ads, personalisation, moderation); on-prem tier for the rest It is not a category — nobody has budget for "streaming ML" High Sell the outcome: "never stale," "no retrain pipeline." The mechanism stays under the hood

docs.title: 10. Positioning
docs.text:
Detects staleness Removes staleness Model keeps learning Per-entity models Retrain pipelines (the status quo) ✖ ✖ (only at the tick) ✖ ✖ Real-time feature platforms ✖ ✖ ✖ ✖ Drift monitors (incl. DriftDeck) ✔ ✖ (tells you to retrain) ✖ ✖ Vowpal Wabbit / River (OSS) — ✔ ✔ ✔ EverLearn ✔ (built-in, as a by-product) ✔ by construction ✔ ✔ native

The honest position: EverLearn does not compete with drift monitors — it is the thing they tell you to do, done automatically. The research's own pairing is the strategy: DriftDeck prices the decay, EverLearn deletes it. A customer that buys one is one sentence away from buying the other.

docs.title: 11. The build order
docs.text:
Ordered so the product de-risks itself and the research's next experiments become the product's first milestones:

Phase Build Exit criterion De-risks A — Shadow SDK + engine + label-join + damage accounting, on one real stream (CreditCard fraud), shadow mode only The self-learning model measurably beats the customer's scheduled-retrain baseline on staleness saved — without being deployed The mechanism survives real data; the killer demo exists B — Live Snapshots, rollback, one pilot model learning in production The pilot runs live with an owner who can revert it in one action Governance under fire; first real dollars attached to staleness saved C — Platform Multi-model, per-entity models, alerts, integrations (registry, feature stores), auth/tenancy Several models, one customer, zero retrain jobs left for them Product–market fit signal D — Distribute Hosted + on-prem; OSS the SDK and engine Paying customers Business

The research roadmap slots straight in: Exp-05 (label delay) is Phase A's core engineering risk; Exp-03/04 (baseline ladder, real streams) are Phase A's shadow-mode validation written in academic form. No wasted work — the experiments are the product's first build phases.

docs.title: 12. Business model (brief)
docs.text:
• OSS core — the SDK and the engine. Cheap to give away (the algorithms are the research; River is already OSS) and it builds distribution in the MLOps community.
  • Paid — the operational layer: the label-join infrastructure, snapshots and rollback, the audit log, multi-model management, SSO, support. Hosted or on-prem.
  • Pricing — per model or per event, not per seat: the value scales with the staleness the customer avoids, and the "staleness saved" dollar figure the product reports is the ROI number that justifies the subscription.

docs.title: 13. One-screen recap
docs.text:
Product. EverLearn — a self-learning serving layer. Models that learn from every prediction, in bounded memory, with no retraining pipeline.

Why it exists. Every production model is frozen between retrains, silently leaking money through the staleness window, and the retrain machinery that fights it is itself expensive and always behind.

The wedge. Real-time ML made features real-time; EverLearn makes the model's own knowledge real-time. The last mile nobody sells.

The offer. Drop-in SDK, River/DeepRiver engine, and governance (shadow mode, snapshots, rollback, audit) that makes self-modifying models safe to deploy.

The metric. Staleness saved — damage area avoided × cost-per-error, in dollars.

The evidence. E01: a streaming model self-heals after drift (8/11 seeds with a real excursion; the other 3 never left the band); a frozen model never does (0/11), paying ≈6.9× more corrected damage_ref. The mechanism is measured, not promised.

The honest gaps. Delayed labels weaken the learner exactly when it matters (the Delay Tax — the project's open problem), and self-modifying models need governance before any team will ship them. Both are Phase A.

The build order. Shadow mode on fraud → live pilot → platform → distribute — with the research's own experiments as the first milestones.

docs.title: EverRank — per-user personalization as a drop-in reranking layer
docs.text:
Product doc — EverLearn's flagship application: a personalization layer that sits between any recommendation system's ranking and its serving.

One line: EverRank is a drop-in reranking layer. Your existing recsys keeps generating candidates; EverRank reorders them with one tiny streaming model per user — and per session — so the feed reacts to you, not your demographic.

(Working name — rename in one edit if you want a different one.)

docs.title: 1. TL;DR
docs.text: What A reranking layer on top of any existing recommendation system Who E-commerce, feeds, streaming, ads — anyone with a ranked list and a user The gap Personalization stops at the global model: one model serves everyone, retrained monthly The wedge Zero-risk adoption — the layer is a pass-through at worst, so a customer can try it without betting their pipeline The engine Per-user + per-session streaming adaptors (KB-scale), learned one interaction at a time, IPS-corrected The metric Per-user lift in CTR/conversion, and drift recovery time — how many interactions until the feed notices your taste changed The moat The measured self-healing mechanism (Exp-01/02) applied at the level of a single user The build order Shadow rerank on one feed → live A/B → session layer → platform

docs.title: 2. The idea
docs.text:
Modern recommendation systems are already staged: retrieval → ranking → reranking. Retrieval finds a few hundred candidates, ranking scores them with the global model, reranking does a final polish before serving.

EverRank inserts itself at that last seam — the one every real system already has. The customer's retrieval and ranking keep working untouched; EverRank takes their top-K and reorders it:

existing system:  retrieval ──► global ranking ──► [EverRank] ──► feed
                    (theirs)      (theirs)          (ours)

The layer shape is not a compromise — it is the product. Three properties fall out of it, each of which is a hard-won answer to a classic objection:

  • Zero-risk adoption. At worst the layer reproduces the incumbent's ranking, so the customer's downside is "exactly what I have today." No data migration, no rip-and-replace, no trust leap. Integration is one API call between their ranking and their serving.
  • The echo chamber is solved upstream. The candidate list still comes from the global system — trending items, new inventory, collaborative "people like you" — because EverRank can only reorder what it is given. Explore and exploit map cleanly onto the two layers: upstream explores, EverRank exploits. The feed cannot become a filter bubble because the layer cannot narrow the candidate pool.
  • Cold start degrades gracefully. A new user has no data, the adaptor sits at its prior, and the layer reproduces the global ranking. EverRank only diverges from the incumbent when the user gives it evidence — a provable no-harm property, and the sentence that closes a sale.

docs.title: 3. The problem — personalization stopped at the last mile
docs.text:
Every mainstream recsys is one global model plus per-user state: your embedding, your last-fifty-items history, your bandit posteriors. The state is personal; the function mapping state → score is shared by everyone. The consequences:

  • You get the feed of "people like you," never yours. The global model learns the average of its users. Quirks, niche tastes, and the one weird thing you love are noise to it.
  • One user's taste drift is invisible. When your life changes — new city, new baby, new hobby — that shift is a drop in the aggregate. A monthly retrain cannot see it, and the feed quietly rots for weeks.
  • The retrain cycle is always behind. Between retrains the model is stale by construction, and "retrain more often" only shrinks the window — it keeps the machinery and the delay.

The customer's feed therefore reacts to the segment, not the person. EverRank's answer is the obvious one: stop learning one model for everyone and start learning one tiny model per person, online, all the time.

docs.title: 4. The architecture — global, user, session
docs.text:
Three levels, each with a different learning clock:

global model          (not ours)   items, trends, cold start — retrained monthly
  └─ per-user adaptor (ours)       slow taste — weeks — KB-scale, one step per interaction
       └─ per-session adaptor (ours)  current intent — seconds — ephemeral

Per-user adaptor. A linear probe on the incumbent's features or embeddings — a vector of a few thousand numbers, a few KB. Each interaction is one gradient step. With 10M users × ~5 KB the whole fleet is tens of GB: object storage plus an LRU hot cache. Small capacity is not a compromise — a user hands you hundreds of samples, and a model bigger than this would have nothing to learn from. The tininess is forced by the data, and it is the right answer.

Per-session adaptor. The strongest predictor of your next action is your last five. Within a session the feedback is dense and fast (clicks in seconds, not purchases in weeks), so a per-session layer — conditioned on context, reset when the session ends — is where the "current intent" lives. This is the level where engagement platforms actually win, and it is pure streaming: you cannot retrain a batch model mid-session.

On "every mood." Users are multi-intent (browsing for self vs. gifts, work vs. leisure, 1am doomscroll vs. morning utility), but detecting mood is the wrong frame — it fragments an already-sparse signal. The right version is conditioning on observable context: time of day, device, current category, query terms, session length. The model learns "this user at 1am on a phone" as an implicit intent state, no mood labels required.

The loop, with the honesty built in:

serve reorder ──► observe (click: seconds · purchase: days · churn: weeks)
                        │
                        └─► learn_one(x, y), IPS-weighted

The delayed, partial labels here are the research's Delay Tax, per user — and the IPS weighting is non-negotiable: a reranker only sees clicks on what it chose to show, so its own policy biases its labels. An uncorrected online learner amplifies its own mistakes; this is how reranking layers silently fail in production. EverRank learns counterfactually (inverse propensity scoring, maintained online) from day one.

docs.title: 5. Why the research is the engine
docs.text:
This product is the project's findings applied at the level of a single user:

Research result EverRank feature E01 — streaming self-heals, frozen never does (frozen 0/11; real streaming recovery 8/11; ≈6.9× less corrected damage_ref) The per-user adaptor recovers within a bounded number of interactions when the user's taste changes; the incumbent's monthly retrain literally cannot see one user's drift in the aggregate damage_ref / recovery rate The product's headline metric: interactions × skill lost for this user, while their feed was stale The Delay Tax Clicks land in seconds, purchases in days, churn in weeks — the adaptor learns on yesterday's truth, and the honest promise is "bounded staleness," not zero lag Selective/biased labels literature The IPS-corrected learner — feedback is conditioned on what EverRank itself chose to show Prequential harness The shadow-rerank engine: replay the customer's own interactions, prove per-user lift offline before a live A/B

The Exp-02 story, told as a product: the frozen model is the customer's feed today; the streaming model is EverRank; the drift is a user whose life changed. One heals, the other never notices.

docs.title: 6. The honest gotchas
docs.text: Problem Severity Status & mitigation Position bias / feedback loop — the reranker shapes its own labels High IPS online from day one; treated as load-bearing, not an add-on Lift concentrates on active users — the long tail stays on the global model Medium By design: active users drive the revenue. The pitch says it plainly Per-user evaluation & governance — global NDCG hides that 3% of users got worse Medium Per-user metrics, per-user rollback, versioned snapshots — EverLearn's governance, scaled to millions of models Per-mood fragmentation — one model per intent state shatters the data Medium Context conditioning, not mood detection; one adaptor per user, context as features Depth ceiling — with ~100 samples per user the adaptor learns coarse taste, not semantics Low The global tower carries the semantics; EverRank is the last mile

docs.title: 7. Positioning
docs.text:
Reranks your list Per-user model Learns online Notices per-user taste drift The incumbent (your customer's system) — ✖ (per-user state, one model) ✖ ✖ Algolia / Constructor / Recombee / Amazon Personalize ✔ ✖ (one global LTR model) ✖ (periodic retrain) ✖ TikTok's engagement engine ✔ (in-house) ✖ (global, ultra-fast retrain) partial partial EverRank ✔ ✔ ✔ every interaction ✔ headline feature

One-liner for the sales deck: their reranker is one model for all your users, retrained monthly; ours is one model per user, updated every interaction — and it notices when that user changed.

And the ecosystem note: EverLearn is the engine and the governance, EverRank is the flagship application, DriftDeck can watch the global model upstream (and, one day, the fleet of per-user adaptors). Three docs, one story: detect the decay, price it, delete it — per user.

docs.title: 8. The killer demo
docs.text:
Two scenes, both runnable on the customer's own logged data:

Scene 1 — the drift. Find a user whose behavior changed on a real date (moved city, new baby, new category of purchases). Replay: the incumbent's monthly-retrained feed stays stale for weeks after that date; EverRank's adaptor pivots within a bounded number of interactions. Show the damage area as engagement lost, priced in churn risk. This is Exp-02, rerun on one real user.

Scene 2 — the session. Replay a single session. Watch the feed pivot on the last five actions: the user was shopping for themselves, then searched a gift category, and the incumbent's session-blind ranking keeps serving the old intent for the rest of the evening while EverRank's session layer has already turned. No drift needed — just speed. This is the demo that makes product teams feel the gap.

docs.title: 9. The build order
docs.text:
Phase Build Exit criterion De-risks A — Shadow rerank Offline replay of a real feed: global ranking vs EverRank's per-user adaptor, IPS-corrected, on held-out interactions Per-user lift vs incumbent on real data — without a single live request The mechanism survives real data; the demo exists B — Live A/B The layer in production, same candidates, two orderings; per-user rollback and snapshots Statistically honest lift in CTR/conversion; rollback proven in anger Governance under fire; first dollar value attached C — Session layer Per-session adaptor on top, context conditioning Measurable mid-session pivot lift The second, defensible moat (speed, not just drift) D — Platform Multi-customer, on-prem tier, integrations with the major recsys stacks Paying customers Business

The research roadmap slots straight in: Exp-05 (delayed labels) is Phase A's core learning risk, and the selective-labels literature already in the review is Phase A's IPS design. The experiments are the product's first milestones.

docs.title: 10. Business model (brief)
docs.text:
• Pricing per request or per lift — the layer's value scales with traffic and with the engagement it recovers, not with headcount.
  • The ROI number is built in — per-user lift × traffic = recovered engagement, reported by the product itself, and that figure is the subscription justification.
  • Land-and-expand — the zero-risk layer is the wedge into an account that already runs a recsys; EverLearn's governance platform and DriftDeck's monitoring are the expansion.

docs.title: 11. One-screen recap
docs.text:
Product. EverRank — a drop-in reranking layer. The customer's recsys generates the candidates; EverRank reorders them with one tiny streaming model per user, and per session.

Why it exists. Personalization stops at the global model: one model for everyone, retrained monthly, so you get the feed of "people like you" — and it can't notice when your taste changed.

The wedge. Zero-risk adoption: worst case the layer is a pass-through, integration is one API call, and with no user data it provably reproduces the incumbent's ranking.

The architecture. Global (theirs, explores) → per-user adaptor (slow taste, KB-scale, learns online) → per-session adaptor (current intent, seconds). Echo chamber solved by construction: the layer can only reorder, never narrow.

The metric. Per-user lift in CTR/conversion, plus drift recovery time — how many interactions until the feed notices your life changed.

The honest parts. IPS-corrected learning is mandatory (the reranker shapes its own labels); lift concentrates on active users; per-user governance at millions-of-models scale is the real engineering.

The evidence. Exp-01/02's self-healing mechanism — streaming recovers in bounded time, frozen never does — applied at the level of one user, whose taste drift is exactly the concept drift the project measures.

The build order. Shadow rerank on one feed → live A/B → session layer → platform.

docs.title: ML.md — the machine-learning reference
docs.text:
What this is: everything ML about this project in one self-contained file — the problem framing, every model used and planned, why each was chosen and what the alternatives were, the pseudocode behind every number, the metric definitions, and the honest defects. Written so it can answer a traditional ML question without any other context.

Status of claims: ✅ = measured in this project · 📋 = planned / spec'd · 📚 = from the literature.

docs.title: 1.1 The task
docs.text:
Supervised binary classification on a non-stationary data stream.

Not regression, not clustering, not recommendation — classification only, locked deliberately as a scope guard. Multi-class is allowed later; everything else is out.

docs.title: 1.2 The regime: online / streaming learning
docs.text:
Standard (batch) ML assumes the dataset is a finished object: finite, available all at once, drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution. Streaming ML drops all three. An algorithm is "streaming" only if it respects three hard constraints:

Constraint Meaning Single pass Each sample is seen exactly once. You cannot revisit sample #5. Bounded memory Memory must not grow with the number of samples seen. Bounded time per sample Processing must keep up with arrival rate, or you fall behind forever.

A useful test: if this ran for a year without restarting, would it still work? If the answer involves "well, memory would…", it is not a streaming algorithm.

docs.title: 1.3 The formal setting
docs.text:
The model estimates P(X, y), usually decomposed as P(y|X) · P(X).

Concept drift is when that distribution changes over time:

P_t(X, y) ≠ P_{t+Δ}(X, y)

Two flavours that matter, and they drive everything downstream:

Flavour What changes Effect Real drift P(y|X) — the input→output rule Genuinely breaks the model. Accuracy suffers. Virtual drift / covariate shift P(X) only — the inputs move, the rule is intact May not cost any accuracy, but input-watching detectors still fire on it.

Drift shapes (the standard taxonomy):

Shape Behaviour Detectability Sudden / abrupt Concept A flips to B instantly Easiest to detect, most damaging Gradual A and B interleave with shifting probability over a window Hard — error rises slowly and noisily Incremental A deforms continuously through intermediate states Hard Recurring Old concepts return (seasons, day/night) Forget-and-restore territory

There is also the blip — a one-off anomaly that is not drift. A good detector must not fire on it. This sensitivity/false-alarm tension is the stability–plasticity trade-off and it is measurable.

docs.title: 1.4 Detection vs adaptation — two separate things
docs.text:
A very common confusion, worth having straight:

  • Detection = noticing the change. Watches a signal and raises an alarm. This is a statistical hypothesis test over a stream.
  • Adaptation = doing something about it. Reset, retrain, reweight, or just keep learning with a forgetting factor.

They are independently designable: you can adapt blindly (no detector at all — sliding windows, fading factors, a learning rate that never reaches zero) or informed (explicit detector triggers a reaction). The project's Exp-01/02 ship an adaptation with no detector at all — see §4.7, this is the single most attackable design choice in the work.

docs.title: 1.5 How models adapt — the three strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Mechanism Strength Weakness Blind / passive Keep learning; recent data outweighs old Always on, simple, no tuning Slow on sudden drift; permanently discards still-valid old knowledge Informed Detector fires → reset / retrain / swap Sharp, fast on the drift it detects A false alarm throws away a good model Ensemble Pool of models, weighted by recent performance; drop worst, add fresh Drift handling is emergent; strongest general baseline More compute, more memory

This project's streaming model uses blind adaptation with a bounded memory window — which is why it recovers without any detector.

docs.title: 2. Models USED (measured)
docs.text: Two models, one race, same data, same order. ✅

docs.title: 2.1 Streaming model — DeepRiver RollingClassifier
docs.text:
Library deep-river 0.3.4 (River + PyTorch) Architecture RNN 3 → 16 → Linear(16→2), logits Parameters ~2.3k Update rule one optimiser step per sample: predict_one → metric.update → learn_one Forgetting mechanism rolling window of 500 samples — old samples fall out Optimiser / loss / lr Adam / cross-entropy / 1e-3 Warm-up learns from sample 1 onward Measured cost 99.1 s for the 48k-loop on an RTX 3050 = 484 samples/s; 1,089 s / 44 samples/s on CPU (~11× slower); peak process RSS 1,074 MB

Why this model: it is a deep streaming learner — it demonstrates that the thesis mechanism (bounded recovery via continuous refit) holds for a neural model, not just for the classical trees the literature usually tests. The rolling window is the drift-adaptation mechanism: it needs no detector, and its memory is bounded by design.

Why the window is the mechanism: a window of 500 means the model is always trained on roughly the last 500 samples. After a drift, the old-concept samples age out within ~500 samples, and the net is refit on the new concept automatically. That is why the recovery is bounded and why no detector is required.

Alternatives considered:

Alternative Why not chosen DeepRiver per-sample Classifier (no rolling window) This is the interesting comparison, not the baseline — per-sample SGD with no explicit window is a different forgetting story. Deferred to a follow-up experiment. River HoeffdingTree The canonical static streaming learner — a deliberate control, belongs in Exp-03's matrix River HAT (Hoeffding Adaptive Tree) The canonical adaptive streaming learner; stronger literature pedigree. Should be added as a classical arm in Exp-03 so the claim isn't deep-net-specific River ARF (Adaptive Random Forest) Strongest general streaming baseline, but ~2.2× the runtime of a retrained XGBoost 📚 and heavier to run; reserved as an accuracy ceiling River SRP, LeveragingBagging, online LogisticRegression In the planned Ch1 matrix; not needed for the pilot

Known deviation from spec: the specified "MLP 2 → 16 → 2" is not expressible in DeepRiver's RollingClassifier — its feature-incremental layer handling requires the module's first layer to take n_features units, and it feeds the net a temporal window. The RNN head is the architecture DeepRiver documents for rolling models. Capacity (16) and learning rate are unchanged. ✅ documented in the Exp-01 write-up.

docs.title: 2.2 Frozen batch model — scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier
docs.text:
Library scikit-learn 1.9.0 Config n_estimators=100, random_state=seed Training fit once on the first 12,000 samples (20% warm-up) Thereafter predict_one only — never updated Measured cost 0.17 s to fit; near-zero per-sample prediction cost

Why this model: it is the frozen baseline — the canonical "train once, deploy, never touch" deployment. It is the weakest possible opponent, and that is the point: Exp-01 was designed as the weakest form of the claim. If the thesis mechanism can't show up against this, the bigger experiments are pointless.

Why RandomForest specifically (rather than another frozen model):

Candidate Why not the primary XGBoost Reserved as the oracle-tuned upper bound (the Amekoe-style honest opponent). Spending it as the frozen strawman wastes the strongest baseline. Logistic Regression A linear model can't express the SEA rule (x₀+x₁ > threshold needs only a linear boundary — but with 10% label noise and a rolling comparison it underfits relative to a tree ensemble); weaker baseline makes the win less credible SVM Poor fit for a streaming/one-shot comparison: no incremental story, scaling sensitivity, and cost grows with training set Decision Tree (single) Too high-variance — a single tree's post-drift collapse would be confounded with its own instability rather than the drift Random Forest ✔ Robust to feature scaling, needs no tuning, handles the non-linear threshold rule, deterministic given a seed, cheap to fit, and the field's default tabular baseline

docs.title: 2.3 Summary of the measured race
docs.text:
Streaming (DeepRiver rolling) Frozen (RF) Pre-drift baseline κ₀ 0.751 ± 0.017 0.767 ± 0.018 Dip depth Δκ 0.045 ± 0.015 0.173 ± 0.018 (~3.8× deeper) Min rolling κ after τ 0.706 ± 0.015 0.594 ± 0.013 Recovery time median 0, mean 319 ± 765 never, 11/11 Damage area 13 ± 31 (max 103) 3,710 ± 592 (min 2,439) Full-run accuracy 0.8830 ± 0.0021 0.8539 ± 0.0017 Full-run Cohen Kappa 0.7530 ± 0.0044 0.6850 ± 0.0035

(Frozen wins the stationary phase slightly; streaming wins everything after the drift.)

docs.title: 3. Models PLANNED
docs.text: 📋 From the locked Ch1 protocol. None of these is measured yet.

docs.title: 3.1 Streaming learners (River)
docs.text: Model What it is Role Hoeffding Tree One-pass decision tree; constant memory per leaf via the Hoeffding bound Canonical static streaming learner — the control HAT (Hoeffding Adaptive Tree) Hoeffding tree with ADWIN at each node Canonical adaptive learner ARF (Adaptive Random Forest) Ensemble with adaptive operators + resampling Strongest general baseline / accuracy ceiling SRP (Streaming Random Patches) Ensemble with random subspaces + patches Diversity in the ensemble arm Leveraging Bagging Online bagging with λ-boosting Classic ensemble baseline kNN + ADWIN Lazy learner gated by a detector Non-parametric counterpoint Logistic Regression Online linear model Deliberately blind/passive — the no-detector control

docs.title: 3.2 Batch baselines (the ladder)
docs.text: Baseline Definition What it tests (a) Frozen Fit on warm-up, predict-only forever No adaptation at all — done ✅ (b) Scheduled-retrain Refit every k samples on a sliding window, no detector Clock-driven adaptation — the honest industrial baseline (c) Oracle-tuned XGBoost / EBM tuned with Optuna, frequently retrained The honest upper bound; reported so no one can accuse us of an easy opponent

docs.title: 3.3 Drift detectors
docs.text:
Detector Mechanism Notes ADWIN (2007) Adaptive window; when two sub-windows differ statistically, drop the older Rigorous guarantees, no window-size parameter; de-facto standard DDM (2004) Statistical process control on the error rate; warn at 2σ, alarm at 3σ Simple, cheap; weak on gradual drift; assumes independent Bernoulli errors EDDM (2006) Tracks the distance between errors Fixes DDM's gradual-drift weakness Page-Hinkley (1954) CUSUM-family: accumulates deviation from the running mean Classical sequential analysis; threshold-sensitive KSWIN (2020) Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between a sliding window and a reference Non-parametric, distribution-based HDDM Hoeffding-bound drift detection Also available in River; optional

The guaranteed finding: no detector wins on delay, false alarms and misses simultaneously. Sensitivity trades against false alarms. Reporting that trade-off with real numbers is a legitimate result — and it becomes the baseline the hybrid is judged against. 📚

docs.title: 4. "Why A and not B" — the decision table
docs.text: This is the section that answers the traditional viva question. Every entry is a design choice, its justification, and the alternative.

docs.title: 4.1 Why streaming/online at all, instead of batch?
docs.text:
Because on a drifting, unbounded, label-scarce stream, a batch model's update schedule does not depend on what the data is doing. Batch models update on a clock; streaming models update on evidence.

The quantitative content of the whole project is one ratio:

Streaming damage        ≈ (d + a) × Δe          # d = detection delay, a = adaptation time
Scheduled-batch damage  ≈ (r_next − τ) × Δe     # r_next = next retrain tick
Frozen-batch damage     = unbounded (never recovers on its own)

Streaming wins whenever d + a < r_next − τ — the generic case, since d + a is tens to low hundreds of samples while r_next − τ spans a whole retrain interval.

The honest counter: a tuned, frequently retrained batch model can beat streaming under delayed labels and rare classes 📚 — retrained XGBoost AUC-ROC 92.81 vs ARF 91.02 (no delay); delayed fraud AUCPR 23.41 vs 14.23. That is exactly why the Delay Tax is the project's open problem rather than a solved one.

docs.title: 4.2 Why prequential evaluation instead of a train/test split?
docs.text: Random shuffling a temporal stream is invalid — it leaks future information into training, and on a drifting stream it estimates a quantity that never existed. The accepted protocol is prequential (test-then-train): score each sample before it trains the model. Every sample is used for testing then training, in that order; nothing wasted, nothing leaked. 📚 Gama, Sebastião & Rodrigues (2013).

docs.title: 4.3 Why Cohen's Kappa instead of accuracy?
docs.text:
• Kappa is chance-corrected — it subtracts the agreement you'd get by guessing.
  • It is robust to class imbalance (critical for the fraud/CreditCard case).
  • Accuracy alone overstates learning on temporal streams, because temporal persistence creates a strong "predict the previous label" baseline that a naive model can exploit. This is the known Kappa+/Elec2 trap.

Accuracy is still reported (§6), just never as the headline.

docs.title: 4.4 Why a rolling (windowed) metric as well as a cumulative one?
docs.text: Cumulative metrics converge and hide drift. Over 48,000 samples, a permanent collapse spreading over thousands of samples is averaged down to a couple of percentage points. The rolling metric (w = 1,000) makes the shape visible — dips and recoveries. In this field, the accuracy-over-time curve is itself the result; almost every good figure plots something against "number of samples seen".

docs.title: 4.5 Why SEA as the stream?
docs.text:
• Synthetic streams are the only way to get ground-truth drift positions. Without a known τ, detection delay and recovery time are uncomputable.
  • SEA is the standard abrupt-drift benchmark — 3 features, only 2 relevant, a linear threshold rule with constructive noise.
  • But it is deliberately simple: a linear boundary in 2 features. That is a weakness (see §11), not a strength.

Alternatives: Agrawal (different rule families), Hyperplane (incremental drift), RandomRBF (gradual), STAGGER, LED, and ConceptDriftStream compositions for recurring drift. All planned for the Ch1 matrix; SEA serves the pilot.

docs.title: 4.6 Why 60,000 samples, τ at 50%, 20% warm-up, noise 0.1?
docs.text: Choice Value Why Stream length 60,000 Long enough that the drift window (5,000) is a small slice; short enough to run 11 seeds on a laptop GPU Drift position τ 30,000 (50%) Symmetric: equal pre- and post-drift room, so κ₀ is well estimated and there's ample post-drift region Warm-up 12,000 (20%) Enough to fit the RF properly; a standard 20–30% warm-up in the protocol Label noise 0.1 (10%) Makes the problem non-trivial — without noise, the frozen RF could memorise the SEA rule perfectly and the drift would be the only error source. Balanced classes by construction.

docs.title: 4.7 Why is there no drift detector in Exp-01/02? (the attackable bit)
docs.text:
Straight answer: the recovery came entirely from the rolling window — blind adaptation, no detector. It was a deliberate minimal design (Exp-01 documents itself as "no detector, no delay, no oracle tuning, no statistics").

Defence available: it is consistent with the literature that the learner matters more than the trigger — with per-sample incremental updates, the retraining policy becomes irrelevant 📚 (54 paired comparisons, no practical difference vs no-retrain).

Honest weakness: the project is fundamentally about detectors, and neither concluded experiment runs one. The detector matrix (RQ1) is genuinely unrun. Do not oversell this as "intentional".

docs.title: 4.8 Why 11 seeds and not more? Why not the full statistical protocol?
docs.text: The pre-registered bar was ≥10 seeds, and 11 were run (42 plus 0–9). That bar is met. But the accepted protocol for comparing many methods over many datasets is Friedman + Nemenyi with ≥10 seeds across multiple datasets and multiple learners 📚 Demšar (2006). Eleven seeds on one stream is a within-stream distribution — call it a distribution, not statistical significance.

docs.title: 4.9 The metric constants — why 0.95, 500, 5,000?
docs.text:
Constant Value Justification Recovery band κ ≥ 0.95 · κ₀ "Effectively back to baseline" — 5% tolerance Sustained stretch 500 consecutive samples Prevents a single lucky sample counting as recovery Lookahead budget 5,000 samples from τ The pre-registered falsification budget — set before the run, so recovery couldn't be judged against a moving target

All three were fixed before the run. That is the defence. The gap is that no sensitivity analysis over these constants has been done — a known next step.

docs.title: 5.1 The prequential loop (the core protocol)
docs.text:
for x, y in stream:
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)      # model has NEVER seen this sample
    metric.update(y, y_pred)           # so this score is honest
    model.learn_one(x, y)              # now let it learn  (frozen model: skipped)

The ordering is the whole point. Note the river API convention: metric.update takes the true label first.

docs.title: 5.2 Stream generation (SEA, one abrupt drift)
docs.text:
# One continuous feature draw; only the LABEL RULE switches at tau.
# (river 0.25's synth.SEA reseeds its RNG per generator, so concatenating two
#  variants REPLAYS identical feature vectors -> the frozen model would have
#  already seen its "test" chunk during warm-up. Hence: draw once, switch the rule.)
X = uniform(0, 10, size=(60000, 3), seed=seed)
y = where(X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 8, 1, 0)          # concept 0  for t < tau
y[tau:] = where(X[tau:, 0] + X[tau:, 1] > 9, 1, 0)  # concept 1  for t >= tau
y = flip_labels(y, p=0.10, seed=seed)             # 10% label noise

docs.title: 5.3 Drift-window metrics
docs.text:
kappa0 = mean(rolling_kappa[tau-1000 : tau])                 # pre-drift baseline
dip    = min(rolling_kappa[tau : tau+5000])                   # worst after drift
dk     = kappa0 - dip                                         # dip depth

# recovery: first sample from which kappa stays >= 0.95*kappa0 for 500 consecutive
recovery = None
run = 0
for i in range(tau, tau + 5000):
    if rolling_kappa[i] >= 0.95 * kappa0:
        run += 1
        if run >= 500:
            recovery = i - 500 + 1
            break
    else:
        run = 0

# damage area: skill lost x time spent below baseline
if recovery is not None:
    window = range(tau, recovery + 1)
else:
    window = range(tau, len(stream))                          # never recovered
damage = sum(max(kappa0 - rolling_kappa[t], 0) for t in window)

⚠️ This exact code has a defect — see §11.1. The recovery truncation collapses damage to ~zero whenever recovery fires at τ.

docs.title: 5.4 Blind adaptation (what the streaming model actually does)
docs.text:
class RollingAdaptation:
    def __init__(self, window=500):
        self.window = deque(maxlen=window)     # bounded memory: old samples fall out

    def learn_one(self, x, y):
        self.window.append((x, y))
        for _ in range(1):                     # one optimiser step per sample
            loss = cross_entropy(self.net(sequence(self.window)), y)
            loss.backward(); self.optimizer.step(); self.optimizer.zero_grad()

The deque(maxlen=window) is the drift mechanism: after a change, old-concept samples age out within ~window samples and the net refits on the new concept. No detector needed — that is why recovery is bounded.

docs.title: 5.5 Detector integration (planned)
docs.text:
detector = ADWIN()
for x, y in stream:
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)
    error = int(y_pred != y)
    detector.update(error)
    if detector.drift_detected:
        model.reset()                          # or retrain on a recent buffer
    model.learn_one(x, y)

docs.title: 5.6 The hybrid detector (planned — the Ch3 contribution)
docs.text:
# Stage 1: label-free early warning on P(X). Fires FAST but also on virtual drift.
# Stage 2: supervised confirmation on the DELAYED error stream. Reliable but LATE.
for t, x in enumerate(stream):
    if stage1_warns(t, x):                     # KS / MMD-style two-sample test
        pending.append(t)                      # unconfirmed warning
    for y_true, t0 in labels_arriving_at(t):   # label for sample t0 lands now
        err = int(pred[t0] != y_true)
        if t0 in pending and stage2_confirms(err):
            adapt()                            # confirmed -> act
        elif t0 in pending:
            revoke(t0)                         # unconfirmed -> revoke, cost it

The design is justified by the lemmas: L4 says stage 1 can never confirm (pure posterior drift is invisible to P(X)), and L1 says stage 2 can never be early (it cannot fire before the labels land). So the hybrid is the only architecture that is both early and reliable given the information available.

docs.title: 6.1 Predictive quality (per-sample, inside the prequential loop)
docs.text: Metric What it proves River class Prequential accuracy overall correctness on the live stream metrics.Accuracy Cohen Kappa chance-corrected agreement — the headline metrics.CohenKappa Rolling Kappa (w=1,000) recency-biased view; reveals recovery metrics.RollingCohenKappa AUC-ROC / AUC-PR ranking quality; PR for rare classes metrics.ROCAUC, metrics.PrecisionRecallAUC F1 / recall / precision per-class utility (e.g. fraud-class recall) metrics.F1, metrics.Recall

docs.title: 6.2 Drift-response metrics (what batch models structurally cannot report)
docs.text:
Metric Definition Good Detection delay samples from true τ to first alarm ↓ False positives alarms with no drift nearby ↓ Missed detections (MDR) drift points with no alarm inside the tolerance window ↓ MTFA / MTD mean time between false alarms / mean time to detect MTFA ↑, MTD ↓ Recovery time samples from τ until rolling Kappa returns to the pre-drift band ↓ Damage area Σ (κ₀ − κ(t)) over the drift window, in samples·κ ↓

Why damage area is the "money metric": recovery time tells you how long the model was wrong; damage area tells you how much skill × time it lost — it prices the whole drift in one number. It is also the metric where streaming's advantage is structural rather than incidental.

docs.title: 6.3 Resource metrics (the three streaming constraints)
docs.text: Metric Constraint Memory footprint (bytes/model) bounded memory Throughput (samples/s), per-sample latency bounded time Number of passes over the data single pass

docs.title: 6.4 Label-efficiency metric
docs.text: Metric What it proves Performance vs fraction of labels used (l_access sweep) streaming keeps working when labels are scarce

docs.title: 6.5 The tolerance window — state it explicitly
docs.text: A drift at index 5000 with an alarm at 5040 is a successful detection with delay 40. An alarm at 9000 is a false positive plus a missed detection. Papers vary; stating and justifying the window is a mark of rigour, not a detail. 📚

docs.title: 7.1 Synthetic (ground-truth drift — required for detector metrics)
docs.text:
Generator Drift type it gives SEA Abrupt (used in Exp-01/02) Agrawal Abrupt, different rule families Hyperplane Incremental drift RandomRBF Gradual STAGGER Abrupt over discrete concepts LED Abrupt, irrelevant-feature control ConceptDriftStream Compositions — recurrence, multi-drift

Why synthetic is non-negotiable for the detector chapter: without a known τ, detection delay is uncomputable. Synthetic gives ground truth; real streams give external validity.

docs.title: 7.2 Real streams
docs.text:
Dataset Role Caveat Elec2 Classic electricity-price drift stream Known temporal autocorrelation — must report a "predict-the-previous-label" no-change baseline and Kappa+, never accuracy alone. Treat as secondary. Phishing Real drift, moderate size — Forest Covertype Larger, multi-class — Airlines Arrival-delay stream — CreditCard Extreme imbalance (~0.17% fraud) Accuracy is meaningless → AUC-PR. Provides the natural delayed-label story (chargebacks).

Protocol difference on real data: there is no ground-truth τ, so drift is inferred from rolling-metric dips and detector alarms, and the comparison targets post-dip behaviour — dip depth, recovery slope, and the fraction of the post-drift window spent below each model's own baseline.

Scope note: the locked scope says ≤3 real datasets (Elec2, Phishing, CreditCard); the README roadmap lists 5. That inconsistency should be resolved before the viva.

docs.title: 8. Statistical protocol
docs.text:
Requirement Value Seeds ≥10 (synthetic). Exp-02 ran 11. ✅ Reporting mean ± SD, plus median and counts — a heavy-tailed, zero-floored distribution makes the mean an unstable centre Multi-dataset comparison Friedman test + Nemenyi post-hoc, critical-difference diagram Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank Effect sizes reported, not just p-values Budgets fixed stream lengths, fixed drift positions, exact versions recorded

📚 Demšar (2006), JMLR 7:1–30 — single runs are noise; this is the field's convention.

Where the project stands: ≥10 seeds ✅, mean±SD ✅, Friedman+Nemenyi ❌ (needs multiple datasets — Exp-04/05), Wilcoxon ❌, effect sizes ❌.

docs.title: 9. The four lemmas (the Ch3 theory)
docs.text:
Formal setting: the concept is C_t ∈ {C₀, C₁} with real drift at τ; instantaneous error e_t = 1[ŷ_t ≠ y_t]. Under immediate labelling the detector seeks a stopping time T — classical quickest detection (Page 1954; Lorden 1971; Shiryaev). Under label delay, each error becomes observable only at t + L_t, so the detector's filtration is

F_t = σ( e_s : s + L_s ≤ t )

— quickest detection with delayed observations, a variant the literature has barely touched.

# Lemma Statement Novelty 1 Reaction floor T ≥ τ + L_τ pointwise. No error-stream detector can alarm before the drift's labels arrive. Novel as a theorem (trivial to prove — that's the point); the phenomenon is already known empirically 📚 2 Power loss Sensitivity degrades by 1/√p: Δ_min ∝ 1/√(pW) instead of 1/√W. Appears genuinely novel — but check Alencar 2026 first (scoop risk) 3 False-alarm inflation Batch arrival of size b inflates error-rate variance by the design effect 1 + (b−1)ρ, so DDM fires above its nominal α. Most clearly novel — no prior treatment found 4 Identifiability ceiling Pure posterior drift (fixed P(X), changed P(y\|X)) is invisible to any label-free detector: the likelihood ratio is 1, KL = 0. NOT novel — Žliobaitė 2010. Ours is only the use (hybrid justification)

Scope guard: no new change-detection algorithms, no regret bounds, no online convex optimisation, no statistical learning theory, nothing beyond these four. If a lemma resists a clean proof, it degrades to an empirical claim and the project survives.

Known scoop risks to state proactively: Alencar et al. 2026 (DSP) is an unread experimental survey of exactly the Ch3 setting — HIGH risk. Botacin & Gomes 2024 already quantified label-delay cost on a real pipeline (~50% exposure increase), so never claim "we show delayed labels hurt."

docs.title: 10. Why this is not just a tutorial — the gap
docs.text:
The field lacks three things:

  1. A detector-level benchmark under label-observation regimes (delayed, partial, selective).
  2. Formal bounds connecting label latency/coverage to detection quality.
  3. A standard confirmation protocol for early-warning + delayed-confirmation hybrids.

Sharpened in 2026: a standard benchmark now exists for immediate-label drift detection (Cerqueira et al., KDD'26 — 14 detectors × 7 real datasets, 4 drift types, each abrupt and gradual). It does not exist for delayed/partial/selective labels. That refinement is the honest gap statement.

Of 33 catalogued papers in the project's review, only 4 study drift detectors under delay at all, and none provides a detector-level benchmark, a formal detection bound, or a built hybrid.

docs.title: 11. Known defects and honest caveats
docs.text: Read this before claiming anything.

docs.title: 11.1 ⚠️ The damage-area metric is truncated — the headline ratio is inflated
docs.text:
The defect. damage_area is summed from τ to the recovery point. But recovery is defined as the first 500-long in-band run starting at τ — so if the model is already in-band at τ and never leaves for 500 samples, recovery = τ, and the integration window is a single sample. Damage collapses to ≈ 0.

Proof from the committed artifact (experiments/exp02/results.json):

Seed Dip depth Δκ Recorded damage 1 0.027 0.0 3 0.071 0.0 7 0.053 0.0

A 0.071 excursion below baseline cannot integrate to zero over any non-degenerate window. 8 of 11 streaming seeds sit on this floor, while the frozen model — which never recovers — always integrates the full window.

Consequences (resolved by E01):

  1. The comparison was asymmetric: truncated integral (streaming) vs complete integral (frozen). Both the 294× mean ratio and the 24× worst-vs-best ratio were upper bounds; both are retired.
  2. E01 corrected it with a fixed 5,000-sample window and a panel-shared κ_ref: damage_ref 74.8 ± 61.8 vs 515.0 ± 97.1 (≈6.9×); damage_full 321.4 vs 3,472.9 (≈10.8×); worst-vs-best 0.74×. See Reports/E01-metric-v2.md.
  3. The claim that "damage area and dip depth are the trustworthy metrics" is too generous — the legacy damage area was defined in terms of the same τ-anchored recovery rule. damage_ref and damage_full are the trustworthy ones now; recovery time is meaningful only conditional on an exit.
  4. Untouched: frozen recovered on 0 of 11 seeds, and the streaming dip is consistently ~3.8× shallower. Those stand.

The fix is done: E01 integrates over a fixed window regardless of recovery and keeps the old artifacts for auditability. Do not quote 294×/24× except as a retired upper bound.

docs.title: 11.2 "Recovery = 0" does not mean "instant recovery"
docs.text:
It means the model never left its pre-drift band. 0 is the metric floor, not a speed. 8 of 11 seeds sit on it. Reading it as a latency is the easiest way to misinterpret the results.

Related: the recovery rule is anchored at τ, so a model that stays in band for the first 500 samples and dips afterwards is scored 0. Seven of eleven seeds did leave the band after τ, but only three are credited with a recovery time. Recovery time is therefore not monotone in dip depth (seed 3 dips deeper than seed 9 yet scores 0).

docs.title: 11.3 The frozen opponent is a strawman by construction
docs.text: "A model that never updates never recovers" is true by definition ✅ measured, 0/11. It is the weakest possible form of the claim and it is documented as such. The informative comparison is a scheduled-retrain model (Exp-03), where streaming's d + a is measured against the batch model's r_next − τ — and where the batch recovery time should scatter uniformly over [0, k] as pure phase noise.

docs.title: 11.4 No detector, one synthetic stream, one drift type, one drift position
docs.text: Both concluded experiments: SEA only, abrupt only, τ at 50% only, two models, no scheduled baseline, no label delay, no detector. This is existence evidence and a first distribution — not a field-wide claim.

docs.title: 11.5 Cost is unfavourable and reported as such
docs.text: 484 samples/s on an RTX 3050 for a 2.3k-parameter net (44/s on CPU) versus 0.17 s to fit the RF. A streaming model that is slower than the batch one is a real tension — and per the literature, ARF is ~2.2× slower than a retrained XGBoost 📚. The cost column stands even though it is unflattering. At this window size the GPU is effectively required.

docs.title: 11.6 H2 was refuted, then restored
docs.text: On seed 42 the two models were level pre-drift (0.755 vs 0.759) → "batch wins steady state" was refuted. On 11 seeds the frozen model does lead (0.767 vs 0.751) → H2 supported. Not a flip-flop: n=1 was noise. The honest reading is that the frozen model wins the stationary phase slightly and still loses the run because it collapses permanently at τ. Streaming pays a small steady-state tax and earns it back on drift.

docs.title: 11.7 The scope guard says no deep learning — the pilot uses it
docs.text: The locked scope lists "❌ Deep learning / deep-river" as out of scope, yet DeepRiver is the subject of both experiments. Acknowledged in the Exp-01 write-up as a deliberate extension, but it is not formally amended in the scope document — and an undocumented scope reversal reads as drift, which is unfortunate in a drift project.

docs.title: 11.8 Duplicated metric code
docs.text: The recovery/damage definitions exist twice (once per runner), copied by hand. Any definition change must be made in both or Exp-01/Exp-02 stop being comparable. There is no shared config-driven harness — that is the main missing development artifact.

docs.title: 12. Quick-fire ML Q&A
docs.text: Question Answer What is concept drift? P_t(X,y) ≠ P_{t+Δ}(X,y) — the joint distribution changes over time. Real vs virtual drift? Real changes P(y\|X) (the rule) and breaks the model. Virtual/covariate shift changes only P(X) — the rule is intact, but input-watching detectors still fire on it. Why is prequential evaluation correct? Random splits leak future information on ordered data. Test-then-train scores each sample before it trains, so the score is honest. Why not cross-validation? There is no "end" to hold out, the order is meaningful, and folds would leak across time. Why Kappa over accuracy? Chance-corrected and imbalance-robust; accuracy overstates learning when temporal persistence gives a strong no-change baseline. What is a drift detector, mechanically? Mostly a 1-D change detector on the model's error stream — it asks "has this Bernoulli mean changed?" Detection vs adaptation? Detection notices; adaptation responds. Independently designable — blind adaptation needs no detector. What is damage area? Σ (κ₀ − κ(t)) over the drift window in samples·κ — skill lost × time wrong. The one number that prices a whole drift. (Mind §11.1.) Why does a rolling window adapt? Old samples age out, so after a drift the model is refit on recent (new-concept) data within ~window samples. Memory stays bounded. Why does a frozen model never recover? It has no mechanism that reads the data. Recovery requires an external retrain decision. Why is label delay a problem? Every detector reads the error stream; late labels mean a late error stream, so drift is detected late — and meanwhile the model visibly reinforces the pre-drift concept. Prequential evaluation itself breaks: you cannot even measure your own accuracy in real time. What is the reaction floor? T ≥ τ + L_τ — no error-stream detector can alarm before the drift's labels arrive. A hard lower bound on detection delay, independent of detector quality. What is partial vs selective labelling? Partial: each label arrives with probability p. Selective: only samples the model flagged get labelled — an endogenous policy, so the detector learns the review policy, not the deployed model. Why can't label-free detection confirm drift? Pure posterior drift leaves P(X) identical, so any P(X)-based test has zero power (KL = 0). Label-free signals can only ever be an early warning. What is the hybrid and why is it maximal? Label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation. L4 says stage 1 can't confirm; L1 says stage 2 can't be early — so the hybrid is the information-maximal architecture given the available information. Why SEA / synthetic at all? Only synthetic streams have known drift positions, which makes detection delay and recovery time computable. Real streams validate external validity. Why is Elec2 treated as secondary? Known temporal autocorrelation; a "no-change" baseline and Kappa+ must be reported, and accuracy alone overstates learning. Why binary classification only? Scope guard — focus. Imbalance is a secondary axis, not a separate task. Why is single-run evidence meaningless here? Synthetic streams are random (draws + label noise), so one replica can't separate a model property from a draw property. ≥10 seeds, mean±SD is the field's convention (Demšar 2006). What would falsify the thesis? Streaming recovery comparable to a sane retrain interval (d + a ≥ r_next − τ); no dip at τ (dataset problem, not a model win); no significant difference under Friedman/Nemenyi; or the reactivity win not worth the resource cost. What if the hybrid loses? A complete negative result: "we quantified how delayed labels break existing methods, and why the obvious fix is insufficient." Lemmas 1–3 hold regardless — Ch3 cannot fail.

docs.title: 13. Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Prequential Test-then-train evaluation: score each sample, then learn from it Concept drift Change over time in P(X,y) Real drift Change in P(y\|X) — the rule itself Virtual drift / covariate shift Change in P(X) only; rule intact Abrupt / gradual / incremental / recurring The four drift shapes over time κ₀ Pre-drift baseline rolling Kappa Δκ Dip depth — how far below κ₀ the model falls Damage area Skill lost × time below baseline, in samples·κ Reaction floor T ≥ τ + L_τ — detection cannot precede label arrival τ The true drift onset time L_t Label latency process (fixed, stochastic, or policy-driven) d, a Detection delay, adaptation time (d + a = streaming recovery) r_next, k Next scheduled retrain; retrain interval Tolerance window W How close an alarm must be to a true drift to count as a detection MTFA / MDR Mean time between false alarms / missed-detection ratio Rolling Kappa Kappa over a sliding recent window (w = 1,000) — reveals drift Blind vs informed adaptation Adapt without a detector vs triggered by one Delay Tax The project's problem: the cost of learning from late, partial, selective labels Hybrid detector Label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation

docs.title: 14. One-screen recap
docs.text:
Problem. Supervised binary classification on a non-stationary stream — single pass, bounded memory, bounded per-sample time, with the distribution allowed to change.

Models.

  • Used (measured): DeepRiver RollingClassifier (RNN 3→16→2, rolling window 500, Adam 1e-3, 1 step/sample) as the streaming learner; sklearn RandomForest(100) fit once on the first 20% as the frozen batch baseline.
  • Planned: Hoeffding Tree / HAT / ARF / SRP / Leveraging Bagging / kNN+ADWIN / online LR (streaming); frozen / scheduled-retrain / oracle-tuned XGBoost (batch ladder); ADWIN / DDM / EDDM / Page-Hinkley / KSWIN (detectors).

Why those. The streaming model was chosen to test the thesis mechanism with a deep learner; its rolling window is the drift mechanism, so no detector is needed. The frozen RF is deliberately the weakest possible opponent — the pilot is the weakest form of the claim. XGBoost is held back as the honest oracle-tuned upper bound.

Metrics. Cohen Kappa (headline, chance-corrected), rolling Kappa w=1,000 (recency), κ₀ / Δκ / recovery time / damage area (drift-window family), accuracy and AUC-PR (secondary), memory / throughput / passes (resource), label efficiency (planned). Detector metrics: delay, FP, MDR, MTFA.

Method. Prequential test-then-train on SEA with one abrupt drift at τ = 30,000 (60k samples, 20% warm-up, 10% label noise), 11 seeds, rolling window w = 1,000, recovery = first 500-sample sustained return to 0.95·κ₀ within a pre-registered 5,000-sample budget; damage area = the integral of skill lost over the drift window.

Result. Frozen recovered 0/11; streaming 11/11 inside budget (median 0 — never left its band). Dip 0.045 vs 0.173 (~3.8×). Damage 13 ± 31 vs 3,710 ± 592. Full run 0.883/0.753 vs 0.854/0.685. Seed 42 reproduced exactly (delta 0).

Three things to say before being asked. (1) The damage ratio is an upper bound — the metric is truncated by the recovery rule on 8 of 11 seeds. (2) The frozen baseline is a strawman by construction; scheduled-retrain is the real opponent and it is next. (3) These are one synthetic stream, one abrupt drift, no detector, no label delay — existence evidence, not a field-wide claim.

docs.title: Datasets — what the project actually runs on
docs.text:
What this page is: a reference for every dataset used in the project — the synthetic generators, the River real streams, and the seven KDD'26 benchmark sets. Shapes, class balances, feature spaces, drift injection, and the caveats are all taken from the experiment configs and the cached artifacts under experiments/data/kdd/ and experiments/results/.

Synthetic configs experiments/registry/e01_metric_v2.yaml, e02_no_drift.yaml, e03_ladder.yaml, e04_detectors.yaml Real-stream configs experiments/registry/e14_real_streams.yaml, e17_real_detector_map.yaml Benchmark runner experiments/kdd_bench.py, experiments/kdd_env/ Cached benchmark data experiments/data/kdd/*.npz, *.csv, usp_ds.zip Standalone Covtype copy data/covtypeNorm.arff (99 MB, untracked)

Important: every real-stream experiment here is semi-synthetic. The real rows are shuffled per seed to remove the original temporal order, and a drift is then injected at a known position. The project is measuring detector/model response to a known change, not natural drift in the wild.

docs.title: 1.2 Synthetic streams
docs.text:
Generator Rows Features Classes Used in Concept change SEA 60,000 3 2 Exp-01, Exp-02, E01–E04 Decision threshold on x₀ + x₁ Hyperplane 60,000 10 2 E02, E03, E04 Random weight vector rotated RandomRBF 60,000 10 2 E04 Centroid set swapped Agrawal 60,000 9 2 E04 Classification function switched

Rows are the available rows before the KDD per-trial 100k cap. Covtype and Posture are the two datasets that hit the cap.

docs.title: 2. The shared synthetic protocol
docs.text:
All controlled streams use the same skeleton unless a config overrides it.

Parameter Value Length 60,000 samples Warm-up 12,000 samples (20%) Drift position τ = 30,000 Label noise 10% (including the no-drift control) Evaluation Prequential: predict → score → learn, every sample Drift shapes abrupt, gradual, incremental, recurring Gradual width 2,000 samples Incremental width 10,000 samples, 10 steps Recurring period 8,000 samples, 2 episodes Detection windows δ_max abrupt 1,000 · gradual 2,000 · incremental 4,000 · recurring 2,000 Seeds 5 (0–4) for the completed slices; E01 uses 11 (42, 0–9); E03's full plan is 11 (0–10)

How the change is generated. The feature process is drawn once per stream. Each sample is labelled by a mixture of concept A and concept B with a weight p(t):

  • Abrupt: p(t) = 0 before τ, 1 after.
  • Gradual: p(t) ramps linearly from 0 to 1 over the width.
  • Incremental: the same ramp, snapped into 10 discrete steps.
  • Recurring: alternating blocks of concept A and B after τ.

This mixing design avoids the River generator RNG-replay confound found during Exp-02: the feature vectors are not replayed under a new label rule, so the frozen model cannot memorise its test chunk.

docs.title: 2.1 SEA
docs.text:
• Features: 3 continuous features, x₀, x₁, x₂ ~ U(0, 10).
  • Label rule: y = 1[x₀ + x₁ > threshold].
  • Concepts: thresholds 8.0, 9.0, 7.0, 9.5 for concept variants 0–3.
  • Used by: Exp-01/02 and E01/E03 with an abrupt change 8.0 → 9.0 at τ; E02 is the stationary control; E04 uses all four shapes.
  • Why: the smallest possible drift testbed — two features actually matter, the decision boundary is exact, and the drift is visible in a rolling metric.

docs.title: 2.2 Hyperplane
docs.text:
• Features: 10 continuous features, xᵢ ~ U(0, 1).
  • Label rule: two random weight vectors w_A, w_B; the active weight vector is mixed with p(t), and y = 1[Σ wᵢxᵢ ≥ 0.5 · Σ wᵢ].
  • Used by: E02 (stationary control), E03 (abrupt, position jittered), E04.
  • Why: a high-dimensional linear boundary that changes direction rather than threshold — a different failure mode from SEA.

docs.title: 2.3 RandomRBF
docs.text:
• Features: 10 continuous features.
  • Concepts: two independently drawn RBF worlds, each with 20 centroids and 2 classes; a sample is a centroid plus a Gaussian offset.
  • Drift: the active centroid set is switched with p(t).
  • Used by: E04.
  • Why: locally clustered classes with overlapping Gaussians — harder for a tree to separate than SEA/Hyperplane.

docs.title: 2.4 Agrawal
docs.text:
• Features: 9 mixed numeric/categorical features (salary, commission, age, elevel, car, …) from River's synth.Agrawal.
  • Concept: one of 10 classification functions; the function is switched with p(t).
  • Used by: E04.
  • Why: a non-linear, rule-based generator with categorical structure.
