docs.text: Experiment Streams Difference from the skeleton Exp-01 / Exp-02 SEA abrupt only Seed 42 + 0–9; legacy metric E01 SEA abrupt only 11 seeds; clean three-model panel E02 SEA + Hyperplane, stationary No drift; every alarm is a false alarm E03 SEA + Hyperplane, abrupt Drift onset jittered by ±7,000 samples per seed to vary the retrain phase E04 SEA, Hyperplane, RandomRBF, Agrawal × 4 shapes 4 generators × 4 shapes × 2 hosts × raw/EWMA, 5 seeds

docs.title: 3. The real streams in E14 and E17
docs.text: Both experiments use River datasets, shuffle the rows per seed, then inject a known drift. This is the semi-synthetic protocol of the KDD'26 benchmark.

docs.title: 3.1 Elec2 — electricity market
docs.text:
Source River Elec2 (remote dataset) Rows 45,312 Features 8: date, day, period, nswprice, nswdemand, vicprice, vicdemand, transfer Target Binary class: electricity price moves up/down Class balance 26,075 / 19,236 in the KDD export (45,311 rows; one row fewer than River's 45,312) Used by E17 (detectors), E14 (models)

E17 configuration. 45,312 rows; warm-up 9,062; drift at τ = 22,656; label swap 0 → 1; five seeds 0–4; four shapes:

Shape Width Notes Abrupt 0 One-step label swap Gradual 2,000 Swap probability ramps over 2,000 rows Incremental 10,000 10 discrete swap steps Recurring 8,000 period, 2 episodes Concept A/B alternate after τ

E14 configuration. 45,312 rows; warm-up 9,062; drift at τ = 30,000; abrupt; five seeds; two mechanisms: label_swap (0 → 1) and feature_permutation (all feature columns permuted).

Caveat. Shuffling removes the original time order, so date and day stay in the feature vector as numbers but no longer carry temporal meaning. This is a known property of the semi-synthetic protocol, not a modelling mistake.

docs.title: 3.2 Phishing — website classification
docs.text:
Source River Phishing (bundled file; UCI Website Phishing) Rows 1,250 Features 9: empty_server_form_handler, popup_window, https, request_from_other_domain, anchor_from_other_domain, is_popular, long_url, age_of_domain, ip_in_url Target is_phishing (binary) Class balance 702 non-phishing / 548 phishing Used by E14 only

E14 configuration. 1,250 rows; warm-up 250; drift at τ = 625; abrupt; five seeds; label_swap and feature_permutation.

Caveat. Phishing is very small (1,250 rows) and contributes only one drift episode per run. It is a second real dataset for external validity, not a stand-alone benchmark; E14's aggregate is dominated by Elec2's 45k rows.

docs.title: 3.3 Injection mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism What happens after τ label_swap Every label equal to the source class is changed to the target class (with the shape's probability p(t)) feature_permutation All feature columns are permuted; labels are untouched class_prior A chosen class is dropped with probability 0.75 (KDD only) feature_filtering Rows above the pre-onset median of a chosen feature are dropped (KDD only)

The first two are used in E14/E17; all four are used in the KDD'26 reproduction. Because the change is injected, the true drift position and the end of the transition are known exactly.

docs.title: 4. The KDD'26 benchmark datasets
docs.text: The KDD'26 reproduction uses seven real datasets. Five come from the USP DS Repository archive; Covtype and Electricity are exported from CapyMOA. Every trial shuffles the rows, caps the stream at 100,000 rows, draws a drift onset uniformly from 50–80% of the stream, and injects one of four drift types.

docs.title: 4.1 Shapes and class balances
docs.text:
Dataset Rows Features Classes Class counts (label-encoded) δ_max Asfault 8,564 64 6 [2335, 1002, 4761, 273, 1, 192] 500 Covtype 581,012 54 7 [211840, 283301, 35754, 2747, 9493, 17367, 20510] 2,500 Electricity 45,311 8 2 [26075, 19236] 2,500 GasSensorArray 13,910 128 6 [2565, 2926, 1641, 1936, 3009, 1833] 1,500 NOAA 18,159 8 2 [12461, 5698] 1,500 Posture 164,858 3 11 [2973, 54480, 6168, 5210, 27244, 1706, 11779, 18359, 1381, 2848, 32710] 2,500 Rialto 82,250 27 10 [8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225, 8225] 2,500

Shares are computed on the full cached data, before the per-trial 100k cap. The encoded labels are arbitrary; the colours are only to show balance.

Effective rows per trial. Asfault, Electricity, GasSensorArray, NOAA and Rialto are used in full. Covtype is truncated from 581,012 to 100,000 and Posture from 164,858 to 100,000. A 50-trial run therefore sees many different 100k slices of those two datasets, not the full records.

docs.title: 4.2 What is in each dataset
docs.text:
Dataset Feature composition Things to know Asfault 64 numeric features; original column names are not preserved by the CSV loader (F1…F64) Class 4 has 1 example; class 2 dominates (4,761 of 8,564). Any per-class metric is unstable. Covtype 54 features: 10 numeric terrain features, 4 binary wilderness-area flags, 40 binary soil-type flags 7 forest-cover classes; the standard UCI Covertype schema, normalized. Electricity 8 features, same schema as Elec2 (date, day, period, nswprice, nswdemand, vicprice, vicdemand, transfer) Binary; 45,311 rows in the CapyMOA export vs 45,312 in River. GasSensorArray 128 numeric sensor features 6 gas classes; high-dimensional and correlated; 13,910 rows. NOAA 8 numeric weather features Binary; 18,159 rows; the smallest feature set after Posture. Posture 3 features 11 classes; 164,858 rows but only 3 features, so the problem is intrinsically hard and the cap to 100k matters. Rialto 27 numeric features 10 perfectly balanced classes (8,225 each); 82,250 rows.

The original column names for Asfault, GasSensorArray, NOAA, Posture and Rialto are replaced with F1…Fn by experiments/kdd_bench.py; the cached .npz files therefore store positional feature names, not semantic ones. The shape and class counts above are read directly from those .npz files.

docs.title: 4.3 The four injected drift types
docs.text:
Drift type Mechanism What changes class_prior After onset, each row of the selected class is dropped with probability 0.75 The class distribution shifts; the stream gets shorter label_swap Every row of the selected class is relabelled to another class P(y|X) changes; P(X) is unchanged feature_permutation All feature columns are permuted The feature→label relationship is destroyed feature_filtering Rows whose chosen feature exceeds its pre-onset median are dropped The conditional feature distribution changes; the stream gets shorter

Transitions. An abrupt drift applies the mechanism at the onset. A gradual drift applies it with probability p(t) that ramps from 0 to 1 over width = δ_max. The onset is drawn uniformly from the middle 50–80% of the stream, so the drift never falls in the first half or the last fifth.

docs.title: 4.4 Protocol summary
docs.text:
Parameter Value Datasets 7 (Asfault, Covtype, Electricity, GasSensorArray, NOAA, Posture, Rialto) Drift types 4 (class_prior, label_swap, feature_permutation, feature_filtering) Transitions 2 (abrupt, gradual) Trials 50 per dataset × drift type × transition Row cap 100,000 per trial Shuffle Every trial independently Headline detectors ADWIN, DDM, HDDM-A, HDDM-W, SEED, STEPD Configured detectors 13, including ABCD and ABCD(X) Stop rule δ_max after the drift end Result rows 16,800 (2,800 tasks × 6 detectors)

The 50-trial run completed 2,800 tasks with 0 failures in 13m33s on 14 workers. The ABCD/ABCD(X) arm is cited from the paper, not reproduced; it is the expensive part of the matrix and overheats the laptop CPU. The full ranking is in E17 §7 and the global Results page.

docs.title: 5. What the data does not contain
docs.text:
These are deliberate limitations, not oversights.

Limitation Consequence No natural temporal drift in E14/E17 Real rows are shuffled and drift is injected; the results measure detector/model response to a known change, not natural drift in Elec2/Phishing No natural-drift benchmark yet E14 has two real datasets (Elec2, Phishing); Covertype, Airlines and CreditCard are not in the model comparison No label delay Labels arrive immediately in every dataset above; the Delay Tax experiments (E15) have not run No missing/partial/selective labels The Delay Tax regimes are future work No train/test split Evaluation is prequential with a warm-up; there is no held-out test set No per-class stratification in E14/E17 Rows are shuffled per seed, so class balance varies slightly by seed KDD uses at most 100k rows Covtype loses ~83% of its rows per trial; Posture loses ~39% KDD labels are encoded Class indices are arbitrary; do not attach semantic meaning without the source table Synthetic streams are controlled SEA has 3 features and 2 classes; a win there is existence evidence, not a field-wide claim

docs.title: 6. Where the data lives and how to rebuild it
6.1 Paths
docs.text:
Path Contents experiments/data/kdd/*.npz Cached numeric arrays + feature names used by the KDD runner experiments/data/kdd/*.csv Original CSVs for the five USP datasets and Electricity experiments/data/kdd/usp_ds.zip 600 MB USP DS Repository archive (do not commit) data/covtypeNorm.arff 99 MB normalized Covtype ARFF (do not commit) experiments/results/e17/ Elec2 detector-map artifact experiments/results/e14/ Elec2 + Phishing model-comparison artifact experiments/results/kdd_bench_full/ 50-trial benchmark artifact

The .npz caches are the canonical numeric form. The standalone data/covtypeNorm.arff is a reference copy, not the KDD runner's input — the runner exports Covtype from CapyMOA into experiments/data/kdd/Covtype.npz. Both the .npz caches and the ARFF are untracked and should stay that way: the repository should not carry the 600 MB zip or the 99 MB ARFF.

docs.title: 6.2 Commands
docs.text:
# synthetic experiments
uv run python -m experiments.run --exp e01
uv run python -m experiments.run --exp e02
uv run python -m experiments.run --exp e03 --resume

# KDD'26 benchmark

    --signal correct --gradual-anchor code \

docs.title: 6.3 Sources
docs.text:
• River — Elec2 and Phishing datasets (river.datasets).
  • CapyMOA — CovtypeNorm and Electricity exports used by the KDD runner.
  • USP DS Repository — the Google Drive archive referenced in experiments/kdd_bench.py; supplies Asfault, GasSensorArray, NOAA, Posture and Rialto.
  • UCI / original dataset pages — the provenance behind River's Phishing and the Covertype schema; use the source pages for semantic feature names and class meanings.

Shapes, row counts and class balances on this page come from the cached experiments/data/kdd/*.npz arrays and the River dataset metadata; the drift settings come from experiments/registry/*.yaml and experiments/kdd_bench.py. Re-run make_dataset_figures.py after refreshing a cache.

docs.title: struct.md — what every file in this repo does
docs.text:
Scope: everything in the repo except docs/ (the documentation site has its own 38-page structure and is deliberately excluded here). Covers the state as of 2026-09-22.

Repo: github.com/Priyansh6747/Streaming-machine-learning- — a research + development project on streaming machine learning, concept drift, and the "Delay Tax". Published site: https://priyansh6747.github.io/Streaming-machine-learning-/.

docs.title: 0. Where the actual work lives
docs.text:
Four things matter; everything else is tooling around them:

Path Role experiments/ The experiments — runners, data artifacts, figure generators docs/ The evidence — write-ups, literature review, results (excluded from this doc) .agentInstructions/ Agent tooling — skills, taste, house rules (not part of the project) root config Packaging, CI, docs build (pyproject.toml, mkdocs.yml, uv.lock, .github/)

main.py is a stub and does nothing. The project is not an application — it is an experiment suite plus a documentation site.

docs.title: 1. Root files
docs.text:
File What it does README.md The project vision page — plain language, no code (deliberate). Status table, the mechanism argument, headline evidence, the roadmap. First thing an examiner reads. CLAUDE.md Agent-facing instructions for this repo: points agents at .agentInstructions/, forbids new top-level dot-folders, and lists the mkdocs commands. main.py Stub. print("Hello from major!"). No real entry point — an experiment is run by invoking its script directly. pyproject.toml uv project definition. Deps: deep-river, river (pinned transitively <0.26), torch, scikit-learn, matplotlib, pytest (a workaround — deep-river imports it at package-import time but omits it from its own deps), mkdocs-material, mkdocs-exporter. Also restricts [tool.uv] environments to Linux + Apple-Silicon arm64 to avoid the Intel-Mac torch wheel blocker. uv.lock Locked, fully-resolved dependency graph (~122 KB). Makes the environment reproducible. .python-version 3.12 — pinned because deep-river's torch <2.6 has no cp313 wheels. mkdocs.yml The docs site config: Material theme, MathJax + Mermaid, admonitions/tables/footnotes, the exporter plugin (per-page PDFs + optional aggregated documentation.pdf via headless Chromium), and the full nav tree. A page under docs/ is invisible on the site unless it is in this nav. .gitignore Three entries only: site/, .venv/, __pycache__/. notes.pdf 26-page generated PDF — "The Delay Tax — Literature Review". Produced 2026-08-25 by the pdf-notes skill (workspace/run1). Covers scope, the gap verdict, lemmas 1–4, scoop risk, closest prior work, baseline pick, go/no-go, and every reviewed paper with its numbers.

Not a source of truth: notes.pdf is a generated artifact. Its content is derived from the literature-review notes in docs/Phase0:Research/. Regenerating it means re-running the skill, not editing the PDF.

docs.title: 2. experiments/ — the experiment suite
docs.text:
One directory per experiment, plus shared scripts/ and figures/. Every claim in the docs traces to a results.json in here.

experiments/
├── exp01/results.json       # Exp-01 artifact
├── exp02/results.json       # Exp-02 artifact
├── figures/                 # shared figure source
│   └── make_thesis_schematic.py
└── scripts/                 # all runners + figure generators
    ├── exp01_deepriver_vs_frozen_sea.py
    ├── exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py
    ├── make_exp01_summary_chart.py
    ├── make_results_figures.py
    └── make_sept9_report_graphs.py

docs.title: 2a. Data artifacts
docs.text: File What it holds exp01/results.json Exp-01 (seed 42): the full per-sample rolling-Kappa series plus all drift-window and full-run metrics. The per-sample series is what makes the rolling-Kappa curve re-renderable. exp02/results.json Exp-02 (11 seeds): per-seed rows (recovery, Δκ, damage, full-run acc/κ), all aggregate distributions (mean/SD/median/min/max), the acceptance scorecard, the Exp-01 cross-check, and the scenario/model spec. Does not retain the per-sample series — which is why the metric fix in ML.md §11 needs a rerun.

docs.title: 2b. Runners
docs.text:
File What it does scripts/exp01_deepriver_vs_frozen_sea.py Exp-01: builds the SEA stream with one abrupt drift at τ=30,000, runs DeepRiver rolling vs frozen RF prequentially over 48k post-warm-up samples, records per-sample metrics, writes exp01/results.json. Flags: --device cuda\|cpu. scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py Exp-02: the same experiment as a loop over 11 seeds. Writes results.json and re-renders the 9-figure suite. Flags: --require-cuda, --limit (dev slice), --figure-only (regenerate all figures from the committed artifact with no rerun), --figures-dir. scripts/make_exp01_summary_chart.py Figure generator: the Exp-01 recovery-time vs damage-area summary chart. scripts/make_results_figures.py Figure generator for docs/Reports/Results.md — process-flow and headline-scoreboard figures. scripts/make_e18_e19_figures.py Figure generator for E18/E19 — AUC gate, FAR-calibrated timing diagnostic, overall rank/FAR, feature-cell and per-dataset robustness. scripts/make_e21_delay_figure.py Figure generator for E21 — label-free warning vs error-only detection under fixed label delay L, from the E19 trial artifacts. scripts/make_e22_report_figures.py Figure generator for E22 — overall rank/F1-FAR and feature-cell/drift-type profile against the requested classical panel. scripts/make_sept9_report_graphs.py Figure generator for the Sept-9 milestone report — roadmap and expected-vs-measured charts. figures/make_thesis_schematic.py Draws the illustrative three-curve recovery schematic (streaming / scheduled / frozen) used in thesis.md and the README. Note it lives in figures/, not scripts/ — the only figure script not in scripts/.

Run an experiment: uv run experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py --require-cuda Re-render figures only: uv run experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py --figure-only

Known structural weakness: exp01 and exp02 duplicate the metric code (drift_metrics) by hand — the Exp-02 docstring says the definitions are "copied verbatim from the Exp-01 script so Exp-02 is a sweep of one experiment, not a new one". There is no shared, config-driven harness yet; that is the Chapter-1 exit criterion and the main missing development artifact.

docs.title: 3. .agentInstructions/ — agent tooling (not project content)
docs.text:
Policy (from README.md): this is the single home for anything instructing an AI agent — prompts, skills, taste. No new top-level dot-folders; keep it in version control.

Path What it does README.md The policy itself, plus one hard project rule: every experiment must produce a plot or data artifact — no experiment may end with only prose. taste/taste.md Index file; points at the category file. taste/taste/taste.md Captured preferences about research and documentation style — verify citations before marking them verified, flag risks loudly, dense/numbers-first deliverables, figures in docs, structured markdown over prose, etc.

docs.title: 3a. skills/pdf-notes/ — a complete PDF-generation skill
docs.text:
A self-contained sub-project (its own .venv, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version) that turns "notes-as-code" into polished PDFs. It produced notes.pdf.

File What it does SKILL.md Skill metadata + trigger description + quick start + the helper-category table. README.md Install and usage: system deps (poppler-utils, graphviz), the init/build/validate workflow. plan.md 40 KB architecture doc — v2 design with graphics: helper catalogue, rendering recipe, asset cache, validation heuristics, design tokens, decision log. plan_detailed_mode.md The chapter-stitched generation mode: instead of one giant content.py, plan a manifest and write one small .py chapter per turn. func.md 27 KB snippet library the agent copies verbatim, editing only the data strings. notes_kit.py Core rendering: design tokens, styles, text helpers, NotesCanvas, generate_notes_pdf, and re-exports from the two modules below. graphics_kit.py Charts (matplotlib), diagrams (graphviz), math (mathtext), Venn, timeline. The largest module (~58 KB). highlighting.py Pygments → ReportLab-XML syntax highlighting (monokai) for add_code(highlight=True). file_tree.py Pure-vector file-tree diagram Flowable — draws drive/folder/file nodes with connectors and arrowheads, no image deps. runner.py CLI: init / build / validate. Emits JSON contracts on stdout, diagnostics on stderr. schemas/generate_spec.py Pydantic request/response models for the JSON contract. schemas/__init__.py Empty package marker. tests/ Pytest suite: test_detailed_mode.py, test_file_tree.py, test_highlighting.py. main.py Stub — print("Hello from pdf-skill!"). Legacy, unused by the skill. pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version, .gitignore The skill's own isolated environment (Python 3.13), independent of the project's. workspace/run1/ The actual generation run that produced notes.pdf. workspace/run1/book.json The manifest: title, subtitle, theme, and the ordered chapter list. workspace/run1/chapters/ch01…ch16_*.py 16 chapter sources — overview, gap, lemma1–lemma4, scoop, closest_prior, baseline, gono, papers_ch1, ch1b, ch2, ch3, ch3b, hybrid. workspace/run1/assets/*.png Rendered math/chart assets, cache-keyed by hash. workspace/run1/preview_p1…26.png Per-page preview renders (one per page of the 26-page PDF).

workspace/run1/ has no notes.pdf in it — the built PDF was copied up to the repo root as notes.pdf.

docs.title: 4. .commandcode/ — legacy duplicate of the taste files
docs.text:
Path What it does taste/taste.md Index pointer (identical content to the .agentInstructions/ one). taste/taste/taste.md Captured preferences about experiment and execution style — persist experiment code as real scripts in experiments/scripts/, use the GPU, keep script docstrings lean, one narrative per figure, draft commit messages but don't commit, keep CI in sync with build deps, a page in docs/ is only "done" when it's in the nav.

Inconsistency worth knowing: .agentInstructions/README.md states this folder was renamed to .agentInstructions and rule 1 forbids new top-level dot-folders for agent tooling. It nonetheless exists again — recreated by the tooling. The two taste/ trees are not mirrors: they hold different captured preferences. Treat both as live.

docs.title: Other dot-paths
docs.text:
Path What it does .claude/settings.local.json Editor-managed permission allowlist (currently one entry: WebFetch(domain:riverml.xyz)). .github/workflows/ci.yml Deploy job: on push to main when docs/**, mkdocs.yml, or the workflow changed, installs mkdocs-material + mkdocs-exporter, installs the Playwright Chromium, then mkdocs gh-deploy --force with PDF export on.

Consequence for adding pages: a commit that only touches, say, experiments/ will not trigger a redeploy. Only changes under docs/ or to mkdocs.yml do.

docs.title: 5. Environment and commands
docs.text:
Command Effect uv sync Install/refresh the project environment uv run experiments/scripts/exp0N_*.py Run an experiment (GPU if present) uv run experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py --figure-only Re-render the Exp-02 figure suite from the committed artifact — no rerun uv run mkdocs serve Local docs preview (needs the Playwright browser for PDFs) MKDOCS_EXPORTER_PDF=false uv run mkdocs serve Fast local preview, no PDF rendering uv run mkdocs build --strict Build; fails on broken links uv run playwright install chromium One-time setup for the PDF export feature

Hardware reality: the DeepRiver loop needs the GPU. 484 samples/s on the RTX 3050 vs 44 samples/s on CPU for the same 48k-sample loop — ~11× — so --require-cuda on Exp-02 exists to fail fast rather than silently take an hour.

docs.title: 6. Things to know before touching this repo
docs.text:
1. docs/ is the published artifact, not a scratch folder. Anything placed there is built into the site and, with the exporter on, into downloadable PDFs.
  2. A page in docs/ without a nav entry is invisible — it builds and is reachable by URL, but nothing links to it. Three pages are currently in that state: papers/dasari-2026-when-to-retrain.md, papers/read-2012-batch-vs-instance.md, and Reports/_milestone-template.md.
  3. main.py does nothing. The real entry points are the scripts in experiments/scripts/.
  4. The two runners duplicate the metric code. Any change to how recovery or damage is defined must be made in both, or the comparison between Exp-01 and Exp-02 breaks.
  5. notes.pdf is generated, not authored — it is the output of skills/pdf-notes/workspace/run1, not a hand-written document.
  6. .commandcode/ shouldn't exist per the repo's own policy, but does, and holds unique preferences. Don't delete it without moving its content.
  7. Figure scripts live in two places (experiments/scripts/ and experiments/figures/) for no documented reason.
  8. exp02/results.json has no per-sample series — a metric-definition fix there requires re-running the sweep, not post-processing.
  9. Do not edit .agentInstructions/taste/ or .commandcode/taste/ by hand. They're managed by the learning system.

docs.title: explore/ — Deep-dive notes
docs.text:
Working notes on topics we're exploring beyond the core streaming-learning curriculum. Read alongside the numbered notes in notes/.

# File What it covers 01 01-transformers-bridge.md Using existing transformer knowledge in quant trading — what transfers, what breaks, where attention genuinely helps 02 02-quant-trading.md Financial quant fundamentals — the pipeline, key concepts, data types, backtesting pitfalls, the honest math 03 03-streaming-finance-bridge.md Why finance IS a streaming problem — regime drift, delayed labels, and where the project's research fits

docs.title: 01 — Mapping transformer knowledge onto quant trading
docs.text: One-line version: your transformer knowledge transfers to quant trading through the habits (learned representations, attention over context, the eval mindset) — but the problem shape is different: financial data is non-stationary, low signal-to-noise, and the ground truth (future returns) is only knowable in hindsight.

docs.title: The good news: the fit is real
docs.text: Finance is a data-stream problem at its core. Prices tick continuously, regimes change, and a model that doesn't adapt dies. The streaming ML skills you've been building are directly market-shaped. And your transformer background gives you a head start on the representation side. This is not a stretch — the two fields genuinely overlap.

docs.title: What your transformer knowledge already covers
docs.text: Transformer muscle Quant trading equivalent Transfers? Learned embeddings of tokens Learned feature representations of market state Yes, core skill Attention over a context window Attention over recent price/order-flow context Yes, with care The train / val / test split ritual Walk-forward / backtest with no leakage Concept, re-tooled The eval harness (accuracy, F1) Sharpe, drawdown, hit rate, per-trade stats Concept, re-tooled Positional encodings Time features — time-of-day, session, calendar effects Yes Sequence modeling (LSTM/attention) Modeling price paths as sequences Yes, but overfit-prone The loss as a training signal The P&L / alpha as the real objective Re-framed Batching, epochs, i.i.d. assumption Non-stationary, ordered, drifting data No — must unlearn

docs.title: Where attention genuinely helps in markets
docs.text:
Attention is not useless in finance — it's just differently useful than in NLP. Three places it earns its keep:

  1. Cross-sectional attention (over assets, not time): which of 500 stocks matter most right now for predicting a target? Cross-sectional attention is a natural, defensible use — the "context" is the market, and which assets matter shifts with regime.
  2. Feature selection over windows: attention over a rolling window of features (not raw prices) to decide which recent context matters — e.g., "the last 3 days of volatility matter more than the last 20."
  3. Regime detection: attention weights as a soft indicator of which regime the model thinks it's in — a bridge to the drift-detection side of the project.

The trap to avoid: attention over raw prices as a universal sequence model is where overfitting lives. Markets are not language; the "next token" is noise-dominated, and attention's power to memorize long patterns becomes a liability, not an asset.

docs.title: The honest differences (what's new)
docs.text:
• Non-stationarity. NLP data is mostly stationary. Markets are non-stationary by construction — the distribution that generated yesterday's prices is not today's. This is the single biggest shift.
  • Low signal-to-noise. A good predictive edge is a tiny edge over noise. Transformers are built to extract strong structure; markets have weak structure. The failure mode is fitting noise.
  • Hindsight ground truth. In NLP, labels are in the data. In trading, the label (future return) is a realized value you can only know after the fact — the delayed-label problem in its purest form.
  • Survivorship and leakage. The dataset itself lies: delisted stocks vanish from history, and look-ahead bias is everywhere. Your transformer instinct (clean split, careful features) is the right instinct here.
  • The eval metric is money, not accuracy. Accuracy doesn't compound. Sharpe, drawdown, and win rate do. The objective function changes shape.

docs.title: How to use transformer knowledge as leverage
docs.text:
Concrete moves that work:

  1. Steal the eval mindset, upgrade it to walk-forward. The habit of "never evaluate on training data" becomes "never let future data leak into the past." Walk-forward / expanding-window evaluation is the market version of your hold-out discipline.
  2. Reuse the representation layer. Whatever feature engineering you did (embeddings, normalized columns, time features) maps to the market-input pipeline. The model changes; the input hygiene survives.
  3. Think of drift detection as regime monitoring. You know what a rising validation loss means. Drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM) are the streaming version: watch the error/P&L distribution, react when the regime shifts.
  4. Port the optimizer discipline, not the architecture. Start with linear models and gradient-boosted trees on good features before attention. The edge in quant is usually in the features and the risk model, not the architecture.

docs.title: The bridge summary
docs.text:
Transformer world Quant trading Data Fixed dataset, reusable Ticking, non-stationary, non-reusable Samples i.i.d., shuffleable Ordered, drifting, regime-dependent Ground truth In the data Realized later (delayed labels) Signal Strong structure Weak structure, noise-dominated Eval Accuracy / loss Sharpe, drawdown, P&L The research problem Scale, generalization Drift, adaptation, edge decay, risk

What transfers: the eval mindset, representation learning, attention as a concept, time-feature discipline, the toolkit. What doesn't: the i.i.d. assumptions, the "one model fits all" instinct, training to accuracy. What's new (and where the project is): non-stationarity, delayed labels, edge decay, regime detection, risk-aware evaluation.

docs.title: Open questions for us
docs.text:
• Is cross-sectional attention (over assets) a defensible use of transformers in a market model, or does it overfit as badly as temporal attention?
  • Can drift detection double as regime detection — giving a trading signal ("the regime changed, adapt the model") rather than just a warning?
  • How does the delayed-label problem (see notes/02-concept-drift.md, research/02-delayed-labels.md) bite quant models specifically — and can the project's delayed-label research be a market research project?
  • What does a minimal honest backtest look like — one that can't be accused of look-ahead bias — for a streaming market model?

docs.title: 02 — Financial quant fundamentals
docs.text: One-line version: quant trading is using math and data to make statistically disciplined bets on markets — the edge is small, the data is noisy and non-stationary, and the difference between a good quant and a gambler is the evaluation, risk, and leakage hygiene around the model.

docs.title: What "quant" actually means
docs.text:
Quantitative trading = making trading decisions from numerical models and data rather than gut feel. The spectrum:

  • Statistical arbitrage — find and exploit temporary mispricings between related assets (pairs, baskets).
  • Momentum / trend following — the market's tendency to continue in a direction for a while; classic systematic strategy.
  • Mean reversion — the market's tendency to snap back to an average; the statistical opposite of momentum.
  • Market making — profit from the bid/ask spread by providing liquidity.
  • High-frequency (HFT) — microstructure, sub-second edges. Not our lane with streaming ML at sample rates like one bar per minute.
  • Factor investing — long/short portfolios tilted toward known factors (value, momentum, size, volatility).

For a research project, the accessible lanes are statistical arbitrage, momentum, and mean reversion on moderate-frequency data (minutes to days). HFT is out — it's a latency/microstructure game, not an ML problem.

docs.title: The quant pipeline (the mental model to keep)
docs.text:
raw data → features → model → position sizing → execution → P&L
                ↑                                   ↓
                └────── risk & evaluation loop ←─────┘

Every stage is a discipline:

  1. Raw data — prices, volumes, order flow, fundamentals, alternative data. Hygiene here is everything: adjusted prices (splits/dividends), no look-ahead, survivorship-free universes.
  2. Features — returns, volatility, momentum, ratios, spreads, time-of-day, regime indicators. This is where edges live. Most quant alpha is feature engineering, not architecture.
  3. Model — predicts a target: direction, return magnitude, volatility, or a mispricing signal. Linear models, trees, and (carefully) neural nets. The model is usually the smallest contributor to edge.
  4. Position sizing — how much to bet, given the edge and the uncertainty (Kelly, fractional Kelly, vol targeting). Model confidence alone is not enough.
  5. Execution — actually trading without eating the edge in costs (spread, fees, slippage).
  6. Risk & evaluation — the loop that keeps you honest: Sharpe, drawdown, exposure, leakage checks, out-of-sample discipline.

docs.title: Key concepts, in plain terms
docs.text:
• Alpha — the part of a return that isn't explained by the market; the edge your model adds. "Alpha decay" = the edge fading as others find it.
  • Beta — the market's general direction; a long-only portfolio has market beta. Quant strategies try to isolate alpha net of beta.
  • Sharpe ratio — (excess return) / (volatility). The standard scorecard. A Sharpe above 1 is good; above 2 is great. It's the risk-adjusted return.
  • Drawdown — peak-to-trough loss. A strategy with great Sharpe but a 40% drawdown is psychologically and practically hard to run. Drawdown is what actually kills funds.
  • P&L / returns — log returns (continuous compounding) are the natural scale for models; simple returns for portfolio math. Log returns are roughly additive over time, simple returns aren't.
  • Volatility — the standard deviation of returns; the thing that scales with risk. Vol is itself forecastable (GARCH, realized vol) and mean-reverts.
  • Regime — a persistent market state (bull/bear, high/low vol). Regime shifts are concept drift wearing a suit.
  • Bid/ask spread — the cost of trading. If your edge per trade is smaller than the spread, you lose regardless of model quality.
  • Slippage — the difference between your intended and actual fill price. Backtests that ignore slippage are fiction.

docs.title: Data types (and their character)
docs.text:
Type Frequency Character Notes Ticks ms Noisy, huge HFT lane; microstructure OHLCV bars 1m–1d Standard for ML The workhorse: open/high/low/close/volume Fundamentals quarterly Sparse, lagged, survivorship-heavy Point-in-time data is the only honest version Order book ms Microstructure Depth, imbalance; HFT-ish Alternative mixed Novel, sparse Sentiment, satellite, search trends Options mixed Derivative structure Implied vol is a rich feature source

The two data traps that end projects:

  1. Survivorship bias — backtesting only stocks that still exist today. Delisted stocks (which often failed) vanish from the historical dataset, inflating returns. You must include delisted names and mark them dead.
  2. Look-ahead bias — using information not available at the time (future prices, restated fundamentals, same-day close to predict same-day return). The fix is strict time-ordering: features computed before the prediction point, labels after it.

docs.title: Backtesting: the honest version
docs.text:
A backtest is a simulation of a strategy on history. It is not proof — it's a sanity check that's easy to fool. The disciplines:

  • Walk-forward evaluation — train on a window, test on the next, roll forward. Never train and test on overlapping periods.
  • Expanding vs rolling window — expanding = use all history so far (more data, adapts slower to regime); rolling = fixed recent window (less data, adapts faster). Streaming ML maps to this directly.
  • Transaction costs — model spread + slippage + fees explicitly. A strategy profitable in zero-cost backtest often dies with realistic costs.
  • Out-of-sample discipline — final evaluation on data never touched during development. This is the quant version of your hold-out test set.
  • Multiple-testing honesty — trying 500 features/strategies and reporting the best one is p-hacking by another name. Report the distribution, not the winner.

docs.title: The honest math (what wins and what doesn't)
docs.text:
• The edge is small. A great strategy wins 52–55% of the time, or has a Sharpe of 1–2. Anyone promising much more is selling something.
  • Volatility is the enemy of compounding. Deep drawdowns need larger recoveries: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to break even. Risk management is not optional — it's the strategy.
  • More complexity = more overfitting risk. Linear models on good features routinely beat deep models on mediocre features, in production.
  • Transaction costs are a tax on frequency. High-frequency strategies die first when costs are realistic. Lower frequency (bars/days) tolerates costs better.
  • The market is adaptive. Whatever edge you find decays as it's exploited — alpha decay is the reason streaming adaptation is required, not optional.

docs.title: Tooling landscape
docs.text:
• Python — the ecosystem: pandas (data), numpy (math), scikit-learn / lightgbm / xgboost (models), statsmodels (econometrics).
  • Backtesting — backtrader, vectorbt, zipline, bt.
  • Data — yfinance (free, fine for learning), ccxt (crypto), paid feeds for production (Polygon, EOD, Bloomberg/Refinitiv).
  • Streaming ML — River (our framework) — a natural fit for the online loop that live markets are.
  • Research infra — Jupyter, mlflow (experiment tracking), wandb.

docs.title: Open questions for us
docs.text:
• Momentum, mean reversion, or stat-arb as the first strategy family? (Each maps differently onto streaming models.)
  • Which data source: free daily bars (yfinance), free crypto (ccxt), or a synthetic stream (generate regimes ourselves) for a clean research setup?
  • How do we measure a streaming trading strategy — Sharpe computed prequentially, per-bar, with realistic costs?
  • Does the delayed-label angle (labels arrive after the trade decision) make our project uniquely suited to markets, or uniquely unsuited? (I suspect suited — see 03.)

docs.title: 02 — Quantization fundamentals, then streaming angles
docs.text: One-line version: quantization is trading a little accuracy for a lot of memory and speed by storing weights and activations in fewer bits — and the streaming world wants exactly that, because streaming models run on constrained devices under a permanent memory budget.

docs.title: Why quantization exists
docs.text:
Neural networks are trained in float32 (4 bytes per value). Most of that precision is wasted: a trained model's weights are robust to small rounding. Quantization stores each value in fewer bits — typically 8, 4, or even 2 — and the model gets smaller, faster, and cheaper to run.

The three things you buy:

  • Memory. A 1B-parameter model at float32 is 4 GB. At int8 it's 1 GB. At int4 it's 500 MB. For a device (or a streaming budget) this is the whole game.
  • Speed. Integer math is faster than float math, and 8-bit values move through memory faster than 32-bit. On CPU especially, int8 is a big win.
  • Energy. Less memory traffic + cheaper arithmetic = less power. Relevant for edge devices, which is where streaming models live.

docs.title: The core idea: scale and zero-point
docs.text:
A float value x in a known range [min, max] maps to an integer q via:

q = round(x / scale) + zero_point
  • scale is the step size — how much one integer step is worth.
  • zero_point is the integer that represents the float 0.0.

So instead of storing the float, you store the integer plus the (scale, zero_point) pair for the whole tensor. Two tensors with different ranges get different scales — that's why per-channel and per-tensor quantization differ.

The two questions that define a quantization scheme:

  1. What range do we assume? Fixed-range (per tensor/channel) vs dynamic.
  2. What precision? 8-bit (safe), 4-bit (tight), 2-bit (extreme).

docs.title: 1. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)
docs.text:
Quantize an already-trained model. No retraining. Calibrate the ranges by running a small amount of data through it and recording activation ranges.

  • Pros: trivial to do, no training cost.
  • Cons: accuracy loss can be significant at low bit-widths, especially for small models (the model can't adapt to the rounding).

docs.title: 2. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)
docs.text:
Simulate the quantization during training — the forward pass uses fake quantized values (rounding injected), the backward pass uses the straight- through estimator (STEs around the rounding) so gradients still flow. The model learns weights that are robust to being rounded.

  • Pros: much better accuracy at low bit-widths.
  • Cons: needs the training pipeline, which streaming models (which learn online) already have — a natural fit.

docs.title: 3. Dynamic vs static quantization
docs.text:
• Static: ranges are fixed after calibration (from PTQ or QAT).
  • Dynamic: activations are quantized on the fly per layer using the actual observed range. More accurate, slightly more compute at inference.

docs.title: The memory math (useful to internalize)
docs.text:
Precision Bytes/value 1M params 1B params float32 4 4 MB 4 GB float16 / bfloat16 2 2 MB 2 GB int8 1 1 MB 1 GB int4 0.5 0.5 MB 500 MB int2 / 1.58-bit ~0.25 ~0.25 MB ~250 MB

Note: weights aren't the only cost. Activations and optimizer states (Adam keeps two float32 moments per parameter) also consume memory. For streaming models, the model is usually small; the bounded-memory constraint is about the whole system over infinite time.

docs.title: When quantization costs you
docs.text:
• Small models are more fragile. A large model has redundancy; a small streaming model has less slack, so the same rounding hurts more.
  • Outliers kill the range. If one weight is far outside the pack, the scale stretches and everything else loses precision. This is the reason "per-channel" and "outlier-aware" schemes exist.
  • The last layers hurt most. Output layers and softmax are sensitive to precision — often kept at higher precision.

docs.title: Streaming-specific angles (the part we care about)
docs.text:
This is where quantization meets the project:

  • Streaming models are small. They run on constrained devices with a permanent memory budget — exactly the profile quantization is built for.
  • The bounded-memory constraint is the constraint. Quantization is a direct lever on it: a 2-bit model is a fraction of the size of a float32 one, forever, not just at inference.
  • Online learning + QAT is a natural pair. QAT needs training-time simulation; streaming models are always training. A streaming model that keeps adapting at low precision is a coherent research direction.
  • Drift detection is numerical. Detectors watch error statistics over time. If quantization changes the error distribution, it changes what the detector sees — a real interaction worth studying.

docs.title: Tooling to know
docs.text:
• River — the streaming framework; supports linear, tree, neural models but quantization is not its focus.
  • PyTorch — torch.quantization (PTQ/QAT), torchao for low-bit work.
  • Hugging Face — bitsandbytes, GPTQ, AWQ for LLMs (the industry is pushing to 4-bit and below).
  • ONNX Runtime — int8 quantization for deployment.
  • keras / TF — tf.lite quantization for edge.

docs.title: Quick mental model
docs.text:
float32  --train-->  weights (full precision)
                          |
             PTQ: quantize after      QAT: simulate during
                          |
                     int8 / int4 / int2  weights + scale/zero-point
                          |
              smaller, faster, cheaper -- with a little accuracy loss

docs.title: Open questions for us
docs.text:
• Which models in River are worth quantizing — and does quantizing them break their online update rules (e.g., trees that store histograms)?
  • Does low-precision training change drift detection — either the detector's sensitivity or the model's adaptation speed?
  • Can QAT-style "robust to rounding" training make a streaming model more stable under drift, not just smaller?
  • Is there a streaming-specific quantization scheme — one that re-quantizes as the data distribution drifts?

docs.title: 03 — Bringing the two together: low-precision streaming models
docs.text: One-line version: streaming ML's bounded-memory, constrained-device, always-learning profile is exactly the profile quantization was built for — and the interesting research is not "quantize a transformer," it's "quantize the online loop and see what breaks."

docs.title: Why these two fit so well
docs.text:
Streaming ML and quantization have matching constraints:

Streaming constraint What it needs What quantization gives Bounded memory, forever Small model, small state 2–8× smaller weights & activations Runs on constrained devices Cheap compute Integer math, less memory traffic Always learning Adaptation without retraining cost QAT-style robustness at train time Drift detection on error stats Stable, accurate error signal A lever (and a risk) on that signal

The fit is structural, not incidental. A streaming model that must run forever on a small device under a fixed budget is the canonical quantization use case. The LLM world (4-bit models) is the loud version; streaming is the quiet one where it's arguably more natural.

docs.title: Concrete directions (what we could actually do)
Direction A — Quantize the streaming model, measure the drift behavior
docs.text:
Take a River model (e.g., linear.LogisticRegression, tree.HoeffdingTree, neural.MLP), quantize it (PTQ or QAT), and run it through the standard streaming loop with a drift detector. Measure:

  • Accuracy cost of quantization at 8-bit / 4-bit / 2-bit.
  • Memory saved — model size plus activations.
  • Drift detection behavior — does the detector fire at the same points? Does low precision make the error signal noisier (more false alarms) or smoother?

This is a clean, empirical, publishable-shaped result: "quantizing streaming models to X bits costs Y accuracy and changes drift detection in Z way."

docs.title: Direction B — Quantize the drift detector itself
docs.text: Drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley) track running statistics over the error stream. Quantize those statistics and ask: how much precision does a detector actually need before it stops detecting? This is a genuinely underexplored question — most quantization research targets models, not detectors.

docs.title: Direction C — QAT-style streaming: learn to be robust to rounding
docs.text: The insight: a streaming model is always training. Use quantization-aware training online — the model learns under simulated rounding, so it stays accurate at low precision while adapting to drift. The research question is whether "rounding-robust" learning also makes the model more stable under drift (fewer catastrophic resets, smoother adaptation).

docs.title: Direction D — Streaming-aware quantization: re-quantize as the data drifts
docs.text: Standard quantization fixes the scale/range once. But in a stream, the data distribution moves — so the optimal scale moves too. A scheme that re-calibrates ranges as drift is detected is a novel angle: quantization and drift detection collaborating instead of just coexisting.

docs.title: What's genuinely researchable (our honest filter)
docs.text:
For each direction, the question is: would a competent practitioner be able to answer this from existing docs, or is it open?

  • A is mostly implementation — a well-built experiment on known tools, with a measured result. Good for a first project; the contribution is the numbers and the analysis, not a new method.
  • B and C are genuinely open — no standard answers exist, and the setup (streaming + quantization) is niche enough that the results would be new.
  • D is speculative but high-value — needs the most care, and might be a stretch goal rather than a first target.

docs.title: The honest risk: quantization is mostly irrelevant to small models
docs.text:
The uncomfortable truth from the LLM world: quantization shines when models are large. A small streaming model (a few thousand parameters) is already tiny — cutting it from 40 KB to 10 KB may save nothing that matters, while the accuracy loss is relatively bigger (small models have less redundancy to absorb rounding).

So the research case for quantization in streaming is not "make it smaller." It's:

  1. The device reality — streaming models run on edge hardware (sensors, phones) where every bit and every watt counts, even for small models.
  2. The drift interaction — quantized models may drift-detect differently, which is a scientific question regardless of size.
  3. The always-training angle — QAT-in-the-loop is genuinely different from quantize-once-and-deploy.

If we want a project that's both honest and interesting: lead with the drift interaction (B/C), use the memory savings as the motivation, not the goal.

docs.title: How this connects to the existing project
docs.text:
• The project (see notes/ and research/) is about delayed labels and drift — how detectors degrade when ground truth arrives late.
  • Quantization adds a second axis of degradation: precision loss on top of label delay. "How do delayed labels + low precision interact?" is a question nobody has answered, and it's a natural extension of the current direction.
  • The River framework gives us the streaming loop; PyTorch gives us quantization; the intersection is where our contribution would live.

docs.title: Open questions (for the next exploration session)
docs.text:
• Which River models are quantizable with existing tools, and which break (trees with histograms, non-differentiable learners)?
  • How much precision does ADWIN/DDM actually need? (Direction B — quickest win, most novel per unit effort.)
  • Does QAT-online change the speed of adaptation to drift, not just the steady-state accuracy?
  • Is there a streaming library (or a way to hack River) that exposes the online update in a quantizable form?

docs.title: 03 — Why finance IS a streaming problem (the bridge)
docs.text: One-line version: live markets are the purest streaming ML problem that exists — data arrives one bar at a time, forever, the distribution drifts (regimes), and the ground truth arrives late (future returns). Everything the project has been studying applies to markets directly, with zero translation.

docs.title: The mapping is almost embarrassingly direct
docs.text:
Streaming ML concept Market equivalent How direct? Data stream, one sample at a time Price bars, one per interval Identical Concept drift Regime shifts (bull/bear, vol expansion) Identical mechanism Delayed labels Future returns realized after the decision Identical, worse Bounded memory Can't store the full tick history Identical constraint Prequential eval (test-then-train) Walk-forward, out-of-sample discipline Identical idea Model adaptation / reset Regime-aware retraining, model re-weighting Identical need Forgetting management A model stuck in the old regime trades badly Identical failure

The whole point of the project — "the model must notice when it becomes wrong and adapt" — is the entire job of a live trading model. A fund that doesn't adapt to regime is a fund that blows up. Markets are not an application of streaming ML; they are its natural habitat.

docs.title: The three-way intersection that makes this project special
docs.text:
The project has three threads. In markets, all three are live simultaneously:

  1. Streaming learning — the online loop (predict → score → learn) is exactly how a live model trades: predict next bar's move, act, learn from what actually happened.
  2. Concept drift / regime detection — drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley) are regime detectors wearing a different name. A drift alarm in a market model is a regime-change signal — actionable, not just diagnostic.
  3. Delayed labels — in trading, the label is the future return, and it is inherently delayed: you decide now, the outcome arrives later. The project's core research problem is not an edge case in trading — it's the definition of the trading problem.

This is the strongest possible fit: the research question the project is already chasing (how do delayed labels break streaming models?) is the exact question a live trading system faces every single bar.

docs.title: Direction A — Delayed labels in trading: the honest framing
docs.text: A trading model's label (future return) arrives after the trade. The project's delayed-label work applies verbatim: quantify how label delay degrades a streaming trading model's decisions, and whether drift detectors can still catch regime change when the error signal is stale.

docs.title: Direction B — Drift detection as regime detection
docs.text: Drift detectors as a trading signal, not just a warning: when ADWIN fires, the regime changed — what should the model do (reset, reweight recent data, shift to a different strategy)? This is the "adapt" side of the streaming loop given a concrete, financial meaning.

docs.title: Direction C — The quant + streaming + transformer triangle
docs.text: A model that combines: streaming adaptation (regime-aware learning), delayed labels (the honest trading constraint), and transformer-style representation (cross-sectional attention over assets, carefully used). The contribution is the combination, not any single piece — and it's a combination nobody has cleanly built.

docs.title: Direction D — The degenerate case nobody checks
docs.text: What happens to a streaming trading model when the label delay is longer than the regime? (E.g., labels arrive after the regime has already flipped.) If detectors can't keep up, the model systematically trades on stale truth — a clean, publishable negative result, in the spirit of the project's existing scope (notes/08-scope.md, idea/synopsis.md).

docs.title: The honest risks (keep these visible)
docs.text:
• Backtest overfitting is the #1 killer. Any strategy can be made to look great in hindsight. The disciplines in 02-quant-trading.md (walk-forward, costs, out-of-sample, multiple-testing honesty) are not optional.
  • Data quality is half the battle. Adjusted prices, survivorship-free universes, point-in-time fundamentals. Garbage data = confident garbage results.
  • The edge is small and decays. Even a good project's results will be modest. That's normal; the research value is in the mechanism (how delay and drift interact), not in claiming a money machine.
  • Costs decide everything. A backtest without realistic spread/slippage is fiction. Especially at bar-level frequencies.
  • "Quant" tempts shortcuts. A fake backtest with a great curve is the quant equivalent of a p-hacked result. Our hygiene is our credibility.

docs.title: The practical starting recipe
docs.text:
A minimal, honest, research-grade setup:

  1. Synthetic or free data first. Either generate a stream with known regimes (clean science: we control the ground truth), or use free daily bars (yfinance) / free crypto (ccxt). Synthetic first isolates the method; real data validates it.
  2. A streaming baseline. A River model (e.g., linear.LogisticRegression on engineered features) through the prequential loop, with a drift detector attached.
  3. A delayed-label regime. Feed labels with delay τ; measure how accuracy, drift detection, and simulated P&L degrade as τ grows.
  4. The bridge result. Show where the model breaks and whether drift detection can rescue it — the same shape as the project's existing delayed- label research, but on a market-flavored stream.

docs.title: Open questions (next exploration session)
docs.text:
• Synthetic regime stream vs real market data first — which gives a cleaner research answer?
  • Which strategy family (momentum / mean reversion / stat-arb) maps most cleanly onto a streaming model with delayed labels?
  • Do drift detectors meaningfully predict regime changes in markets, or only confirm them after the fact?
  • What's the minimal honest cost model (spread + slippage + fees) for a bar-frequency backtest?

docs.title: Scope — The Delay Tax
docs.text:
Working title: The Delay Tax: drift detection and adaptation when labels are late, partial, and biased.

Status: scope locked — pending only the teacher-dependent questions in §12. This document supersedes notes/08-scope.md (kept as the draft it was). It consolidates the research phase (now complete) into a single reference.

Thesis spine: Streaming ML works in simulation. Does it work in production? Build the system, find where it breaks, fix one thing properly.

The one thing we fix: production labels arrive late, partially, and selectively — and the field's detectors, metrics, and evaluation protocol quietly assume they arrive instantly, completely, and unbiased.

docs.title: 1. The problem in one page
docs.text:
Streaming ML rests on a hidden assumption:

Sample x arrives, and its true label y arrives with it. The model predicts, is immediately told whether it was right, and learns.

That assumption is false in every real deployment:

  • Fraud: a transaction is approved now; the chargeback lands 30–90 days later.
  • Ads: an impression is served now; the conversion arrives next week.
  • Intrusion: a login is flagged now; the analyst verdict comes later, or never.

Follow the consequences, because they cascade:

  1. Detection is late. Drift detectors watch the error stream. If labels are late, the error stream is late, so drift is detected only after the labels catch up — meanwhile the model is silently wrong.
  2. Evaluation breaks first. Prequential scoring (predict → score → learn) requires the label in the same tick. Under delay you cannot even measure your own accuracy in real time, so the field's own instrument for success fails in the setting the field claims to serve.
  3. Adaptation compounds the error. While labels are pending, the model keeps learning stale samples — after a drift, it is actively reinforcing the pre-drift concept.
  4. The label process itself misbehaves. Labels arrive in bursts, out of order, or only for flagged cases. That injects autocorrelation and selection bias into the error stream — which detectors misread as drift (false alarms) or miss entirely.

The research phase (done — §2) confirms this is a real, under-populated gap, not a tutorial topic.

docs.title: 2. What the research established
docs.text:
Findings from research/01-landscape.md and research/02-delayed-labels.md.

The gap is real and open. The delayed/partial-label literature is fragmented — terminology alone spans verification latency, delayed labelling, label latency, extreme verification latency, partially labelled streams — and no widely accepted benchmark or protocol exists. The most relevant syntheses are Gomes et al. (2022, ACM CSUR survey on delayed partially labelled streams) and a dedicated 2026 experimental survey in Digital Signal Processing. The area is active but not converged: no canonical problem formulation, no dominant method.

Well-established (safe to build on):

  • Prequential evaluation is the right protocol for ordered streams; random train/test splits are invalid (temporal leakage).
  • No drift detector dominates. Delay / false-alarm / missed-detection trade-offs depend on drift type, noise, imbalance, and configuration.
  • ARF, SRP, Leveraging Bagging, HAT are the strong adaptive baselines; Hoeffding Tree is the canonical static one.
  • Synthetic generators give ground-truth drift → detection delay is computable; real streams give external validity but unknown drift positions.
  • Elec2 has known temporal-autocorrelation problems (a "no change" baseline and Kappa+ must be reported; accuracy alone overstates learning).

The specific holes this project targets:

  • Detector-level degradation under delay is unquantified. There is no clean curve of detection delay vs label latency, or false-alarm rate vs label coverage. Existing work studies classifiers or active-learning systems, not the detector in isolation.
  • No standard confirmation protocol combining a label-free early warning with delayed supervised confirmation. Research names this architecture explicitly as a promising, unbuilt direction.
  • The operational cost of continual learning is under-measured. Papers rarely report the latency, memory, and divergence costs of adaptation — the field is populated by ML researchers, not infrastructure people. This is our home turf.

The bet, confirmed: the two strongest gaps (delayed labels, operational cost) both lie exactly where the field's standard assumptions diverge most sharply from production reality — and neither requires deriving novel algorithms.

docs.title: 4. Research questions
docs.text:
Three questions, one spine. Each is falsifiable and measurable.

  • RQ1 (baseline, guaranteed). Under controlled synthetic drift — sudden, gradual, incremental, recurring — how do ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, KSWIN compare on detection delay, false-alarm rate, and missed detections, and how do adaptive models (HAT, ARF) recover compared to static ones (Hoeffding Tree, Naive Bayes)? This is the control condition: "what the literature says happens."

  • RQ2 (system, novel-by-measurement). What does running continual learning as a real service cost — p50/p99 prediction latency during adaptation, throughput ceiling, memory growth, checkpoint/restart cost, and how fast do scaled-out replicas diverge? Where does it break first?

  • RQ3 (contribution, the gap). By how much does delayed, partial, and selective labelling degrade drift detection and adaptation — exactly — and can a hybrid detector (label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation) recover the immediate-label baseline, or come provably close?

The math (§6) turns RQ3 from "degrades a lot" into four specific, provable claims about how and by what factor it degrades.

docs.text:

docs.title: Chapter 2 — The system (infrastructure spine)
docs.text:
A real, containerised, reproducible continual-learning service:

  • Event source: Redis Streams (zero-JVM friction) or Kafka/Redpanda — decided in Phase 2, pinned early.
  • Model service: POST /predict + a learning consumer; the same model that serves is the model that learns, one pass.
  • Live drift monitor (a real service, not an offline script).
  • Prometheus metrics + Grafana dashboard; load generator to push it until it breaks.
  • Versioned, seeded, reproducible end to end (docker-compose).

Deliverable: the running system + the "reality tax" chapter — the operational cost the literature never reports: adaptation latency cost, replica divergence, backpressure behaviour (drop learning or drop serving?), restart/recovery cost.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — The delayed-label contribution (the research)
docs.text:
The core novel work, built on Chapter 1's harness:

  1. Delay regimes — fixed (d = 10/100/1000), stochastic (geometric mean d), partial (label probability p ∈ {1, .5, .1}), selective (only "flagged" samples labelled — the endogenous-bias case).
  2. Measure the degradation — detector delay/FP/FN and model recovery vs. the d = 0 control, at detector level and downstream accuracy level.
  3. Build the hybrid — label-free early warning on the input stream P(X), supervised confirmation on the delayed error stream, with an explicit confirmation protocol (warning within tolerance window, confirm on labels).
  4. Evaluate — hybrid vs. naive-delayed-supervised vs. label-free-only vs. immediate-label control; test the §6 lemmas empirically.

Fallback (safe): if the hybrid does not beat the naive baselines, that is a publishable negative result — "we quantified how much delayed labels break existing methods and why the obvious fix is insufficient." Chapter 3 cannot fail, which is why it is the bet.

docs.title: 6. The mathematical angle — the delay tax
docs.text: The project's theory. Deliberately applied math — probability, concentration bounds, hypothesis testing — squarely within reach, and every claim is empirically verifiable in Chapter 3. This is not a bet on novel theory; it is a bet on formalising the obvious correctly and measuring the constants.

docs.title: 6.1 The formal setting
docs.text:
Let the concept be C_t ∈ {C₀, C₁}, with a real drift at time τ. The model predicts ŷ_t; the instantaneous error is

e_t = 1[ŷ_t ≠ y_t].

Under immediate labelling a detector observes (e_t) in real time and alarms at a stopping time T — the classical quickest detection problem (Page 1954; Lorden 1971 minimax; Shiryaev). The field's "detection delay vs false-alarm trade-off" is the empirical image of Lorden's criterion: minimise worst-case delay subject to a false-alarm constraint (average run length).

Under label delay, each error e_t becomes observable only at t + L_t, for a latency process L_t (fixed, stochastic, or driven by a review policy). The detector's filtration is

F_t = σ( e_s : s + L_s ≤ t ).

This is quickest detection with delayed observations — a variant the literature has barely touched. Four claims follow, each provable with undergraduate/early-grad probability and each with a Phase-3 experiment attached.

docs.title: 6.2 Lemma 1 — The reaction floor
docs.text:
Any detector that observes only the error stream cannot alarm before the drift's labels arrive: T ≥ τ + L_τ pointwise, hence E[T] ≥ τ + E[L].

Proof idea: e_τ ∉ F_t for t < τ + L_τ; the alarm is a stopping time w.r.t. F_t. Trivial — and that triviality is the point: it is a hard lower bound on detection delay that no algorithm can beat, independent of how good the detector is. It converts "you detect drift a month late" from a complaint into a theorem.

Experiment: for each delay regime, measure detection delay of every detector and confirm it never dips below d (fixed case) / E[L] (stochastic case).

docs.title: 6.3 Lemma 2 — The power loss (effective sample size)
docs.text:
Under stochastic per-sample delay, a windowed detector's confidence band widens by the factor 1/√p, where p is the fraction of the window's labels that have arrived — equivalently, its minimum detectable mean shift grows from Δ_min ∝ 1/√W to Δ_min ∝ 1/√(pW).

Proof idea: the observed error stream is a randomly thinned version of the true one; a window of W arrivals contains only ~pW distinct fresh errors, and any mean-estimate test (Hoeffding/CLT based — ADWIN's threshold is a constant times √(ln(1/δ)/W)) has standard error σ/√n with n = pW. Delay degrades sensitivity by the factor 1/√p — a clean, checkable constant.

Experiment: for p ∈ {1, .5, .25, .1} and a fixed drift magnitude, measure ADWIN's detection delay; verify it tracks the predicted 1/√p inflation.

docs.title: 6.4 Lemma 3 — False-alarm inflation under batch arrival
docs.text:
If labels arrive in batches of size b, the observed error stream inherits intra-batch correlation ρ > 0, inflating the variance of the estimated error rate by 1 + (b−1)ρ (the standard clustered-data factor). Detectors calibrated for i.i.d. errors then fire spuriously: DDM's alarm rate rises above its nominal α.

Proof idea: the variance of a clustered sample mean; DDM's thresholds assume e_t independent Bernoulli. Batch arrival is exactly what daily/weekly label reconciliation does in production.

Experiment: feed detectors a delayed-error stream under batch arrival with no actual drift; measure FP rate vs. b.

docs.title: 6.5 Lemma 4 — The identifiability ceiling (why the hybrid is maximal)
docs.text:
If P(X) is unchanged but P(Y|X) differs between concepts (pure posterior drift), no label-free detector has any power: the likelihood ratio of the X-observations is identically 1, so the KL divergence between the two hypotheses is 0.

Proof idea: the X-marginal cannot distinguish joints that share it. This is the formal content of Žliobaitė's detectability result (2010) — and it justifies the hybrid by construction: label-free signals can only be an early warning; confirmation requires labels. The hybrid is the information-maximal architecture available, which is the strongest design statement a scoping document can make.

Experiment: construct a generator with pure posterior drift (e.g. flip P(y|x) in a region while keeping the marginal fixed); confirm label-free detectors miss it while the hybrid's delayed confirmation catches it.

docs.title: 6.6 What the math is for
docs.text:
• It gives the report a theory section with four lemmas it can actually prove, each with an empirical counterpart — rigorous, but no dependence on novel analysis (a systems-strength fit).
  • It converts Chapter 3's headline from a table of numbers into a narrative: detection is bounded below by the reaction floor, weakened by 1/√p, distorted by batch autocorrelation, and capped by identifiability — and the hybrid is the best possible response.

docs.title: 6.7 Explicitly not in scope (math)
docs.text: • No new change-detection algorithms, no regret bounds, no online convex optimisation, no statistical learning theory, no proofs of novel theorems beyond the four lemmas above. If a lemma resists a clean proof, it degrades to an empirical claim — the project survives.
