docs.title: The Delay Tax
docs.text:
Drift detection and adaptation when labels are late, partial, and biased

Project synopsis — streaming (online) machine learning with a systems engineering spine

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
Almost all machine learning assumes the dataset is a finished object: it sits on disk, you load it, you split it, you fit a model, and you are done. Streaming machine learning drops that assumption. Data arrives one sample at a time, potentially forever, and is too large or too fast to store. The model must learn incrementally, in a single pass, using bounded memory — and because the world that generates the data keeps changing, it must also notice when it becomes wrong and adapt. That last part, concept drift, is the research problem.

This project targets a specific, under-studied failure of the field's core assumption. Nearly every paper on drift detection and adaptation assumes labels arrive instantly, completely, and without bias alongside each sample. In production they do not: fraud is confirmed 30–90 days after the fact, ad conversions arrive a week later, analyst verdicts sometimes never come. This project asks what happens when that assumption breaks — formally, measurably, and end to end — and whether a practical remedy exists.

The project has three parts, in increasing order of novelty:

  1. Baseline. A rigorous detector-and-adaptation benchmark under controlled synthetic drift (the field's "what happens" reference numbers).
  2. System. A real, containerised continual-learning service — the same model that serves predictions is the model that learns — with live drift monitoring, measured for the operational costs the literature never reports: adaptation latency, memory growth, replica divergence, recovery cost.
  3. Contribution. A formal model of delayed, partial, and selective labelling as a delay tax — four provable lemmas describing exactly how detection degrades — plus a hybrid detector that pairs a label-free early warning with delayed supervised confirmation, evaluated against the baseline.

The mathematical contribution is deliberately applied: concentration bounds, quickest-detection theory, and hypothesis testing, all of which can be verified empirically. The systems contribution is measurement the field lacks because the field is populated by ML researchers rather than infrastructure engineers. Every chapter has a survivable failure mode; no single bet can sink the project.

docs.title: 2. Background: what streaming machine learning is
2.1 The three constraints
docs.text:
Standard batch learning rests on an assumption so common it is usually invisible: the data is finite, available all at once, and drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution that will not change. Streaming ML drops all three parts. Any algorithm that claims to be a streaming algorithm must respect three hard constraints:

  1. Single pass. Each sample is seen exactly once; you cannot go back and revisit sample #5.
  2. Bounded memory. Memory usage must not grow with the number of samples seen. A model that processed ten billion rows must occupy roughly the same space as one that processed ten thousand.
  3. Bounded time per sample. Processing must keep up with the arrival rate, or the learner falls behind forever.

A useful test: if this ran for a year without restarting, would it still work? If the answer involves "well, memory would…", it is not a streaming algorithm.

docs.title: 2.2 Why it matters
docs.text:
There are two distinct motivations, often confused:

  • The engineering motivation — scale and latency. The data does not fit in RAM, arrives too fast, or needs a model updated now rather than after tonight's retraining job. Clickstreams, sensors, network packets, financial ticks.
  • The statistical motivation — the world changes. Even if the data did fit in memory, a model trained on last year's data may be wrong about this year, because the process generating the data has changed. Batch learning has no mechanism to notice this. Streaming learning does.

The statistical motivation is the spine of this project. In streaming ML, the central question is not "how accurate is my model?" — a single number — but "how does accuracy behave over time?" — a curve. Accuracy becomes a time series; drops, recoveries, and recovery speed are the interesting phenomena. Almost every good figure in this field plots something against "number of samples seen."

docs.title: 2.3 The River framework
docs.text:
River is "scikit-learn for data streams" — the standard Python library for online machine learning (Montiel et al., JMLR 2021; merger of creme and scikit-multiflow). It is the instrument for this project, not the subject. Its core API is four methods:

model.learn_one(x, y)        # update the model with ONE labelled sample
model.predict_one(x)         # predict a label for ONE sample
model.predict_proba_one(x)   # predict class probabilities
metric.update(y, y_pred)     # update a running score — TRUE label first

where x is a Python dict — a deliberate design choice that lets features appear, disappear, or stay sparse without reshaping. River ships the models this project needs (Hoeffding trees, adaptive forests, linear models), the drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, KSWIN), synthetic generators with ground-truth drift, real datasets, and incrementally-updated metrics.

docs.title: 3.1 Definition
docs.text:
A model estimates a joint distribution \(P(X, y)\), usually decomposed as \(P(y \mid X) \cdot P(X)\). Concept drift is when that distribution changes over time:

\[P_t(X, y) \neq P_{t+\Delta}(X, y).\]

The world that produced the training data is not the world being predicted in.

docs.title: 3.2 Two flavours that matter
docs.text:
• Real drift — \(P(y \mid X)\) changes. The input–output relationship itself changed, which genuinely breaks the model.
  • Virtual drift / covariate shift — \(P(X)\) changes while \(P(y \mid X)\) holds. The inputs have shifted but the rule is intact; accuracy may not suffer.

The distinction drives detector design: detectors that watch the input distribution fire on virtual drift (false alarms from the model's point of view); detectors that watch the error stream only fire on drift that actually costs accuracy. This tension is central to this project.

docs.title: 3.3 Types by shape over time
docs.text:
The standard taxonomy, in terms of which concept is active:

SUDDEN (abrupt)         GRADUAL                 INCREMENTAL             RECURRING

 ────┐                   ──┐ ┌┐ ┌──┐             ──╲                 ──┐   ┌──┐   ┌──
     │                     └─┘└─┘  └───            ╲___                └───┘  └───┘
     └────────                                        ╲──

concept A flips        A and B interleave,      A morphs smoothly     A and B alternate
to concept B           B wins over time         into B                (e.g. seasonal)
instantly
  • Sudden / abrupt — an instantaneous switch; easiest to detect, most damaging.
  • Gradual — a transition window during which samples come from A or B with shifting probability; hard to detect, because error rises slowly and noisily.
  • Incremental — the concept deforms continuously through intermediate states.
  • Recurring — old concepts return (day/night, seasons). Forgetting the old concept is actively wasteful, motivating archive-and-restore approaches.

There is also the blip — a one-off anomaly that is not drift. A good detector must not fire on it. This is the stability–plasticity trade-off: react fast enough to catch real drift, but not so fast that noise triggers a reset.

docs.title: 3.4 How detectors work
docs.text:
Most detectors do not look at the features at all. They watch a one-dimensional stream of the model's errors (\(1\) = wrong, \(0\) = right) and ask: has this stream's mean changed?

Detector Idea Notes DDM (2004) Track error rate \(p\) and its std \(s\); warn at \(p + s > p_{min} + 2s_{min}\), alarm at \(3s\) Simple, cheap; weak on gradual drift EDDM (2006) Track the distance between errors instead Designed to fix DDM's gradual-drift weakness ADWIN (2007) Adaptive window; when two sub-windows have statistically different means, drop the older part Rigorous guarantees, no window-size parameter; the de-facto standard Page-Hinkley (1954) CUSUM-family: accumulates deviation from the running mean Classical sequential analysis; threshold-sensitive KSWIN (2020) Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between a sliding window and a reference Non-parametric, distribution-based

The trade-off is always the same: sensitivity vs. false alarms. Tune a detector to catch drift faster and it fires on noise. That trade-off curve is measurable, and measuring it is part of this project's baseline chapter.

docs.title: 3.5 How models adapt
docs.text:
Three responses to drift:

  1. Blind adaptation (no detector). Keep learning and let recent data outweigh old data — sliding windows, fading factors, a learning rate that never reaches zero. Always-on, simple, but adapts slowly to sudden drift and permanently discards old-but-still-valid knowledge.
  2. Informed adaptation (detector + reaction). Run an explicit detector; when it fires, reset the model, retrain on a recent buffer, or swap in a background model trained in parallel. Reacts sharply, but a false alarm throws away a good model.
  3. Ensembles. Keep a pool of models, weight them by recent performance, drop the worst, add fresh ones. Drift handling is emergent. This is what Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) does, and it is the strongest general baseline.

The deep question — whether explicit detection actually beats passive adaptation — is contested in the literature, and this project measures it directly in its baseline chapter.

docs.title: 3.6 How a streaming model is evaluated
docs.text:
Random train/test splitting is invalid for ordered streams: order is meaningful, there is no "end" to hold out, and a random split leaks future information into training. The standard protocol is prequential evaluation (test-then-train):

for x, y in stream:
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)   # model has NEVER seen this sample
    metric.update(y, y_pred)        # so this score is honest
    model.learn_one(x, y)           # now let it learn

Every sample is used for testing and training, in that order — nothing wasted, nothing leaked. Cumulative metrics converge and hide drift; rolling metrics over a recent window reveal dips and recoveries. The accuracy-over-time curve is a result in itself: dip depth and recovery slope are what get compared.

Two evaluation facts anchor this project:

  • Memory and per-sample time are first-class results in streaming ML, not afterthoughts — the field's whole claim is bounded resources.
  • Statistical rigour is expected: multiple seeds reported as mean ± std, fixed experimental budgets, and the Friedman test + Nemenyi post-hoc with a critical-difference diagram (Demšar, 2006) as the accepted convention for comparing many methods over many datasets.

docs.title: 4. The problem: labels are late, partial, and biased
4.1 The hidden assumption
docs.text:
Every paper in the field's canonical evaluation loop assumes the label y arrives in the same tick as the sample x. The detector watches the error stream \(e_t\) in real time; the evaluator scores each prediction immediately; the learner updates immediately. In production, none of this holds:

  • A fraud model approves a transaction now and learns the truth 30–90 days later, when the chargeback lands.
  • An ad model serves an impression now and learns the conversion next week.
  • An intrusion model flags a login now and receives the analyst's verdict later — or never.
  • Labels arrive in batches (overnight reconciliation), out of order, and only for flagged cases — which makes the observed errors a biased sample of true errors.

docs.title: 4.2 The cascade of consequences
docs.text:
Follow the consequence of a late label; it is not obvious and it is nasty:

  1. Detection is late. A drift detector works by watching the error stream. If the error stream is \(d\) days late, drift is detected \(d\) days after it happened — and the model has been silently wrong for a month.
  2. Evaluation breaks first. Prequential evaluation cannot score a prediction whose label has not arrived. The instrument the entire field uses to measure success does not work in the setting the field claims to serve: you cannot even measure your own accuracy in real time.
  3. Adaptation compounds the error. While labels are pending, the model keeps learning from stale samples. After a drift, it is not just slow to adapt — it is actively reinforcing the pre-drift concept with outdated data.
  4. The label process itself misbehaves. Batch arrival injects autocorrelation into the error stream; selective labelling injects bias. Detectors calibrated for i.i.d. errors misread both — false alarms, or missed drift entirely.

docs.title: 4.3 Why this is a research gap, not a tutorial topic
docs.text:
The research phase of this project (a deep literature survey; see the reference list, §12) established three things:

  • The area is active but fragmented. The delayed/partial-label literature spans roughly 2008–2026, but terminology alone is split across verification latency, delayed labelling, label latency, extreme verification latency, and partially labelled streams — and the same problem is studied separately in semi-supervised streaming, stream active learning, and positive-unlabelled learning. No widely accepted benchmark or evaluation protocol exists.
  • The specific degradation is unquantified. Papers show that delayed labels harm classifiers or active-learning systems, but almost none isolates the detector and produces a clean curve of detection delay vs. label latency, or false-alarm rate vs. label coverage.
  • The confirmation protocol is unbuilt. Research explicitly names "a two-stage detector: label-free alarm, delayed supervised confirmation, calibrated action" as a promising, unbuilt architecture. This project builds exactly that.

The most relevant prior syntheses: Gomes et al. (2022), the ACM Computing Surveys survey on semi-supervised learning for delayed partially labelled streams; and a 2026 experimental survey on concept-drift detection in delayed and partially labelled streams (Digital Signal Processing). Both confirm the gap this project targets.

docs.title: 5. Research questions
docs.text:
Three questions, one spine. Each is falsifiable and measurable.

  • RQ1 — Baseline (guaranteed results). Under controlled synthetic drift — sudden, gradual, incremental, recurring — how do the standard detectors (ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, KSWIN) compare on detection delay, false-alarm rate, and missed detections; and how do adaptive models (Hoeffding Adaptive Tree, Adaptive Random Forest) recover relative to static ones (plain Hoeffding Tree, Naive Bayes)? This is the control condition: the idealised numbers the field's papers assume, measured with our own rigour.

  • RQ2 — System (novel by measurement). What does running continual learning as a real service cost — p50/p99 prediction latency during adaptation, throughput ceiling, memory growth, checkpoint/restart cost, and how fast do scaled-out replicas diverge from each other? Where does it break first?

  • RQ3 — Contribution (the gap). By how much — exactly — does delayed, partial, and selective labelling degrade drift detection and adaptation? Can a hybrid detector (label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation) recover the immediate-label baseline, or come provably close? Do the four lemmas of §6 hold empirically?

docs.title: 6. The mathematical angle: the delay tax
docs.text: The project's theory. It formalises "delayed labels are bad" into four provable claims about how and by what factor detection degrades. The mathematics is deliberately applied — probability, concentration bounds, hypothesis testing, classical quickest detection — every lemma has an attached experiment, and none requires novel analysis.

docs.title: 6.1 The formal setting
docs.text:
Let the concept be \(C_t \in \{C_0, C_1\}\) with a real drift at time \(\tau\). The model predicts \(\hat{y}_t\); the instantaneous error is

\[e_t = \mathbb{1}[\hat{y}_t \neq y_t].\]

Immediate labelling. The detector observes \((e_t)\) in real time and raises an alarm at a stopping time \(T\). This is the classical quickest detection problem (Page 1954; Lorden 1971; Shiryaev). The field's "detection delay vs. false-alarm trade-off" is the empirical image of Lorden's minimax criterion: minimise worst-case detection delay subject to a false-alarm constraint (average run length between false alarms).

Delayed labelling. Each error \(e_t\) becomes observable only at time \(t + L_t\), where \(L_t\) is a latency process — fixed (\(L_t = d\)), stochastic (e.g. geometric with mean \(d\)), or driven by a review policy (only flagged samples are ever labelled). The detector's information set at time \(t\) is the filtration

\[\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma\big( e_s : s + L_s \le t \big).\]

This is quickest detection with delayed observations — a variant the literature has barely touched. The four lemmas follow from this setting.

docs.title: 6.2 Lemma 1 — The reaction floor
docs.text:
Any detector that observes only the error stream cannot alarm before the drift's labels arrive: \(T \ge \tau + L_\tau\) pointwise, hence \(\mathbb{E}[T] \ge \tau + \mathbb{E}[L]\).

Proof idea. The first error containing information about the new concept is \(e_\tau\), and it enters \(\mathcal{F}_t\) only at \(t = \tau + L_\tau\). The alarm is a stopping time with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_t\), so it cannot precede that information. Trivial — and that triviality is the point: it is a hard lower bound that no algorithm can beat, independent of detector quality. It converts "you detect drift a month late" from a complaint into a theorem.

Experiment. For each delay regime, measure every detector's detection delay and confirm it never dips below \(d\) (fixed) or \(\mathbb{E}[L]\) (stochastic).

docs.title: 6.3 Lemma 2 — The power loss
docs.text:
With only a fraction \(p\) of labels arriving, a windowed detector's sensitivity degrades by the factor \(1/\sqrt{p}\): its minimum detectable mean shift grows from \(\Delta_{\min} \propto 1/\sqrt{W}\) to \(\Delta_{\min} \propto 1/\sqrt{pW}\).

Proof idea. The observed error stream is a randomly thinned version of the true one: a window of \(W\) arrivals yields only ~\(pW\) distinct fresh errors. Any mean-estimate test has standard error \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\) with \(n = pW\) (Hoeffding / CLT-based; ADWIN's threshold is a constant times \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/W}\)). Thinning inflates the standard error by \(1/\sqrt{p}\).

Experiment. For label coverage \(p \in \{1, .5, .25, .1\}\) and a fixed drift magnitude, measure ADWIN's detection delay and verify it tracks the predicted \(1/\sqrt{p}\) inflation.

docs.title: 6.4 Lemma 3 — False-alarm inflation under batch arrival
docs.text:
If labels arrive in batches of size \(b\), the observed error stream inherits intra-batch correlation \(\rho > 0\), inflating the variance of the estimated error rate by the clustered-data factor \(1 + (b-1)\rho\). Detectors calibrated for i.i.d. errors then fire spuriously: DDM's alarm rate rises above its nominal level \(\alpha\).

Proof idea. The variance of a clustered sample mean carries the standard design effect \(1 + (b-1)\rho\). DDM's thresholds assume independent Bernoulli errors. Batch arrival — exactly what overnight or weekly label reconciliation does in production — violates that assumption, so the detector sees "drift" in pure noise.

Experiment. Feed detectors a delayed-error stream under batch arrival with no actual drift; measure false-alarm rate vs. batch size \(b\).

docs.title: 6.5 Lemma 4 — The identifiability ceiling
docs.text:
If \(P(X)\) is unchanged but \(P(y \mid X)\) differs between concepts (pure posterior drift), no label-free detector has any power: the likelihood ratio of the observed \(X\)-stream is identically 1, so the KL divergence between the two hypotheses is 0.

Proof idea. The marginal \(P(X)\) cannot distinguish between two joints that share it. Formally, the two candidate distributions over \(X\)-observations are identical, so no test can have power above its size. This is the formal content of Žliobaitė's detectability analysis (2010) — and it justifies the hybrid by construction: label-free signals can only ever be an early warning; confirmation requires labels. The hybrid of §8 is the information-maximal architecture available, which is the strongest design statement a scoping document can make.

Experiment. Construct a generator with pure posterior drift (flip \(P(y \mid X)\) in a region while keeping the marginal fixed); confirm label-free detectors miss it while the hybrid's delayed confirmation catches it.

docs.title: 6.6 What the mathematics is for
docs.text:
The lemmas give the report a theory section that is genuinely provable — each with an empirical counterpart — without betting the project on novel analysis. They convert Chapter 3's headline from a table of numbers into a narrative:

Detection under delay is bounded below by the reaction floor, weakened by \(1/\sqrt{p}\), distorted by batch autocorrelation, and capped by identifiability — and the hybrid is the best possible response.

Explicitly out of mathematical scope: new change-detection algorithms, regret bounds, online convex optimisation, statistical learning theory, and any theorem beyond the four lemmas. If a lemma resists a clean proof, it degrades to an empirical claim with a simulation study — the project survives either way.

docs.title: 7.1 Purpose
docs.text: Everything later is measured against "what the literature says happens." Chapter 1 produces those idealised numbers ourselves, with documented rigour, so that Chapter 3 can show reality is worse.

docs.title: 7.2 The run matrix
docs.text: Axis Values Drift type sudden (SEA), incremental (Hyperplane), gradual (RandomRBF), recurring (ConceptDriftStream composition) Detector ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, KSWIN Model Hoeffding Tree (static), Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (adaptive), ARF (ensemble), Logistic Regression (blind/passive) Detector metrics detection delay, false-positive rate, missed detections, MTFA / MTD Model metrics dip depth, recovery time, rolling accuracy, memory, throughput Rigour ≥ 10 seeds, fixed stream length (~100k), fixed drift positions, mean ± std, Friedman + Nemenyi

docs.title: 7.3 Detector metrics — precise definitions
docs.text:
Detector metrics require known ground-truth drift points, which is why synthetic streams are non-negotiable for this part:

Metric Definition Good value Detection delay samples between true drift and first alarm low False positives (FP) alarms with no drift nearby low Missed detections (FN) drift points with no alarm within a tolerance window low MTFA mean time between false alarms high MTD mean time to detection low Recovery time samples until rolling accuracy returns to pre-drift level low

A tolerance window must be defined explicitly: a drift at index 5000 with an alarm at 5040 is a successful detection with delay 40; an alarm at 9000 is a false positive plus a missed detection. Papers vary; stating and justifying the window is a mark of rigour.

The central finding to expect: no detector wins on all three of delay, FP, and FN. Sensitivity trades against false alarms. Showing that trade-off with real numbers is a legitimate result — and it becomes the baseline against which the hybrid is judged.

docs.title: 7.4 Deliverable
docs.text: A reusable, config-driven, seeded experiment harness (one runner serves both Chapter 1 and Chapter 3), plus the first real results: trade-off tables, accuracy-over-time curves, and statistical comparisons.

docs.title: 8. Chapter 3 — The delayed-label contribution (the research)
docs.text: Chapter 2, the system, is described in §9; Chapter 3 is presented here because it is the intellectual heart of the project.

docs.title: 8.1 Step 1 — The delay regimes
docs.text:
Labels are withheld from the baseline streams according to explicit observation processes:

Regime Process Production story Fixed delay \(L_t = d\), for \(d \in \{10, 100, 1000\}\) samples Batch reporting on a fixed schedule Stochastic delay \(L_t \sim\) Geometric(mean \(d\)) Variable human/queue latency Partial labelling label arrives with probability \(p \in \{1, .5, .1\}\) Only some events ever get confirmed Selective labelling only samples the model flagged get labelled "Only flagged cases are reviewed" — the biased case

The selective regime is the subtle one: it is not mere label scarcity but an endogenous observation policy, because the probability of being labelled depends on the model's own prediction. Any detector trained on those labels estimates the review policy, not the deployed model.

docs.title: 8.2 Step 2 — Measure the degradation
docs.text:
For every regime, re-run the Chapter 1 matrix and compare against the \(d = 0\) control, at two levels:

  • Detector level: how do detection delay, FP rate, and missed-detection rate change with \(d\) and \(p\)? This is the clean, largely-unpublished curve the field lacks — and it is exactly where the lemmas live.
  • Downstream level: how does the model's accuracy-over-time curve degrade? Dip depth, recovery time, and whether the model ever returns to baseline.

docs.title: 8.3 Step 3 — Build the hybrid
docs.text:
The hybrid is a two-stage architecture:

input stream x_t ──► label-free early warning (monitors P(X))
                        │
                        ▼
                   "possible drift"   (fast, but fires on virtual drift too)
                        │
                        ▼
        delayed error stream e_{t-d} ──► supervised confirmation
                        │
                        ▼
              confirmed alarm → adaptation (reset / retrain / swap)
  • Stage 1 (label-free, immediate): monitors the input distribution \(P(X)\) (windowed two-sample tests, e.g. KS / MMD-style statistics). Fires early — possibly on harmless virtual drift — but provides a warning within a tolerance window.
  • Stage 2 (supervised, delayed): confirmation from the error stream once the delayed labels arrive. A confirmed alarm triggers adaptation; an unconfirmed warning is revoked (with the false-alarm cost explicitly recorded).

The design is not ad hoc: Lemma 4 shows stage 1 cannot confirm, and Lemma 1 shows stage 2 cannot be early. The hybrid is the only architecture that is both early and reliable, given the information available.

docs.title: 8.4 Step 4 — Evaluate
docs.text: Compare four systems on the full delay matrix: (a) naive delayed-supervised detector, (b) label-free only, (c) the hybrid, (d) the immediate-label control from Chapter 1. Test the lemmas empirically; verify the \(1/\sqrt{p}\) factor and the batch-correlation inflation with real measurements.

docs.title: 8.5 The failsafe
docs.text: If the hybrid does not beat the naive baselines, that is a complete, publishable negative result: "we quantified exactly how delayed labels break existing methods, and showed why the obvious fix is insufficient." Lemmas 1–3 hold regardless and remain the contribution. Chapter 3 cannot fail — which is precisely why it is the bet.

docs.title: 9.1 What is built
docs.text:
A real, containerised, reproducible continual-learning service — the part that makes this a major project rather than a notebook:

events ──► event stream (Redis Streams / Kafka) ──► learning consumer
                                                        │
                                                        ▼
                     POST /predict ◄── model service (serves AND learns, one pass)
                                                        │
                                                        ▼
                          live drift monitor (a real service, not a script)
                                                        │
                                                        ▼
                     Prometheus metrics ──► Grafana dashboard
                     load generator ──► pushes the system until something breaks

The defining property: the same model that serves predictions is the model that learns — not a served snapshot and a separate offline trainer. That is what makes the operational questions real.

docs.title: 9.2 What is measured (the "reality tax")
docs.text:
• Adaptation cost. What do model resets, background retraining, and drift reactions do to p50/p99 prediction latency and throughput? What happens when a reset coincides with peak load?
  • Replica divergence. Scale the service to 3 replicas. Each learns from the events it happens to consume; they diverge. How fast? Which one is "the model"? Nobody has a clean answer to horizontal scaling of a stateful learner — measuring the divergence is itself a publishable observation.
  • Backpressure. When consumers fall behind, do we drop learning or drop serving? What is the cost of each?
  • Recovery. How expensive is checkpointing and restarting model state? A batch model is an immutable artifact you can roll back; a streaming model has no artifact. What does recovery even mean?

docs.title: 9.3 Why it is a research chapter, not a demo
docs.text: The field evaluates by replaying a CSV in a single Python process: labels arrive instantly and always, no network, no queue, no concurrency, no backpressure, and success is measured almost entirely as accuracy. Production violates every one of those assumptions. The system chapter measures the gap — the operational cost the literature never reports — and it exists because the field is populated by ML researchers, not infrastructure people. This is the author's home turf, and it is deliberately scoped to a single node (docker-compose), which is sufficient for the measurements and honest about their limits.

docs.title: 10. Datasets
docs.text:
Kind Data Role Synthetic SEA, Hyperplane, RandomRBF, STAGGER, ConceptDriftStream compositions Ground-truth drift positions → detector metrics, lemmas 1–4 Real Elec2, Phishing, CreditCard (≤ 3) External validity; natural delayed-label story (fraud) Baseline honesty Elec2 Known temporal autocorrelation: report a no-change baseline and Kappa+, never accuracy alone

Synthetic streams are the main experimental tool because drift position is known exactly — detection delay would otherwise be uncomputable. Real streams validate that the findings are not artefacts of generators. Elec2's known flaws are handled by reporting a "predict the previous label" baseline and temporal-aware metrics, rather than treating it as neutral ground truth.

docs.title: 11. Scope guards
docs.text:
The most common way student projects fail is scope creep, not difficulty. Written down and defended:

❌ Out of scope ✅ Instead Deep learning / online neural nets Classical models + ensembles (River) Regression, clustering, recommendation Classification only Distributed training (parameter servers, federated learning) Single-node service; measuring replica divergence is in scope Building a streaming framework River; we build the harness and system around it Kubernetes / multi-cloud production deployment docker-compose on one machine More than ~3 real datasets Exactly 3, chosen and justified Novel adaptation algorithms Hybrid architecture + formal delay model + measurement Theorem-proving beyond the four lemmas The lemmas; anything harder degrades to empirical

docs.text:
Citations from the research phase — each must be verified on Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar before entering the report bibliography.

SDM. - Gama et al. (2004). Learning with Drift Detection (DDM). SBIA. - Baena-García et al. (2006). Early Drift Detection Method (EDDM). - Raab, Heusinger & Schleif (2020). Reactive Soft Prototype Computing (KSWIN). Neurocomputing. - Page (1954). Continuous Inspection Schemes. Biometrika. (Roots of Page-Hinkley / CUSUM.)

Surveys and methodology - Gama, Žliobaitė, Bifet, Pechenizkiy & Bouchachia (2014). A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation. ACM Computing Surveys. The reference. - Lu et al. (2019). ACM Computing Surveys. - Alencar et al. (2026). Concept drift detection in delayed and partially labeled data streams: An experimental survey. Digital Signal Processing.

docs.title: 13. Timeline
docs.text:
Roughly 10–15 hours/week alongside coursework, deliberate slack built in:

Phase Weeks Work Exit criterion 0 — Orientation 1–4 Verify citations; get River running; reproduce one published baseline number A baseline number reproduced; bibliography skeleton 1 — Baseline 5–12 Harness + Chapter 1 run matrix Reusable harness; idealised numbers done 2 — System 13–24 Event stream, model service, live monitor, metrics, load generator Running docker-compose stack 3 — Break it 25–32 Latency / throughput / memory / divergence / recovery measurements "Reality tax" data 4 — Delay tax 33–44 Delay regimes → degradation curves → hybrid → lemma verification The contribution (or the negative result) 5 — Write-up 45–52 Report, figures, statistics, README, demo Submittable project

Phases 2–3 can shrink if the year tightens; Phase 4 keeps its budget. Phase 1 goes first because everything depends on the control condition.

docs.title: 14. Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Experiment harness — config-driven, seeded, reusable; one runner for Chapters 1 and 3.
  2. The running system — docker-compose stack: event stream, model service, live drift monitor, Prometheus/Grafana, load generator.
  3. Results — accuracy-over-time curves; delay/FP/FN trade-off tables; the delay-tax measurements (lemmas 1–3); system cost curves (latency, throughput, memory, divergence).
  4. The report — verified literature review, methodology chapter, the four lemmas with proofs, three results chapters, statistical testing.
  5. Repo hygiene — README, pinned versions, seed policy, one-command reproduction.
  6. Demo — a live drift-and-recovery dashboard, as a viva prop.

docs.title: 15. Risks and fallbacks
docs.text:
Risk Fallback Hybrid does not beat naive baselines Complete, publishable negative result; lemmas 1–3 still hold and are the contribution A lemma's proof does not cleanly go through Degrade to an empirical claim + simulation study; report honestly System chapter overruns Shrink Phase 3; Chapter 2 remains a complete chapter Elec2 results contested Pre-empt with no-change baseline + Kappa+ + exact preprocessing statement Scope creep (the real killer) §11 guards; anything new must pass "which research question does this serve?" Teacher requires novelty beyond the hybrid The hybrid is the novelty; if novelty is mandatory, its weight increases, not the project's size

Every chapter has a survivable failure mode. The project cannot fail as a whole unless it is abandoned — and the safeguards above exist to prevent exactly that.

This synopsis is self-contained. A more detailed working document (idea/scope.md) tracks open decisions, the full literature landscape, and implementation notes.

docs.title: Literature Review Index — The Delay Tax
docs.text:
Systematic catalog for the "Delay Tax" project (streaming ML drift detection under delayed/partial/selective labels). Sorted newest-first within each section.

Verified = ✅ (URL resolves, authors/venue/year cross-checked) or ⚠️ (unverified — flagged why).

docs.title: Section 1 — Ch1: Detector baselines, prequential evaluation, River/MOA tooling
Streaming vs batch / retraining-policy comparisons (Ch1 thesis evidence — added Sep 2026)
docs.text: Direct answer to "has anyone beaten non-streaming models with streaming ones, or compared them on real metrics?" — yes, repeatedly; the honest summary is context-dependent, no universal winner, streaming wins where it has a structural mechanism (per-sample updates), not by detector alone.

docs.title: When to Retrain: An Empirical Study of Retraining Policies for Streaming ML Under Concept Drift, Budget, and Latency Constraints
docs.text:
• Authors: Sawan Dasari
  • Year / Venue: 2026, arXiv:2608.19488 (cs.LG); code public
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (primary — retraining-policy evidence for the thesis), Ch2 (secondary — latency/budget system model)
  • Core claim: Under explicit budgets and training-plus-deployment latency, the retraining policy (periodic vs error-threshold vs ADWIN-triggered vs none) matters far less than whether the model learns incrementally per sample; without incremental updates, simple periodic retraining beats both reactive policies on abrupt and gradual drift, reactive policies winning only under recurring drift.
  • Key numbers: 3,933 runs; 54 paired comparisons; without incremental updates policy choice separates post-drift accuracy by 15–55 pp; latency–budget queueing interaction silently halves effective budgets; immediate labels, linear learner.
  • Method / dataset: Simulator with stale-model-serves-during-latency; 3 drift regimes × 3 budgets × ≤5 latency levels × 3 datasets × 2 learning modes.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Scope-defining for Ch1: our claim must be about streaming learners (bounded recovery via per-sample updates), not drift detectors as batch-refit triggers. Immediate labels only — Delay Tax (Ch3) untouched. Deep note: papers/dasari-2026-when-to-retrain.md.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Online versus batch retraining in one-step-ahead urban water demand forecasting under concept drift
docs.text:
• Authors: Lukas Hans, Dietlind Zühlke
  • Year / Venue: 2026, Water Supply 26(4):255–268
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (primary — deployment-faithful online-vs-batch-retraining evidence), Ch2 (secondary — runtime/latency in ops)
  • Core claim: Deployment-faithful prequential evaluation of incremental updating vs weekly batch retraining (rolling + expanding windows) on 6 years of hourly demand; an online averaging ensemble of three incremental learners achieves the lowest MAE/RMSE and mitigates high-error episodes; several expanding-window batch models are statistically indistinguishable in the milder-drift area, but the online ensemble is consistently faster (seconds vs minutes/hours) and keeps accuracy where batch baselines degrade.
  • Key numbers: Graphical abstract: avg MAE 391.2, runtime 27.6 s; Diebold–Mariano tests; two drift areas (variance/level drift vs distributional/shape drift).
  • Method / dataset: German utility, 6 years hourly consumption + meteorology; MAE/RMSE, DM tests, end-to-end runtime; online ensemble vs weekly batch retrain.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Applied confirmation that online wins under stronger drift and on cost — but regression forecasting, not classification/detector metrics; no recovery-time or damage-area measurement (our Ch1 metrics).
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Digital twin-based anomaly detection under concept drift: A comparison between iterative batch learning and incremental learning approaches
docs.text:
• Authors: Farah Abdoune, Maroua Nouiri, Olivier Cardin
  • Year / Venue: 2026, Expert Systems with Applications 299:130062
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (secondary — applied batch-vs-incremental comparison), Ch2 (secondary — digital-twin/ops context)
  • Core claim: Within a manufacturing digital-twin anomaly-detection framework, compares (i) a statistical threshold baseline, (ii) iterative batch learning (Isolation Forests periodically retrained with operator feedback), and (iii) incremental learning (Half-Space Trees updating in real time) under concept drift.
  • Key numbers: Headline numbers not yet extracted (full text not in vault).
  • Method / dataset: Manufacturing digital twin; threshold baseline vs periodic-batch iForest vs incremental HST.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Same paradigm axis as Ch1 but anomaly detection in a DT setting; supports the "drift favours incremental" applied story; no detector-level or delayed-label metrics.
  • Verified: ✅ (Crossref + publisher record)

docs.title: An Experimental Comparison of Batch and Online Machine Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
• Authors: Thomas Bartz-Beielstein, Lukas Hans
  • Year / Venue: 2024, chapter 9 in Online Machine Learning (Springer, MLFA series), pp. 105–124
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (secondary — methodology of BML-vs-OML experiments), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Book-chapter experimental studies comparing batch and online ML: study 1 predicts bike-sharing demand; study 2 compares on very large datasets in the presence of drift.
  • Key numbers: n/a at abstract level (chapter).
  • Method / dataset: Bike-sharing demand regression; large drifting datasets.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Same-lab companion to the Water Supply 2026 study (Hans co-author); classification/metric framing and recovery-time measurement still ours.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: All Versus One: An Empirical Comparison on Retrained and Incremental Machine Learning for Modeling Performance of Adaptable Software
docs.text:
• Authors: Tao Chen
  • Year / Venue: 2019, SEAMS (14th Intl Symposium on Software Engineering for Adaptive and Self-Managing Systems)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (secondary — "retrained is not always more accurate" evidence), Ch2 (secondary — software/cloud domain)
  • Core claim: First large study comparing full-retrain ("all data, discard old model") vs truly incremental ("tune on each new sample") versions of the same algorithms; refutes the general belief that retrained ⇒ better accuracy: incremental wins on highly fluctuated data (and MLP), retrained wins on stable data (and SVM); incremental is always faster (15% to 3 orders of magnitude) and can dominate on both axes for 3 of 5 performance indicators.
  • Key numbers: 8 learning algorithms (LR/DT/SVM/MLP + bagging/boosting), 5 performance indicators, 3 real adaptable software systems, 1,360 conditions, 10 runs; Wilcoxon + effect sizes.
  • Method / dataset: WEKA/MOA implementations; S-RUBiS, ASOS, C-VARD; MAE + mean training time; drift counted via ADWIN, extent via mRSD.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Regression performance modeling (software domain), not classification streams; no detectors/recovery metrics; complements Read 2012 and reinforces our per-metric/per-context claim structure.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Batch-Incremental versus Instance-Incremental Learning in Dynamic and Evolving Data
docs.text:
• Authors: Jesse Read, Albert Bifet, Bernhard Pfahringer, Geoff Holmes
  • Year / Venue: 2012, IDA (LNCS 7619), pp. 313–323
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (primary — the canonical instance- vs batch-incremental comparison)
  • Core claim: First in-depth comparison of instance-incremental (learn per example) vs batch-incremental (gather batches, retrain) classifiers under drift; papers in both camps typically cite no evidence for the choice — this supplies it, revealing respective advantages/disadvantages with no universal winner.
  • Key numbers: 104 citations (Springer, Sep 2026); headline empirical numbers to be extracted on full read.
  • Method / dataset: MOA; multiple algorithms of each paradigm, drift adaptation focus.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Establishes context-dependence (hence our per-metric win card), not reactivity metrics; immediate labels only. Deep note: papers/read-2012-batch-vs-instance.md.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods
docs.text:
• Authors: Vitor Cerqueira, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Marco Heyden, Bernhard Pfahringer, Albert Bifet
  • Year / Venue: 2026, KDD '26 (Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD, V.2), pp. 8671–8682
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (primary), Ch2 (secondary — reproducible benchmark infra)
  • Core claim: Evaluation of drift detectors is inconsistent (oversimplified synthetic generators, incompatible metrics, hidden hyperparameter choice); proposes a Monte-Carlo drift-injection framework on real data, timing-aware metrics (F1-detection score, normalized detection time), and a leave-one-dataset-out hyperparameter protocol.
  • Key numbers: Benchmarks 14 detectors on 7 real datasets × 4 drift types (class prior, label swap, feature permutation, feature filtering) × abrupt/gradual; KDD'26 acceptance rate 21%; open access, code public.
  • Method / dataset: Drift injected into real streams via Monte Carlo trials.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Immediate-label setting; no delayed/partial labels. Confirms our Ch1 methodology gap (no accepted protocol) and is the strongest candidate baseline harness to reproduce for the Phase-0 "reproduce a published baseline" task.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Practical Machine Learning for Streaming Data (KDD'24 tutorial)
docs.text:
• Authors: Heitor Murilo Gomes, Albert Bifet

docs.title: DeepRiver: A Deep Learning Library for Data Streams
docs.text:

  • Year / Venue: 2025, Journal of Open Source Software 10(105):7226
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (tooling, secondary), Ch2 (secondary)

docs.title: River: Machine Learning for Streaming Data in Python (JMLR 2021)
docs.text:
• Authors: Jacob Montiel, Max Halford, Saulo Martiello Mastelini, Geoffrey Bolmier, Raphael Sourty, Robin Vaysse, Adil Zouitine, Heitor M. Gomes, Jesse Read, TaleL Abdessalem, Albert Bifet
  • Year / Venue: 2021, JMLR 22(110):1–8
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (primary — our chosen tool), Ch2 (secondary — deployment APIs)

docs.title: Adaptive Learning from Evolving Data Streams (HAT)
docs.text:
• Authors: Albert Bifet, Ricard Gavaldà
  • Year / Venue: 2009, IDA (Springer)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (adaptive model baseline)
  • Core claim: Introduces Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT), which uses ADWIN at tree nodes to detect and adapt to drift; a core adaptive baseline.
  • Key numbers: Reports superior adaptability on synthetic and real datasets (Adult, Poker-Hand); HAT-INC, HAT-EWMA, HAT-ADWIN variants.
  • Method / dataset: Incremental decision trees with ADWIN per node.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; a Ch1 baseline model.

docs.title: On Evaluating Stream Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
• Authors: João Gama, Raquel Sebastião, Pedro Pereira Rodrigues
  • Year / Venue: 2013, Machine Learning 90(3):317–346
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (prequential evaluation protocol)
  • Core claim: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation with forgetting mechanisms is the correct protocol for ordered streams; random splits leak temporal information.
  • Key numbers: n/a (methodology).
  • Method / dataset: Formalizes prequential evaluation and sliding-window/fading-factor variants.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — foundational evaluation protocol for Ch1; breaks under delayed labels (our Ch3 motivation).

docs.title: A Comparative Study on Concept Drift Detectors
docs.text:
• Authors: Paulo M. Gonçalves Jr, Silas G. T. de Carvalho Santos, Roberto S. M. Barros, Davi C. L. Vieira
  • Year / Venue: 2014, Expert Systems with Applications 41(18):8144–8156
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (detector comparison baseline)
  • Core claim: Systematic comparison of DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, STEPD, DoF, ADWIN, Paired Learners, ECDD under abrupt/gradual drift, noise, and irrelevant attributes; no detector dominates.
  • Key numbers: n/a reported in abstract; the canonical "no single detector wins" empirical reference.
  • Method / dataset: Synthetic (SEA) and real streams; detector configs matter.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; reusable as Ch1 comparator and to justify our sweep design.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (DOI cross-checked in KDD'26 reference list; full-text not re-fetched)

docs.title: Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing (ADWIN)
docs.text:
• Authors: Albert Bifet, Ricard Gavaldà
  • Year / Venue: 2007, SIAM SDM (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (detector baseline, foundational)
  • Core claim: ADWIN maintains an adaptive window and shrinks it when two subwindows differ significantly; provides false-positive guarantees.
  • Key numbers: n/a (foundational).
  • Method / dataset: Adaptive windowing / change detection on error or feature streams.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; the canonical detector for Ch1 and the natural subject of our Lemma 2 (power loss) experiment.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Learning with Drift Detection (DDM)
docs.text:
• Authors: João Gama, Pedro Medas, Gladys Castillo, Pedro Rodrigues
  • Year / Venue: 2004, SBIA (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (detector baseline, foundational)
  • Core claim: DDM tracks error rate and its std, warns/alarms when error significantly exceeds its minimum; cheap, standard supervised detector.
  • Key numbers: n/a (foundational).
  • Method / dataset: Statistical process control on error stream.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; subject of our Lemma 3 (batch-arrival false-alarm inflation) experiment.

docs.title: Early Drift Detection Method (EDDM) (Baena-García et al., 2006, IWKDDS)
docs.text:

docs.title: Mining High-Speed Data Streams (VFDT / Hoeffding Tree)
docs.text:
• Authors: Pedro Domingos, Geoff Hulten
  • Year / Venue: 2000, KDD (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (static model baseline, foundational)
  • Core claim: Hoeffding Tree learns a decision tree in one pass with constant memory per leaf using the Hoeffding bound; the canonical static stream classifier.
  • Key numbers: Reported constant-time-per-example and high throughput; 1,598 citations on ACM DL.
  • Method / dataset: VFDT on synthetic/large data.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; Ch1 static baseline.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Mining Time-Changing Data Streams (CVFDT)
docs.text:
• Authors: Geoff Hulten, Laurie Spencer, Pedro Domingos
  • Year / Venue: 2001, KDD (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (static/adaptive model baseline, foundational)
  • Core claim: Extends VFDT with a sliding window and alternate subtrees so the tree stays current under drift while still exploiting old data; the original demonstration that an adaptive stream learner tracks evolving concepts better than trees rebuilt periodically on recent data — the ancestor of our frozen-vs-adaptive claim.
  • Key numbers: Constant (amortised) time per example; experiments on synthetic + real evolving streams (e.g., network/data-stream settings).
  • Method / dataset: Hoeffding-tree variant with windowed statistics + alternate-subtree replacement.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Immediate labels; recovery-time/recovery-metrics framing not present — but it is the correct historical citation for "adaptive beats periodically-rebuilt batch," alongside VFDT (2000).
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Learning in the Presence of Concept Drift and Hidden Contexts
docs.text:
• Authors: Gerhard Widmer, Miroslav Kubat
  • Year / Venue: 1996, Machine Learning 23(1):69–101 (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch1 (concept drift foundations)
  • Core claim: Early formal treatment of concept drift and hidden contexts; introduced the notion of context-dependent concepts.
  • Key numbers: n/a (foundational).
  • Method / dataset: FLORA2 algorithm on synthetic streams.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — immediate labels; contextualizes Ch1.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (citation cross-checked in multiple reference lists; not separately fetched)

docs.title: Section 2 — Ch2: Systems / operational cost of continual learning
A High-Throughput Architecture for Anomaly Detection in Streaming Data Using Machine Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
• Authors: Chellammal Surianarayanan, Saranya Kunasekaran, Pethuru Raj Chelliah
  • Year / Venue: 2023 (published online 04 Nov 2023; issue 2024), International Journal of Information Technology 16:493–506
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (primary — streaming architecture, Kafka, throughput)
  • Core claim: Proposes a high-throughput Kafka publish-subscribe architecture for continuous ML anomaly detection, with two alternating subscribers to hide ML computation time.
  • Key numbers: Single-node: avg accuracy 96.7%, computation 37.5 ms; distributed: avg accuracy 98.6%, computation 38.5 ms; Random Forest with threshold-based point anomaly detection.
  • Method / dataset: Apache Kafka pub/sub, RF; single-node vs distributed configs.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — no delayed labels; a concrete reference for our Ch2 event-source/backpressure design (Redis Streams vs Kafka decision).
  • Verified: ✅ (Springer full text fetched)

docs.title: Optimizing Machine Learning Inference Serving Systems: A Survey
docs.text:
• Authors: (survey) Ebadi & Keller (per Semantic Scholar)
  • Year / Venue: 2025 (recent; last-3-years survey)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (serving latency/throughput optimization)
  • Core claim: Surveys techniques for resource optimization and latency reduction in ML inference serving.
  • Key numbers: n/a (survey).
  • Method / dataset: Survey of serving systems literature.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — no delayed labels; informs Ch2's latency/throughput framing, not Ch3.

docs.title: Machine Learning (In) Security: A Stream of Problems
docs.text:
• Authors: F. Ceschin, H. M. Gomes, M. Botacin, A. Bifet, B. Pfahringer, L. S. Oliveira, A. Grégio
  • Year / Venue: 2023, Expert Systems with Applications 212:118590
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (primary), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Argues malware detection must be modeled as an evolving data stream; surveys pipeline realism gaps (drift, delayed labels, imbalance).
  • Key numbers: n/a (survey/positioning); frames the delayed-label production story.
  • Method / dataset: Survey of stream-ML-for-security pitfalls.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none directly — but a strong production-motivation citation for Ch2 and Ch3.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (PDF link from author site; year/venue cross-checked in Botacin & Gomes references)

docs.title: TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification Across Space and Time
docs.text:
• Authors: Feargus Pendlebury, Fabio Pierazzi, Roberto Jordaney, Johannes Kinder, Lorenzo Cavallaro
  • Year / Venue: 2019, USENIX Security (foundational for realistic evaluation)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (evaluation bias), Ch3 (delayed-label motivation)
  • Core claim: Temporal (and spatial) bias in malware ML evaluation inflates results; proposes temporal-aware evaluation and the AUT (area under time) metric.
  • Key numbers: Reports evaluation bias reduction with time-aware splits (details in paper).
  • Method / dataset: Android malware (DREBIN) with temporal splits; AUT metric.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — no delayed labels, but AUT is a temporal metric Ch2/Ch3 should contrast with the exposure metric of Botacin & Gomes.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (USENIX page; content cross-checked via Botacin & Gomes reference list)

docs.title: Challenges in Benchmarking Stream Learning Algorithms with Real-world Data
docs.text:
• Authors: Vinícius M. A. Souza, Denis M. dos Reis, André G. Maletzke, Gustavo E. A. P. A. Batista
  • Year / Venue: 2020, Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 34:1805–1858
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (benchmarking pitfalls), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Real-world stream benchmarks have undocumented preprocessing and ordering issues that confound results; proposes a benchmark repository and methodological fixes.
  • Key numbers: n/a (methodology).
  • Method / dataset: Stream repository (the one used by STUDD).
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: none — but reinforces our Elec2/Kappa+ caution for Ch1.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: MOA: A Real-Time Analytics Open Source Framework
docs.text:
• Authors: Albert Bifet, Geoff Holmes, Bernhard Pfahringer, Jesse Read, Philipp Kranen, Hardy Kremer, Timm Jansen, Thomas Seidl
  • Year / Venue: 2011, ECML-PKDD (tooling)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch2 (infrastructure/tooling contrast), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: MOA is the reference Java framework for stream mining; relevant as the ecosystem River/CapyMOA interoperate with.

  • Verified: ⚠️ (Springer chapter page; cross-checked in Grzenda references)

docs.title: Section 3 — Ch3: Delayed / partial / selective labels + drift detection (the core gap)
Concept Drift Detection in Delayed and Partially Labeled Data Streams: An Experimental Survey
docs.text:
• Authors: Brenno de Mello Alencar, Guilherme Weigert Cassales, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Cássio V. S. Prazeres, Tatiane Rios, Albert Bifet, Ricardo Araújo Rios
  • Year / Venue: 2026, Digital Signal Processing 182:106325
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (primary — the closest existing survey)
  • Core claim: First recent experimental survey organizing drift detectors under delayed and partially labeled streams; provides a taxonomy of detectors and evaluation approaches under label scarcity.
  • Key numbers: DSP 182, article 106325 (verified via dblp).
  • Method / dataset: Experimental survey of detectors under delayed/partial labels.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Directly adjacent to the whole of Ch3. It likely partially covers our Lemma 2 (label-scarcity degradation) empirically; the gap is the formal reaction-floor/identifiability treatment and the hybrid confirmation protocol. Potential partial scoop — must read in full before finalizing Ch3 novelty claims.
  • Verified: ✅ (dblp + ScienceDirect + Semantic Scholar)

docs.title: Towards More Realistic Evaluations: The Impact of Label Delays in Malware Detection Pipelines
docs.text:
• Authors: Marcus Botacin, Heitor Gomes
  • Year / Venue: 2024, Computers & Security (COSE), vol. 147 (per ScienceDirect pii)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (primary — direct empirical measurement of label-delay cost), Ch2 (secondary — queue/pipeline modeling)
  • Core claim: Models malware detection as delayed+partially-labeled evolving stream; quantifies how label delay (from analysis-queue limits) degrades drift-based retraining, proposes the exposure metric, and shows pseudo-labels mitigate delay.
  • Key numbers: Delayed labels increase user exposure ~50% (up to 75% detection decrease); 81 epochs delay → exposure +50% vs immediate (DDM), 61 epochs (EDDM); pseudo-labels reduce loss to ~30% of original; 10% queue ≈ 100+ epochs delay; 10 executions averaged; DREBIN 250×500 samples, Androzoo replication.
  • Method / dataset: DREBIN + Androzoo, RF, DDM/EDDM, epoch-based drift detection, exposure metric, pseudo-label (secondary classifier) mitigation.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Empirically confirms the reaction-floor phenomenon (Lemma 1) and the value of a label-free/early signal (hybrid), but does not derive the formal bounds or the statistical power/identifiability lemmas; its pseudo-label approach is the closest existing thing to our hybrid's Stage-1. Must-cite; do not let Ch3 claim the exposure-style quantification as novel without contrasting.
  • Verified: ✅ (PDF fetched + ScienceDirect record; COSE 2024 confirmed via GitHub repo)

docs.title: A Survey on Semi-supervised Learning for Delayed Partially Labelled Data Streams
docs.text:
• Authors: Heitor Murilo Gomes, Maciej Grzenda, Rodrigo Mello, Jesse Read, Minh Huong Le Nguyen, Albert Bifet
  • Year / Venue: 2022 (published online 21 Nov 2022; issue 2023), ACM Computing Surveys 55(4), Article 75
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (primary — anchor survey), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Formalizes "delayed partially labelled data streams" (immediate/delayed/infinite labels × supervised/semi-supervised); surveys SSL methods, learning guarantees, and evaluation practice; proposes a unified problem setting.
  • Key numbers: 63 citations / 6,779 downloads (ACM DL, Aug 2026). Included a small experiment: with ADWIN + SRP on AGRAWAL (100k instances, 3 drifts), a 10,000-instance label delay shifts detections by ~10,000 instances and causes prolonged prequential accuracy below 50%.
  • Method / dataset: Survey + illustrative delayed-label AGRAWAL experiment.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Confirms the reaction-floor phenomenon empirically (Lemma 1) but does not prove it or bound power loss (Lemma 2) or batch-arrival inflation (Lemma 3). Identifiability (Lemma 4) is discussed via Žliobaitė. The reference to cite as "closest prior work."
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: STUDD: A Student–Teacher Method for Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection
docs.text:
• Authors: Vitor Cerqueira, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Albert Bifet, Luis Torgo
  • Year / Venue: 2022 (online 21 Jun 2022; issue 2023), Machine Learning 112:4351–4378
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (label-free baseline for hybrid Stage-1), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Student model mimics teacher; drift is detected by monitoring the student's mimicking loss (label-free) — a strong candidate for the label-free early-warning stage of our hybrid.
  • Key numbers: 19 benchmark streams (truncated to 150k each); MDR ~19% (3/16), FAR/MTD/MTFA reported; label efficiency best among non-baselines; Bayesian sign test ROPE 5%.
  • Method / dataset: Student-teacher with Page-Hinkley; comparison vs supervised (SS/DSS/WS/DWS) and unsupervised (OS/OF/FF) variants.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Unsupervised only — explicitly notes it cannot catch real (posterior) drift without labels, which is exactly our Lemma 4 and motivates the hybrid. Direct Stage-1 baseline for Ch3.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: ROSE: Robust Online Self-Adjusting Ensemble for Continual Learning on Imbalanced Drifting Data Streams
docs.text:
• Authors: Alberto Cano, Bartosz Krawczyk
  • Year / Venue: 2022, Machine Learning 111:2561–2599
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (secondary — adaptation method under drift+imbalance), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Online ensemble with variable-size random feature subspaces, ADWIN-per-subspace drift detection + background ensemble, per-class sliding windows, and self-adjusting λ bagging for imbalance.
  • Key numbers: 30 ensembles compared; 24 imbalanced real datasets; 36 imbalanced generators; 12 drifting-imbalance generators; Kappa avg 63.65 vs next-best 57.85 (static IR); Wilcoxon/Bayesian significance; 384 GB RAM Xeon runs.
  • Method / dataset: MOA; HoeffdingTree base; prequential Kappa/AUC; Friedman ranks.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Immediate labels; contributes the background-ensemble + drift-detector adaptation pattern relevant to Ch2/Ch3 but not delayed-label detection.
  • Verified: ✅ (full text in Material/)

docs.title: Stream-Based Active Learning with Verification Latency in Non-stationary Environments
docs.text:
• Authors: Rodrigo Mello, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Albert Bifet, Bernhard Pfahringer
  • Year / Venue: 2022 (arXiv:2204.06822; IJCNN 2022)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (selective labeling / active learning under latency), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Proposes PRopagate: estimates query utility under unknown label delay and predicts requested-but-unavailable labels; drift-dependent labeling budget.
  • Key numbers: Reports improvements over active-learning baselines under constant and variable latency (from abstract; per-paper details to be read).
  • Method / dataset: Stream active learning with verification latency.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Addresses label acquisition under latency rather than detector isolation; the "only flagged cases labeled" endogenous-bias scenario connects to our selective-labeling regime. Partially overlaps our selective-labeling chapter.
  • Verified: ✅ (arXiv abstract page resolves)

docs.title: Statistical Drift Detection with Parametric Gamma–Weibull and Adaptive Deep Learning for Malware Detection in IoT Data Streams
docs.text:
• Authors: Friday I. Agu, Robert Andok, Jaromír Klarák, Jean Rosemond Dora
  • Year / Venue: 2026, Journal of King Saud University — Computer and Information Sciences 38:673
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (secondary — hybrid statistical detector + pseudo-label adaptation), Ch2 (secondary — edge/runtime profiling)
  • Core claim: A Gamma–Weibull log-likelihood-ratio CUSUM detector (ARL₀-calibrated) gates lightweight LSTM/CNN adaptation; post-drift buffer, pseudo-labeling + clustering labels, no human labels.
  • Key numbers: Detection delay 6 samples (abrupt), 80 (gradual), 35 (mixed), zero false alarms (noise-free); ADWIN delay 1.1±1.2 but ~1270 false alarms; PHT 125.2±106 delay, 0 FA; DDM 425.9±401 delay, 625 FA; LSTM macro-F1 0.977→0.981, CNN 0.457→0.576; full pipeline 1.43 s CPU; monitoring <150 ms; memory <50 KB.
  • Method / dataset: Simulated Gamma→Weibull streams (T=10k, MC=30); IoT-23 (benign n=451; malware n=14,784; capture 33-1 and 1-1).
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Uses a parametric distribution model (not error-stream detectors) and pseudo-labels (not delayed ground truth); does not treat the four lemmas, but its gatekeeper adaptation is a good contrast for our hybrid architecture. Include as a 2026 "adjacent hybrid" citation.
  • Verified: ✅ (full text in Material/)

docs.title: Delayed Labelling Evaluation for Data Streams
docs.text:
• Authors: Maciej Grzenda, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Albert Bifet
  • Year / Venue: 2020, Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 34:1237–1266
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (evaluation protocol under delay), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Introduces continuous re-evaluation: buffer predictions, re-poll the evolving model before the delayed label arrives, and score binned predictions (initial / periodic / test-then-train). The standard evaluation answer for delayed-label streams.
  • Key numbers: Hyperplane (delay 100), LED (delay 1000), AGRAWAL (delay 1000, 4 gradual drifts), Airlines (natural latency up to 13h), Electricity (~1–2 day latency), Forest cover (delay 1000); K=10 re-polls, B=50 bins recommended. Open-source MOA implementation.
  • Method / dataset: MOA; HT/HAT/ARF/kNN/NB/NC/MC; binned performance λ(T,b).
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Evaluation methodology, not detector analysis; it shows models can refine predictions while labels are pending — directly relevant to our hybrid's confirmation stage and to how we evaluate the delayed-label regimes. Use their evaluation protocol in Ch3.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Credit Card Fraud Detection and Concept-Drift Adaptation with Delayed Supervised Information
docs.text:
• Authors: Andrea Dal Pozzolo, Giacomo Boracchi, Olivier Caelen, Cesare Alippi, Gianluca Bontempi
  • Year / Venue: 2015, IEEE IJCNN
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (delayed labels in fraud — production story), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: In credit-card fraud, immediate investigator feedback and delayed chargeback labels carry different information; training separate models on each and aggregating outputs beats treating them identically.
  • Key numbers: Reports improved performance by separating immediate vs delayed supervision (per abstract; details in paper).
  • Method / dataset: Fraud detection with delayed supervised information.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: An application-specific adaptation strategy, not a general detector benchmark; supports our premise that delayed labels break standard practice, and echoes the two-signal structure of our hybrid. Empirical anchor for the fraud dataset story.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (Semantic Scholar hit a bot-wall on fetch; citation cross-checked in Gomes survey reference list)

docs.title: Online Learning under Delayed Feedback
docs.text:
• Authors: Pooria Joulani, András György, Csaba Szepesvári
  • Year / Venue: 2013, ICML (PMLR 28(3):1453–1461)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (theory — delayed-feedback regret), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Delay increases regret multiplicatively in adversarial online learning and additively in stochastic settings; gives black-box meta-algorithms to handle delay.
  • Key numbers: n/a (theoretical).
  • Method / dataset: Regret bounds for full-information and bandit feedback under delay.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: This is the regret-theoretic cousin of our delay tax, but for learning (not detection); our Lemma 1 (reaction floor) is the detection-side analogue. Cite for the theoretical framing of "delay costs."
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: Change with Delayed Labeling: When is it Detectable?
docs.text:
• Authors: Indrė Žliobaitė
  • Year / Venue: 2010, IEEE ICDM Workshops (foundational)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (identifiability — Lemma 4), Ch1 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Characterizes which drift types are detectable without new labels; pure posterior drift (P(Y|X) changes, P(X) fixed) is not detectable from inputs — the formal basis of our identifiability ceiling.
  • Key numbers: n/a (theoretical/analytical; two drift types empirically evaluated).
  • Method / dataset: Analytical observability conditions + experiments.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Directly establishes Lemma 4's identifiability ceiling; does not propose the hybrid confirmation architecture. The theoretical root of our hybrid's justification.
  • Verified: ✅

docs.title: A Predictive and User-Centric Approach to Machine Learning in Data Streaming Scenarios
docs.text:
• Authors: Davide Carneiro, Miguel Guimarães, Fábio Silva, Paulo Novais
  • Year / Venue: 2021 (preprint May 2021), Neurocomputing (per Material filename)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (secondary — retraining decision support), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Meta-learning approach that predicts whether retraining a model on new data will improve performance, to avoid wasteful retraining in streaming scenarios; pairs it with an explainable interface for human-in-the-loop validation.
  • Key numbers: Meta-model trained on 673 meta-instances from 47 datasets; 10-fold CV RMSE 0.000355, r² 0.98, MAE 0.007; streaming meta-model updated every 2000 instances; 53 datasets total.
  • Method / dataset: pymfe meta-features (57), Random Forest meta-model; regression (binary classification transformed to 0/1); tax fraud case study.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Addresses "when to retrain" via predicted performance rather than drift detection; relevant to Ch2's adaptation-cost framing and Ch3's selective-adaptation angle, but not delayed-label detection per se.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (full text in Material/; DOI inferred from filename — verify before citing)

docs.title: Stream-based Active Learning for Sliding Windows under the Influence of Verification Latency
docs.text:
• Authors: Rodrigo Mello, Heitor Murilo Gomes, Albert Bifet, Bernhard Pfahringer
  • Year / Venue: 2021, Machine Learning (online 2021)
  • Chapter relevance: Ch3 (verification latency in active learning), Ch2 (secondary)
  • Core claim: Forgetting and Simulating: simulates the learner's future state when a queried label arrives, improving utility estimates under latency.
  • Key numbers: Reports improvements under constant and variable latency (per abstract).
  • Method / dataset: Stream active learning with sliding windows.
  • Gap vs. our lemmas: Adjacent — label acquisition under latency, not detector isolation; complements the selective-labeling regime.
  • Verified: ⚠️ (DOI cross-checked in Gomes survey reference list; not separately fetched)

docs.title: Section 4 — Ch3: Hybrid / label-free + confirmation methods

docs.title: How to use this index
docs.text:
• papers/<slug>.md contains deep notes for the load-bearing papers (Ch3 anchors + closest prior work + the KDD'26 benchmark).
  • gap-analysis.md maps every entry to the four lemmas and flags scoop risk.
  • ⚠️ entries need a final verification pass before going into the report bibliography.

docs.title: Literature Review Conclusion — The Delay Tax
docs.text:
Papers reviewed: 38 unique papers — 33 catalogued in the four index sections (the index has 35 entries; STUDD and the Gamma–Weibull paper are each cross-listed in two sections) plus 5 foundational quick-reference items.

Verified: 21 of the 33 catalogued papers are ✅ verified; 12 are ⚠️ flagged unverified; the 5 foundational items carry no individual flag in the index.

Deep-dive notes: 6 papers received full per-paper notes in papers/*.md (Gomes 2022, Botacin & Gomes 2024, Cerqueira KDD'26, STUDD 2023, Agu 2026, ROSE 2022).

Date range: 1954 (Page, foundational) – 2026; the 33 catalogued papers span 1996–2026.

docs.title: Is the gap real?
docs.text:
Verdict: Yes — delayed/partial-label drift detection is confirmed fragmented and unbenchmarked, but the immediate-label side of the field now has a standard benchmark, so the claim must be sharpened.

Of the 33 catalogued papers, roughly 14 address delayed or partial labels in some form, but only 4 study drift detectors under delay at all — Alencar 2026 (results unread), Gomes 2022 (one illustrative experiment), Botacin & Gomes 2024 (DDM/EDDM inside a pipeline), Žliobaitė 2010 (theory) — and none provides a detector-level benchmark across label-observation regimes, none states a formal detection bound under label latency, and none builds and evaluates a two-stage early-warning + delayed-confirmation hybrid. Fragmentation is visible in the terminology alone: verification latency, delayed labelling, label latency, extreme verification latency, and delayed partially labelled streams all name the same area. The important update: Cerqueira et al. (KDD'26) has standardized the immediate-label detector benchmark (14 detectors, 7 real datasets, 4 drift types, abrupt+gradual), so our gap statement becomes "a standard benchmark now exists for immediate labels, but not for delayed, partial, or selective labels."

docs.title: Lemma 1 — Reaction floor (detection cannot precede label arrival)
docs.text:
Verdict: empirically demonstrated by two papers, never stated as a theorem — novel as a formal statement, trivial to prove, and must cite the empirics.

Gomes 2022's AGRAWAL experiment (100k instances, 3 drifts) shows a 10,000-instance label delay shifts ADWIN+SRP detections by ~10,000 instances and holds prequential accuracy below 50%. Botacin & Gomes 2024 shows delay maps near-linearly to harm: exposure reaches +50% at 81 epochs of delay (DDM) and 61 (EDDM), exposure grows ~50k points (DDM) / ~60k (EDDM) per 10 epochs of delay, and beyond 81–91 epochs drift mitigation is fully nullified. Joulani 2013 provides the learning-side analogue (delay multiplies regret in adversarial settings, adds it in stochastic ones). No logged paper states the pointwise bound T ≥ τ + L_τ for error-stream detectors under verification latency; the mathematical root is classical quickest detection (Page 1954, Lorden 1971), which nobody in this literature has applied to delayed-error detectors.

docs.title: Lemma 2 — Power loss (1/√p sensitivity degradation under partial labels)
docs.text:
Verdict: the closed-form 1/√p bound for windowed error-stream detectors appears genuinely novel; adjacent treatments are intuition-level only, and one unread paper may hold the empirics.

Gomes 2022 formalizes only the general SLT intuition that effective sample size equals the labelled count. STUDD 2023 sweeps label access over {1, 10, 25, 50}% and shows relative method ordering shifts — qualitative, no law. The one real risk is Alencar 2026 (DSP): an experimental survey that likely measures detector degradation as label availability decreases; its results are unread (paywalled), and if it already reports a 1/√p-like curve for ADWIN/DDM/KSWIN, our contribution shrinks to formalizing the factor rather than measuring it.

docs.title: Lemma 3 — False-alarm inflation under batch arrival (design effect 1+(b−1)ρ)
docs.text:
Verdict: the most clearly novel lemma — no direct treatment found anywhere in the logged literature.

Nothing logged studies batched or bursty label arrival injecting autocorrelation into the observed error stream and inflating detector false alarms. Botacin & Gomes 2024 is the closest conceptual neighbor but models a different mechanism — queue size → delay (their mapping: 10% queue capacity ≈ 100+ epochs of delay, and queue capacity can drop to 70% with pseudo-labels at the same exposure), not batch correlation → spurious alarms. The clustered-data variance factor 1+(b−1)ρ is classical statistics, but its application to drift detectors under batch-reconciled labels is open territory.

docs.title: Lemma 4 — Identifiability ceiling (pure posterior drift invisible to label-free detection)
docs.text:
Verdict: already established — not novel as a claim; the novelty must be the hybrid's use of it.

Žliobaitė 2010 proves the detectability conditions (pure posterior drift with fixed P(X) is undetectable from inputs); Gomes 2022 reproduces the observability table; STUDD 2023 demonstrates the limitation empirically (missed-detection ratio ~19%, 3/16 datasets) and states it explicitly. Ch3 should present Lemma 4 as a properly credited restatement of Žliobaitė, and the actual contribution is the conclusion that follows from it: label-free signals can only be an early warning, so the hybrid confirmation architecture is the information-maximal response.

docs.title: Scoop risk
docs.text:
Verdict: one high-risk unread paper, one medium-high already-published overlap; the combination we propose remains unclaimed.

  • Alencar et al. 2026 (DSP 182:106325) — HIGH. An experimental survey of exactly our Ch3 setting. Verification status: ✅ that it exists (dblp + ScienceDirect + Semantic Scholar), but results unread — paywalled. If it contains delay-vs-latency and label-coverage-vs-false-alarm curves for standard detectors, part of our "measure the degradation" chapter is scooped as measurement; our remaining novelty would be formal lemmas 1–3 and the hybrid protocol. Must be read in full before finalizing any novelty claim.
  • Botacin & Gomes 2024 (Computers & Security) — MEDIUM-HIGH. Already quantified label-delay cost on real malware pipelines (~50% exposure increase, up to 75% detection decrease; 30% loss with pseudo-labels instead of 70%) and shown pseudo-label mitigation. We must not claim "we quantify that delayed labels hurt."
  • Gomes 2022 (CSUR) — MEDIUM. Covers our formal framing at survey level and explicitly flags the under-explored delayed+partial intersection as open — cite them as naming our gap.
  • Agu 2026 (JKSU-CIS) — LOW-MEDIUM. Architecturally close hybrid (detector-gated pseudo-label adaptation, detection delay 6 samples abrupt / 80 gradual / 35 mixed) but sidesteps delayed ground truth rather than measuring it — must be distinguished.
  • Mello 2021/2022 — LOW. Verification latency in active learning overlaps our selective-labeling regime, not detector isolation.

docs.title: Closest prior work
docs.text:
Verdict: Botacin & Gomes 2024 is the single closest paper; Ch3 must add detector-level isolation, formal bounds, and a confirmation protocol to be a genuine contribution.

Their key numbers: delayed labels increase user exposure ~50% (up to 75% detection decrease); exposure +50% at 81 epochs delay (DDM) and 61 (EDDM); ~50k/60k exposure-point increase per 10 epochs of delay; 10% queue capacity ≈ 100+ epochs of delay; a pseudo-label secondary classifier reduces the detection loss from ~70% to ~30%; exposure metric goes 0.49→0.90 while AUT-F1 goes 0.52→0.18 as delay goes 0→80; results averaged over 10 executions on DREBIN (250 epochs × 500 samples) and replicated on Androzoo (~284k samples, ~270 epochs). What Ch3 must add beyond this: (1) detector-level isolation — clean curves of detection delay vs label latency and false-alarm rate vs label coverage, on synthetic streams with known drift positions; (2) the formal bounds of lemmas 1–3; (3) a confirmation protocol (label-free early warning within a tolerance window → delayed supervised confirmation → calibrated action) evaluated against naive-delayed, label-free-only, and immediate-label controls; and (4) no claim of a novel time-aware metric without contrasting with the exposure metric and Pendlebury 2019's AUT metric.

docs.title: Recommended baseline to reproduce
docs.text:
Verdict: reproduce Cerqueira et al. (KDD'26); fallbacks are Gonçalves 2014 and Gomes 2022's AGRAWAL experiment.

Chosen over the alternatives because it is the most recent (2026), venue-strong (KDD), open-access (CC-BY) with public code, uses immediate labels (the correct control condition for Phase 0), and is naturally extendable — we can take the field's new standard benchmark and break it with delayed-label regimes in Ch3.
