The reproduction target: one detector comparison from it, e.g., ADWIN vs DDM vs KSWIN on one injected-drift real dataset under both abrupt and gradual transitions, using their F1-detection score and normalized detection time; River and CapyMOA both implement all three detectors, so a 2–3 detector, 1–2 dataset subset is realistic. Stretch pilot: reproduce Gomes 2022's delayed-AGRAWAL shift (~10,000 instances) as the first delayed-label sanity check.

docs.title: Overall go/no-go read
docs.text: Proceed with the locked Ch1/Ch2/Ch3 scope, with two conditions before implementation starts: reword the gap claim (immediate-label benchmarks now exist; delayed-label ones do not) and read Alencar 2026 in full before finalizing Ch3 novelty. Ch2 — replica divergence, backpressure, restart/recovery cost — is untouched by the entire delayed-label literature and remains our most defensible novelty with zero scoop risk. Ch3 rests on a combination no single paper has: formal lemmas 1–3 (novel as detector-level statements), lemma 4 (Žliobaitė's result, credited and operationalized), detector-level delay/coverage/batch curves on synthetic ground truth, and a hybrid confirmation protocol that Gomes 2022 and STUDD 2023 explicitly name as open and that no logged paper builds or evaluates. The literature supports proceeding; it does not support claiming the delayed-label measurement itself as new.

docs.title: Ch1 — Detector baselines, prequential evaluation, tooling
docs.text:
[Cerqueira, Gomes, Heyden, Pfahringer & Bifet 2026] — A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods. KDD '26, pp. 8671–8682. Benchmarks drift detection by injecting controlled distributional changes into real datasets via Monte Carlo trials: 14 detectors, 7 real datasets, 4 drift types (class prior, label swap, feature permutation, feature filtering), each abrupt and gradual, with new timing-aware metrics (F1 detection score, normalized detection time) and a leave-one-dataset-out hyperparameter protocol. KDD'26 acceptance rate 21% (1,157 of 5,395 submissions). Bears on Ch1 as the reference protocol and the Phase-0 reproduction target; immediate-label only, which is precisely the gap Ch3 fills. Verified: ✅

[Kulbach, Cazzonelli, Ngo, Halford & Mastelini 2025] — DeepRiver: A Deep Learning Library for Data Streams. Journal of Open Source Software 10(105):7226. Adds PyTorch deep learning to River's streaming API — class-incremental learning, stream-specific optimizers, autoencoder anomaly detection. No quantitative results in the paper (software paper); tooling/background only, since the project excludes deep learning by scope. Verified: ✅

[Gomes & Bifet 2024] — Practical Machine Learning for Streaming Data. KDD '24 tutorial (2 pp.). Demonstrates stream-ML practice via CapyMOA (Python API over MOA): drift detection and evaluation (ADWIN, STUDD), clustering/anomaly methods, and a section on partially and delayed labeled streams using cluster-and-label and incremental self-training. No numbers (tutorial); confirms CapyMOA as a viable supplement to River. Verified: ✅

[Montiel, Halford, Mastelini, Bolmier, Sourty, Vaysse, Zouitine, Gomes, Read, Abdessalem & Bifet 2021] — River: Machine Learning for Streaming Data in Python. JMLR 22(110):1–8. The tooling paper for our chosen framework: dict-based API, incremental models, and the exact detector set Ch1 needs — ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, KSWIN, HDDM — plus Hoeffding trees, ARF, SRP, and prequential metrics. No numbers (library); the version to pin for Phase 0. Verified: ✅

[Gonçalves Jr, de Carvalho Santos, Barros & Vieira 2014] — A Comparative Study on Concept Drift Detectors. Expert Systems with Applications 41(18):8144–8156. Systematic comparison of DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, STEPD, DoF, ADWIN, Paired Learners, and ECDD under abrupt/gradual drift, noise, and irrelevant attributes; the logged conclusion is the canonical "no single detector wins" — qualitative-only in our notes (no accuracy table captured). Ch1 comparator and justification for our sweep design. Verified: ⚠️ (DOI cross-checked in the KDD'26 reference list; full text not re-fetched)

[Gama, Sebastião & Rodrigues 2013] — On Evaluating Stream Learning Algorithms. Machine Learning 90(3):317–346. Establishes prequential (test-then-train) evaluation with sliding-window or fading-factor forgetting as the correct protocol for ordered streams, since random splits leak temporal information. No numbers (methodology). Foundational for Ch1 — and the protocol that breaks under delayed labels, which is our Ch3 motivation. Verified: ✅

[Bifet & Gavaldà 2009] — Adaptive Learning from Evolving Data Streams (HAT). IDA. Introduces the Hoeffding Adaptive Tree, which puts ADWIN at tree nodes to detect and adapt to drift; logged claim is superior adaptability on Adult and Poker-Hand across HAT-INC/EWMA/ADWIN variants — qualitative-only in our notes (no numeric scores captured). Ch1 adaptive-model baseline. Verified: ✅

[Bifet & Gavaldà 2007] — Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing (ADWIN). SIAM SDM. The canonical adaptive-window detector with false-positive guarantees; foundational, no numbers logged. Ch1 detector baseline and the natural subject of our Lemma-2 power-loss experiment. Verified: ✅

[Baena-García, del Campo-Ávila, Fidalgo, Bifet, Gavaldà & Morales-Bueno 2006] — Early Drift Detection Method (EDDM). 4th Intl Workshop on Knowledge Discovery from Data Streams. Detects drift from distances between errors to better catch gradual drift; foundational, no numbers logged. Ch1 detector baseline, and one of the two detectors used in the Botacin & Gomes pipeline. Verified: ⚠️ (cross-checked in KDD'26 and STUDD reference lists; not separately fetched)

[Gama, Medas, Castillo & Rodrigues 2004] — Learning with Drift Detection (DDM). SBIA. Applies statistical process control to the error stream with warn/alarm thresholds; foundational, no numbers logged. Ch1 detector baseline and the subject of our Lemma-3 batch-arrival experiment. Verified: ✅

[Domingos & Hulten 2000] — Mining High-Speed Data Streams (VFDT / Hoeffding Tree). KDD, pp. 71–80. One-pass decision tree using the Hoeffding bound with constant memory per leaf; reported constant-time-per-example and high throughput, 1,598 citations on ACM DL. Ch1 static-model baseline. Verified: ✅

[Widmer & Kubat 1996] — Learning in the Presence of Concept Drift and Hidden Contexts. Machine Learning 23(1):69–101. Early formalization of drift and hidden contexts via the FLORA2 algorithm; foundational, no numbers logged. Background for Ch1's drift framing. Verified: ⚠️ (cross-checked in multiple reference lists; not separately fetched)

[Ditzler, Roveri, Alippi & Polikar 2015] — Learning in Nonstationary Environments: A Survey. IEEE Computational Intelligence Magazine. Foundational quick-reference item: survey of nonstationary learning; no numbers logged. Background only. Verified: — (foundational quick-reference; unflagged in index)

[Lorden 1971] — Procedures for Reacting to a Change in Distribution. Annals of Mathematical Statistics. Foundational quick-reference item: minimax quickest detection, i.e., the detection-delay vs false-alarm trade-off that frames our Lemma 1. No numbers logged. Verified: — (foundational quick-reference; unflagged in index)

[Page 1954] — Continuous Inspection Schemes. Biometrika. Foundational quick-reference item: root of Page-Hinkley/CUSUM and of the quickest-detection framing behind our Lemma-1 reaction floor. No numbers logged. Verified: — (foundational quick-reference; unflagged in index)

docs.title: Ch2 — Systems / operational cost of continual learning
docs.text:
[Ebadi & Keller 2025] — Optimizing Machine Learning Inference Serving Systems: A Survey. (Semantic Scholar). Surveys resource-usage and latency optimization for ML inference serving over the last three years. No numbers logged (survey). Informs Ch2's latency/throughput framing; no delayed-label content. Verified: ⚠️ (author list not independently cross-checked)

[Surianarayanan, Kunasekaran & Chelliah 2023/2024] — A High-Throughput Architecture for Anomaly Detection in Streaming Data Using Machine Learning Algorithms. International Journal of Information Technology 16:493–506 (published online Nov 2023). Kafka publish-subscribe architecture with two alternating subscribers to hide ML computation time, Random Forest threshold-based point anomaly detection. Reported 96.7% accuracy at 37.5 ms computation (single node) and 98.6% at 38.5 ms (distributed). Ch2 reference for our event-source and backpressure design (Redis Streams vs Kafka decision). Verified: ✅

[Ceschin, Gomes, Botacin, Bifet, Pfahringer, Oliveira & Grégio 2023] — Machine Learning (In) Security: A Stream of Problems. Expert Systems with Applications 212:118590. Positions malware detection as an evolving data-stream problem and catalogs pipeline-realism gaps (drift, delayed labels, imbalance). No numbers (survey/positioning, qualitative-only). Production-motivation citation for Ch2 and Ch3. Verified: ⚠️ (author-hosted PDF; venue cross-checked in Botacin & Gomes references)

[Souza, dos Reis, Maletzke & Batista 2020] — Challenges in Benchmarking Stream Learning Algorithms with Real-world Data. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 34:1805–1858. Shows real-world stream benchmarks suffer undocumented preprocessing and ordering that confound results, and supplies the benchmark repository STUDD used. No numbers (methodology). Reinforces our Elec2/Kappa+ caution for Ch1. Verified: ✅

[Pendlebury, Pierazzi, Jordaney, Kinder & Cavallaro 2019] — TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification Across Space and Time. USENIX Security. Argues temporal and spatial bias inflates malware ML evaluation and proposes the AUT (area under time) metric with time-aware splits; our notes record the bias-reduction claim qualitatively, without specific numbers. Ch2/Ch3 metric to contrast against the exposure metric. Verified: ⚠️ (USENIX page; content cross-checked via Botacin & Gomes references)

[Bifet, Holmes, Pfahringer, Read, Kranen, Kremer, Jansen & Seidl 2011] — MOA: A Real-Time Analytics Open Source Framework. ECML-PKDD. The reference Java stream-mining framework that River and CapyMOA interoperate with. No numbers (tooling). Ch2 infrastructure/tooling contrast. Verified: ⚠️ (Springer chapter page; cross-checked in Grzenda references)

docs.title: Ch3 — Delayed / partial / selective labels + drift detection
docs.text:
[Alencar, Cassales, Gomes, Prazeres, Rios, Bifet & Rios 2026] — Concept Drift Detection in Delayed and Partially Labeled Data Streams: An Experimental Survey. Digital Signal Processing 182:106325. The closest survey to all of Ch3: organizes detectors under delayed and partially labeled streams, provides a detector taxonomy, and runs label-scarcity experiments. Existence verified; results unread (paywalled) — if it already reports delay-vs-latency and label-coverage-vs-false-alarm curves for standard detectors, part of our measurement chapter is taken. Highest scoop risk in the review. Verified: ✅ (existence via dblp + ScienceDirect + Semantic Scholar); content unread.

[Agu, Andok, Klarák & Dora 2026] — Statistical Drift Detection with Parametric Gamma–Weibull and Adaptive Deep Learning for Malware Detection in IoT Data Streams. Journal of King Saud University — Computer and Information Sciences 38:673. A Gamma–Weibull log-likelihood-ratio CUSUM detector (ARL₀ ≈ 2000) gates LSTM/CNN fine-tuning on a post-drift buffer labeled by pseudo-labels (τ=0.80) plus K-means. Reported detection delays of 6 samples (abrupt), 80 (gradual), and 35 (mixed) at zero false alarms in noise-free simulation (T=10,000, MC=30); in a 20-replication comparison, ADWIN was fastest (1.1±1.2) but fired ~1,270 false alarms, Page-Hinkley 125.2±106 with 0, KSWIN 176.3±272.9 with ~126, DDM 425.9±401 with ~625; adaptation raised LSTM macro-F1 0.977→0.981 and CNN 0.457→0.576; full pipeline 1.43 s CPU, monitoring <150 ms, pseudo-labeling 2.4 ms, model memory <50 KB. Real data: IoT-23 benign (n=451) and malware (n=14,784) duration streams, first alarm at t=31 vs ADWIN t=7, PHT t=75, KSWIN t=251, DDM none. Adjacent hybrid — must be distinguished from Ch3, which measures delayed ground truth rather than sidestepping it with pseudo-labels. Verified: ✅

[Botacin & Gomes 2024] — Towards More Realistic Evaluations: The Impact of Label Delays in Malware Detection Pipelines. Computers & Security, vol. 147. Models malware detection as a delayed+partially-labeled evolving stream and measures how analysis-queue-driven label delay degrades DDM/EDDM drift retraining on DREBIN (250 epochs × 500 samples) and Androzoo (~284k samples, ~270 epochs), introducing the exposure metric. Delayed labels raised user exposure ~50% (up to 75% detection decrease); exposure hit +50% at 81 epochs of delay (DDM) and 61 (EDDM); exposure grows ~50k points (DDM) / ~60k (EDDM) per 10 epochs of delay; a 10% queue capacity maps to 100+ epochs of delay (queue capacity can drop to 70% at the same exposure with pseudo-labels); a pseudo-label secondary classifier cut the detection loss from ~70% to ~30%; the exposure metric runs 0.49→0.90 while AUT-F1 runs 0.52→0.18 as delay goes 0→80; averages over 10 executions with FPR < 1% enforced. The closest prior work to Ch3 — see the Closest prior work section for what must be added. Verified: ✅

[Cerqueira, Gomes, Bifet & Torgo 2023] — STUDD: A Student–Teacher Method for Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection. Machine Learning 112(11):4351–4378. A student model mimics the deployed teacher and Page-Hinkley (δ=0.001) monitors the mimicking loss — fully label-free. On 19 benchmark streams (truncated to 150k each; W=2000, 500 for small sets), missed-detection ratio ~19% (3/16 datasets, tied with DWS), best label efficiency among non-baselines, and — directly relevant to our Lemma 4 — it explicitly cannot catch posterior drift that leaves P(X) unchanged; sensitivity sweeps over label access {1, 10, 25, 50}% (delay {250..4000}) shift relative method ordering, with STUDD relatively better as label access drops and worst at 50% access (qualitative). Candidate Stage-1 component for our hybrid. Verified: ✅

[Gomes, Grzenda, Mello, Read, Le Nguyen & Bifet 2022] — A Survey on Semi-supervised Learning for Delayed Partially Labelled Data Streams. ACM Computing Surveys 55(4), Article 75. The anchor survey: formalizes the setting (immediate/delayed/infinite labels × supervised/semi-supervised), surveys SSL methods and evaluation practice, and includes an AGRAWAL experiment (100k instances, 3 drifts) where a 10,000-instance label delay shifts ADWIN+SRP detections by ~10,000 instances and holds prequential accuracy below 50%. 63 citations / 6,779 downloads on ACM DL. Names our gap and the under-explored delayed+partial intersection as open. Verified: ✅

[Mello, Gomes, Bifet & Pfahringer 2022] — Stream-Based Active Learning with Verification Latency in Non-stationary Environments (PRopagate). IJCNN (arXiv:2204.06822). Estimates query utility under unknown label delay and predicts requested-but-unavailable labels, with a drift-dependent labeling budget. Our notes hold only the qualitative claim of improvement over active-learning baselines under constant and variable latency — no numeric results logged yet. Bears on the selective-labeling regime ("only flagged cases are labeled"). Verified: ✅ (arXiv resolves); results qualitative-only in our notes.

[Cano & Krawczyk 2022] — ROSE: Robust Online Self-Adjusting Ensemble for Continual Learning on Imbalanced Drifting Data Streams. Machine Learning 111:2561–2599. Online ensemble with variable-size random feature subspaces (μ=0.7), ADWIN-per-subspace drift detection with a background ensemble (replacement after 1000 instances), per-class sliding windows (1000-instance total budget), and self-adjusting λ bagging (λ_min=4; λ = λ_min + log10(#majority/#instance)×λ_min). Compared against 30 ensembles on 24 imbalanced real datasets, 36 imbalanced generators, and 12 drifting-imbalance generators; best mean Kappa 63.65 vs next-best 57.85 (KUE) at static imbalance, 59.95 vs 54.45 (LB) under drifting imbalance, and most noise-robust (Kappa 59.95→36.54 at 0→40% noise, rank 1.70); ablation: 1→10 adaptation epochs raises F1 0.965→0.983; runs on a 384 GB Xeon. Immediate labels only; its background-ensemble adaptation pattern informs Ch2 and the adaptation side of Ch3. Verified: ✅

[Carneiro, Guimarães, Silva & Novais 2021] — A Predictive and User-Centric Approach to Machine Learning in Data Streaming Scenarios. Neurocomputing (preprint May 2021). Meta-learning predicts whether retraining a model on new data will improve performance before spending the compute, paired with an explainable interface; meta-model trained on 673 meta-instances from 47 datasets (53 total), 10-fold CV RMSE 0.000355, r² 0.98, MAE 0.007, re-trained every 2,000 streamed instances; batch-test RMSE predictions 0.111 vs 0.102 observed (wine), 0.321 vs 0.400 (diabetes), 0.093 vs 0.161 (breast cancer). Relevant to Ch2's adaptation-cost framing and selective adaptation, not delayed-label detection. Verified: ⚠️ (full text in Material; DOI inferred from filename — verify before citing)

[Mello, Gomes, Bifet & Pfahringer 2021] — Stream-Based Active Learning for Sliding Windows under the Influence of Verification Latency. Machine Learning (online 2021). Forgetting and Simulating: simulates the learner's future state at label-arrival time to improve utility estimates. Our notes log only the qualitative improvement claim under constant and variable latency. Adjacent to our selective-labeling regime; not detector isolation. Verified: ⚠️ (DOI cross-checked in Gomes survey reference list; not separately fetched)

[Grzenda, Gomes & Bifet 2020] — Delayed Labelling Evaluation for Data Streams. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 34:1237–1266. Continuous re-evaluation: buffer predictions and re-poll the evolving model before the delayed label arrives, scoring binned predictions (initial / periodic / test-then-train). Applied to Hyperplane (delay 100), LED (1000), AGRAWAL (1000, 4 gradual drifts), Airlines (natural latency up to 13 h), Electricity (~1–2 days), Forest cover (1000); recommends K=10 re-polls and B=50 bins (50–100 validated); open-source MOA implementation. The standard evaluation protocol for delayed-label streams — Ch3 should use it, not reinvent it. Verified: ✅

[Dal Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2015] — Credit Card Fraud Detection and Concept-Drift Adaptation with Delayed Supervised Information. IEEE IJCNN. Shows immediate investigator feedback and delayed chargeback labels carry different information, and that separate models with output aggregation beat identical treatment. Our notes hold only the qualitative improvement claim. Empirical anchor for the fraud dataset story and the two-signal structure of our hybrid. Verified: ⚠️ (citation cross-checked in Gomes survey reference list; Semantic Scholar fetch bot-walled)

[Joulani, György & Szepesvári 2013] — Online Learning under Delayed Feedback. ICML, PMLR 28(3):1453–1461. Theoretical: delay multiplies regret in adversarial online learning and adds it in stochastic settings, with black-box meta-algorithms for delayed feedback. No numeric results (theory). The regret-side cousin of our reaction floor — cite for the theoretical framing of delay costs. Verified: ✅

[Masud, Gao, Khan, Han & Thuraisingham 2011] — Classification and Novel Class Detection in Concept-Drifting Data Streams under Time Constraints. IEEE TKDE. Foundational quick-reference item: delayed labels plus concept evolution; no numbers logged. Verified: — (foundational quick-reference; unflagged in index)

[Žliobaitė 2010] — Change with Delayed Labeling: When is it Detectable? IEEE ICDM Workshops. Analytical conditions for which drift types are detectable without new labels — pure posterior drift with fixed P(X) is not — which is the direct basis of our Lemma 4; two drift types empirically evaluated, no numeric results in our notes. Does not propose a hybrid architecture, which is why the hybrid remains open. Verified: ✅

[Kuncheva & Sánchez 2008] — Nearest Neighbour Classifiers for Streaming Data with Delayed Labelling. IEEE ICDM. Foundational quick-reference item: early delayed-label classification work; no numbers logged. Verified: — (foundational quick-reference; unflagged in index)

docs.title: Ch3 — Hybrid / label-free + confirmation methods
docs.text:
[Shen, Ming, Li, Gao & Zhang 2023] — Unsupervised Concept Drift Detectors: A Survey. Springer (survey chapter). Surveys label-free detector families separately from supervised error-based methods. No numbers (survey). Catalogs the Stage-1 options for our hybrid; no delayed-confirmation treatment. Verified: ⚠️ (author list per Gomes survey; not separately fetched)

[Pinto, Sampaio & Bizarro 2019] — Automatic Model Monitoring for Data Streams. arXiv:1908.04240 (Feedzai). Windowed Jensen–Shannon divergence drift monitoring with alarm explanations from an auxiliary classifier. No numbers logged (qualitative-only from abstract). A label-free Stage-1 candidate for the hybrid. Verified: ⚠️ (arXiv abstract; cross-checked in STUDD references)

docs.title: Gap Analysis — The Delay Tax
docs.text: Written after logging the index and per-paper notes. Maps every entry to the four lemmas, confirms/revises the "active but fragmented" claim, flags scoop risk, and recommends the baseline to reproduce.

docs.title: 1. Is the field "active but fragmented, no accepted benchmark"? — CONFIRMED, with one update
docs.text:
The claim in idea/scope.md holds, but must be sharpened in light of 2026 work:

  • Active: Gomes et al. 2022 (CSUR survey), Alencar et al. 2026 (DSP experimental survey), Mello et al. 2021/2022 (verification latency in active learning), Botacin & Gomes 2024 (COSE label-delay measurement), plus the adjacent hybrid line (STUDD 2023; Gamma-Weibull 2026).
  • Fragmented: confirmed. Terminology still split (verification latency, delayed labelling, label latency, extreme verification latency, delayed partially labelled streams). No canonical formulation, benchmark, or protocol — the Gomes survey's unified setting is a proposal, not yet the standard.
  • UPDATE (important): the immediate-label side of the field has now gained a proper benchmarking framework — Cerqueira et al., KDD'26 ("A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods"). So "no accepted benchmark" is no longer true for the immediate-label detector benchmark; it is still true for the delayed/partial-label detector benchmark. Our gap statement must be reworded to: "there is now a standard benchmark for immediate-label drift detection, but no equivalent under delayed, partial, or selective labels."

Revised one-line gap: the field lacks (a) a detector-level benchmark under label-observation regimes, (b) formal bounds connecting label latency/coverage to detection quality, and (c) a standard confirmation protocol for early-warning + delayed-confirmation hybrids.

docs.title: Lemma 1 — Reaction floor (detection cannot precede label arrival)
docs.text:
• Partial treatment exists, empirically:
  • Gomes et al. 2022: AGRAWAL experiment — 10,000-instance delay shifts detections by ~10,000 instances; prequential accuracy dips below 50%.
  • Botacin & Gomes 2024: delay epochs map ~linearly to exposure increase; 81 epochs delay → +50% exposure; delay beyond that fully nullifies drift mitigation.
  • Joulani et al. 2013 (regret side): delay hurts learning multiplicatively (adversarial) / additively (stochastic) — the learning analogue of the floor.
  • No formal stopping-time bound (T ≥ τ + L_τ pointwise) exists in this literature. The classical quickest-detection-with-delayed-observations framing (Page 1954 / Lorden 1971 / Shiryaev) is the mathematical root, but no one has stated the reaction floor as a theorem for error-stream detectors under verification latency.
  • Verdict: the theorem is novel as stated (trivial to prove, novel to publish); the empirical phenomenon is already known — Ch3 must present the lemma as formalizing known behavior, and cite Gomes 2022 + Botacin 2024 as empirical corroboration.

docs.title: Lemma 2 — Power loss (1/√p sensitivity degradation under partial labels)
docs.text:
• Adjacent treatments:
  • Gomes et al. 2022 survey: SLT discussion — effective sample size = labelled count (the same intuition, not a detector-level law).
  • Alencar et al. 2026 (DSP): the experimental survey likely measures detector degradation as label availability decreases — must be read in full; if it reports a 1/√p-like curve for ADWIN/DDM, our contribution shrinks to formalizing the factor (still publishable, but the empirics are taken).
  • STUDD 2023: sensitivity analysis over l_access ∈ {1,10,25,50}% shows relative method ordering changes with label access — qualitative, not a law.
  • Verdict: the 1/√p closed-form bound for windowed error-stream detectors appears genuinely novel. High-priority action: read Alencar 2026 to confirm.

docs.title: Lemma 3 — False-alarm inflation under batch arrival (design effect 1+(b−1)ρ)
docs.text:
• No direct treatment found. Nothing in the logged literature studies batch/ bursty label arrival injecting autocorrelation into the observed error stream and inflating detector false alarms. The clustered-data variance factor is classical statistics, but its application to drift detectors under batch-reconciled labels is open.
  • Botacin & Gomes 2024 model queue size → delay, not batch correlation → false alarms; closest conceptual neighbor but not the same mechanism.
  • Verdict: the most clearly novel lemma. Least prior risk.

docs.title: Lemma 4 — Identifiability ceiling (pure posterior drift invisible to label-free)
docs.text:
• Already established. Žliobaitė 2010 (ICDMW) proves the detectability conditions; Gomes et al. 2022 reproduce the table; STUDD 2023 empirically demonstrates the limitation (cannot catch posterior drift, explicitly stated).
  • Verdict: NOT novel as a claim. The novelty in Ch3 must be the use of it: the hybrid confirmation protocol that makes it actionable (label-free early warning + delayed supervised confirmation is the information-maximal architecture). Present Lemma 4 as a formal restatement of Žliobaitė, credited properly.

docs.title: 3. SCOOP WARNINGS — read these before finalizing novelty claims
docs.text:
1. Alencar et al. 2026 (DSP 182:106325) — HIGH. An experimental survey of exactly our Ch3 setting (delayed + partially labeled streams, detector taxonomy, label-scarcity experiments). We have only verified it exists; we have NOT read its results. If it already contains delay-vs-latency curves and label-coverage-vs-false-alarm curves for ADWIN/DDM/KSWIN, part of our Ch3 "measure the degradation" chapter is scooped as measurement — our remaining novelty is then the formal lemmas (esp. 1–3) and the hybrid protocol. Action: read it in full immediately.
  2. Botacin & Gomes 2024 (COSE) — MEDIUM-HIGH. Already quantified label-delay cost on real malware pipelines + pseudo-label mitigation. Do not claim: "we quantify that delayed labels hurt." Do claim: detector-level isolation, formal bounds, confirmation protocol, synthetic ground-truth delay curves. Also do not claim a novel time-aware metric without contrasting with exposure/AUT.
  3. Gomes et al. 2022 (CSUR) — MEDIUM. The unified setting and the delayed-label AGRAWAL illustration cover our formal framing at a survey level. They explicitly flag "forget outdated labels after drift" and the under-explored intersection (iv) as open — cite them as naming our gap.
  4. Agu et al. 2026 (JKSU-CIS) — LOW-MEDIUM. Pseudo-label adaptation gated by a statistical detector is architecturally close to our hybrid, but it sidesteps delayed ground truth rather than measuring it. Distinguish clearly.
  5. Mello et al. 2021/2022 — LOW. Verification latency in active learning overlaps our selective-labeling regime; not detector isolation.

Net position: the combination of (formal lemmas 1–3) + (detector-level delay/coverage/batch curves on synthetic ground truth) + (a confirmation protocol, evaluated against naive-delayed, label-free-only, and immediate-label controls) remains unclaimed. The biggest single risk is #1.

docs.title: 4. Which published baseline to reproduce for Phase 0
docs.text:
Recommendation: Cerqueira et al., KDD'26 — "A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods."

Why: - It is the most recent (2026), venue-strong (KDD, open access, CC-BY, code public), and directly relevant: reproducing one of its detector comparisons (e.g., ADWIN vs DDM vs KSWIN on one injected-drift real dataset) exercises exactly the harness + metrics Ch1 needs. - It is immediate-label; that's fine for Phase 0 (we need the control numbers first) and it lets us later extend it with delay regimes in Ch3, which is a clean narrative: "we take the field's new standard benchmark and break it with delayed labels." - Feasibility note: it uses MOA-family methods (Java) for some detectors; River and CapyMOA both implement ADWIN/DDM/EDDM/KSWIN/Page-Hinkley, so a River reproduction of a subset (2–3 detectors, 1–2 datasets, abrupt + gradual) is realistic.

Fallback alternatives (if KDD'26 proves too heavy to reproduce): - Gonçalves et al. 2014 (ESWA) — the classic detector comparison; reproducing a headline number (e.g., no detector dominates on SEA) is cheap and citable. - Gomes et al. 2022 survey's AGRAWAL experiment — reproduce the delayed-label shift (~10k instances) as a sanity check that our harness correctly models delay; this doubles as a first Ch3 pilot result.

Recommended Phase 0 checklist: 1. Pin River version; verify ADWIN/DDM/EDDM/KSWIN/PHT implementations exist. 2. Reproduce one KDD'26-style detector comparison on a real dataset with injected drift (or fallback: one ESWA-2014-style SEA comparison). 3. As a stretch: reproduce Gomes 2022's delayed-AGRAWAL shift as the first delayed-label pilot.

docs.title: 5. What stays in the project (post-analysis)
docs.text: Item Status Ch1 baseline benchmark (immediate labels) Valid; now has a reference protocol (KDD'26) to build on Ch2 systems/ops chapter (replica divergence, backpressure, restart cost) Untouched by the whole Ch3 literature — still our most defensible novelty, zero scoop risk Ch3 lemmas 1–3 (floor, 1/√p, batch inflation) Novel as formal detector-level statements; empirics partially adjacent (Alencar 2026 to check) Ch3 lemma 4 (identifiability) Žliobaitė's result; ours only as restatement + hybrid motivation Ch3 hybrid confirmation protocol Architecture named as open by Gomes 2022 and STUDD 2023; no built/evaluated instance found — the central claim Delayed-label evaluation protocol Grzenda et al. 2020 (continuous re-evaluation) is the standard to use, not reinvent

docs.title: 6. Ch1 status update — direct streaming-vs-batch comparisons (added Sep 2026)
docs.text:
After web research logged into index.md §1 (subgroup "Streaming vs batch / retraining-policy comparisons"), the landscape for the Ch1/Phase-1 thesis question ("take non-streaming models and beat them on real metrics") is now clear:

Direct comparisons already exist — Ch1 is not novel as a paradigm comparison.

  • Read et al. 2012 (IDA): instance-incremental vs batch-incremental under drift — no universal winner.
  • Chen 2019 (SEAMS): retrained vs incremental on 1,360 conditions — winner depends on algorithm and drift intensity; incremental faster, often equal-or-better.
  • Amekoe et al. 2024: tuned frequent-retrain batch beats streaming under delay + rare class (already logged).
  • Applied 2024–2026 (Hans & Zühlke 2026 Water Supply; Abdoune et al. 2026 ESWA; Bartz-Beielstein & Hans 2024): online/incremental wins operationally under drift intensity and on runtime.

Scope-defining new evidence — Dasari 2026 (arXiv:2608.19488):

  • With per-sample incremental updates, retraining policy is irrelevant (54 paired comparisons, no practical difference vs no-retrain).
  • Without incremental updates, periodic retraining beats both reactive (drift-triggered / error-threshold) policies under abrupt and gradual drift; reactive only wins under recurring drift.
  • ⇒ The thesis claim must be worded about streaming learners, not about drift detectors used as batch-refit triggers. "Event-driven beats clock-driven" is only true when the learner updates per sample; a detector firing at batch cadence inherits the clock's weaknesses. Our thesis.md §1/§3 mechanism (bounded recovery via per-sample updates) already reflects this; keep it explicit.

What remains ours for Ch1 (defensible, narrow):

  1. The reactivity-metric family applied to this comparison — recovery time, damage area, rolling-Kappa dip depth, detection delay — none of the found studies measure these (they use mean accuracy/MAE and runtime).
  2. A fair, pre-registered protocol with frozen + scheduled + oracle-tuned baselines, ≥10 seeds, Friedman + Nemenyi, and an explicit win card (one claim per metric, dataset + number).
  3. Quantifying the scheduled-batch phase-noise effect (recovery time scatters uniformly over the retrain interval) rather than reporting one lucky schedule.
  4. The Delay Tax (Ch3) remains the project's main novelty; Ch1 is best framed as the rigorous baseline chapter the literature lacks (consistent with KDD'26 as the detector-side benchmark to build on).

docs.title: Statistical Drift Detection with Parametric Gamma–Weibull and Adaptive Deep Learning for Malware Detection in IoT Data Streams
docs.text:
Full citation: Agu, F. I., Andok, R., Klarák, J., & Dora, J. R. (2026). Statistical drift detection with parametric Gamma–Weibull and adaptive deep learning for malware detection in IoT data streams. Journal of King Saud University — Computer and Information Sciences, 38, Article 673. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44443-026-01091-w

Status: ✅ Verified (full text read from Material/)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: A 2026 hybrid drift-detection + adaptation framework that is the closest recent work to our Ch3 architecture in spirit: a statistical detector gates model adaptation, and adaptation uses auto-generated labels (pseudo-labels + clustering) rather than human labels. It is a strong "adjacent hybrid" citation and a useful contrast case.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Detector: Gamma–Weibull log-likelihood-ratio CUSUM. Pre-change modeled as Gamma(α₀, β₀), post-change as Weibull(k₁, λ₁); LLR per observation Λ(X_t) = log(f₁(X_t)/f₀(X_t)); CUSUM recursion S_t = max(0, S_{t−1} + Λ(X_t)); alarm when S_t ≥ h.
  • Threshold calibration: ARL₀ (in-control average run length) target 2000, with approximation ARL₀ ≈ (e^h − 1)/|μ₀|, so h = ln(1 + ARL₀|μ̂₀|).
  • Expected delay: E[D] ≈ h/μ₁ where μ₁ is expected LLR under post-change.
  • Adaptation: on alarm, buffer B of b=300 post-drift sequences; labels generated by confidence-threshold pseudo-labeling (τ=0.80) with K-means clustering for low-confidence samples; only the 66-parameter classifier head of an LSTM/CNN is fine-tuned (backbone frozen).

docs.title: Key numbers
docs.text:
Scenario (simulated, T=10,000) Detection delay False alarms Abrupt Gamma→Weibull 6 samples 0 Distribution mismatch (Lognormal post) 6 0 Gradual (window 500) 80 0 Mixed post-change 35 0 Noisy environment −3941 (false early alarm) 28 Detector comparison (20 replications, abrupt) Delay (mean±SD) False alarms GW–CUSUM (theirs) 43.0 ± 24.0 1.2 Page–Hinkley 125.2 ± 106.0 0.0 ADWIN 1.1 ± 1.2 1270.2 KSWIN 176.3 ± 272.9 126.2 DDM 425.9 ± 401.2 625.5 Model (full stream, simulated) Variant Acc Macro-F1 Weighted-F1 LSTM Baseline 0.987 0.977 0.987 LSTM Adaptive 0.991 0.981 0.991 CNN Baseline 0.823 0.457 0.745 CNN Adaptive 0.838 0.576 0.777
  • MC=30 Wilcoxon signed-rank: all adaptive-vs-baseline p < 5.7e-5.
  • Runtime (CPU): full pipeline 1.43 s; monitoring <150 ms; pseudo-labeling 2.4 ms; model+adaptation memory <50 KB (edge-deployable claim).
  • Real data: IoT-23 benign (n=451) and malware (n=14,784) duration streams; first alarm at t=31 (vs PHT t=75, KSWIN t=251, ADWIN t=7, DDM none); 714 alarms over stream (persistent deviation, not a single transition). Second malware family (Capture-1-1): Gamma fits better than Weibull — family-dependent.
  • Pseudo-label robustness: 30% injected label corruption drops LSTM macro-F1 only 0.0114 (0.8149→0.8035).
  • Honest limitation: Lognormal fits the data better than Gamma/Weibull; the pair is chosen for closed-form tractability, not best fit.

docs.title: How it differs from Ch3 / our lemmas
docs.text:
• Different signal. They detect distributional drift in the input feature (connection duration) via parametric LLR, not drift in a classifier's error stream. Our detectors (ADWIN/DDM/EDDM on errors) are the classical supervised setting; the two are complementary but not directly comparable.
  • No delayed ground truth. Their "labels" are pseudo-labels generated by the model itself — the delay problem is sidestepped, not measured. They do not quantify detection delay vs label latency, power loss vs label rate, or batch-arrival effects.
  • No formal lemmas. The ARL₀ approximation and E[D]≈h/μ₁ are classical CUSUM results, not new bounds about label delay.
  • Their detector-gated adaptation is a useful design contrast: adaptation only on statistically significant alarms (avoids unnecessary retraining) — aligns with our hybrid's "confirm before acting" philosophy.

docs.title: Recommended use
docs.text:
• Cite as 2026 evidence that "statistical detector + auto-labeled adaptation" is an active, viable pattern (and to show we are aware of it).
  • Their ARL₀ calibration discussion is a good reference for detector threshold-setting in Ch1.
  • Explicitly distinguish: they remove the label problem via pseudo-labels; we measure the label problem and confirm with delayed ground truth.

docs.title: Towards More Realistic Evaluations: The Impact of Label Delays in Malware Detection Pipelines
docs.text:
Full citation: Botacin, M., & Gomes, H. (2024). Towards more realistic evaluations: The impact of label delays in malware detection pipelines. Computers & Security, 147 (per ScienceDirect pii S0167404824004279). Author-hosted PDF: https://marcusbotacin.github.io/files/label-delays.pdf · Code: https://github.com/marcusbotacin/ML.delay.experiments

Status: ✅ Verified (full text read; COSE 2024 confirmed via GitHub + ScienceDirect)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: This is the closest published empirical treatment of our exact Ch3 problem: it measures, with real malware data and real drift detectors (DDM/EDDM), what label delay does to a drift-retraining pipeline — and it proposes the closest existing thing to our hybrid (a pseudo-label secondary classifier as an early signal).

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Setting: malware detection modeled as a delayed and partially labelled evolving data stream (explicitly citing the Gomes 2022 survey).
  • Pipelines: Naive Triage (no retraining), Triage-Update (drift detector triggers retrain), Triage-Oracle-Update (sandbox = oracle), and Triage-Oracle-Eager-Update (secondary classifier produces pseudo-labels to bridge the delay before the oracle's ground truth arrives).
  • Data: DREBIN (Android malware, temporally ordered by first-seen), 250 epochs × 500 samples; replicated on Androzoo (~284k samples, ~270 epochs).
  • Detectors: DDM and EDDM, epoch-level drift checks.
  • Classifier: Random Forest, FPR < 1% enforced, 10 executions averaged.
  • New metric: the exposure metric — cumulative sum of False Negatives over samples and days: Exp(samples; days) = Σ_day Σ_sample FN(s, d). Non-decreasing; captures how long a user is exposed to a missed sample.

docs.title: Key numbers (all from the paper)
docs.text:
Finding Number Drift mitigation reduces exposure ~50% Delayed labels increase exposure ~50% (up to 75% detection decrease) Delay at which exposure +50% vs immediate (DDM) 81 epochs (~⅓ of stream) Delay at which exposure +50% vs immediate (EDDM) 61 epochs Exposure increase per 10 epochs of delay ~50k points (DDM), ~60k (EDDM) Pseudo-labels reduce detection loss 30% loss instead of 70% loss 10% queue capacity ≈ equivalent delay 100+ epochs (oracle-only) Queue capacity with same exposure using pseudo-labels down to 70% (vs 100%) Metrics comparison (Table 4) AUT-F1 0.52→0.18 as delay 0→80; Exposure 0.49→0.90

Pseudo-label detail: with 21 epochs delay, mitigation strong; effect weakens to nil at 45 epochs, then reappears for larger delays (secondary model's own predictions become relevant again). Updating the secondary model on drift points matters (un-updated secondary degrades over time).

docs.title: How it differs from Ch3 / our lemmas
docs.text:
• Empirical, not formal. It demonstrates the reaction floor (Lemma 1) but proves no bound, and does not touch power loss (Lemma 2), batch autocorrelation (Lemma 3), or identifiability (Lemma 4).
  • Application-specific. DREBIN/Androzoo + DDM/EDDM only; no synthetic ground-truth drift positions, so no clean detection-delay curve vs label latency.
  • Pseudo-labels, not a two-stage hybrid. Their eager-update secondary classifier is a label-free early signal, but there is no explicit confirmation protocol, no warning-within-tolerance-window machinery, and no calibration of false-alarm cost of unconfirmed warnings.
  • Their exposure metric is a strong candidate for how we should frame Ch2/Ch3 "reality tax" results (time-aware, cumulative) — and we must cite it when introducing any time-aware metric.

docs.title: What Ch3 must NOT claim as novel
docs.text:
• "Delayed labels measurably degrade drift-based retraining" — already quantified here.
  • "A secondary/label-free signal mitigates delay" — already shown (pseudo-labels).
  • "You need time-aware metrics" — already argued (exposure vs AUT).

What remains open (our space): formal reaction-floor bound; power-loss law vs label rate on detectors in isolation; false-alarm inflation from batch arrival; identifiability ceiling; a confirmation protocol (early warning → delayed supervised confirmation → calibrated action) evaluated against both naive delayed-supervised and label-free-only baselines.

docs.title: ROSE: Robust Online Self-Adjusting Ensemble for Continual Learning on Imbalanced Drifting Data Streams
docs.text:
Full citation: Cano, A., & Krawczyk, B. (2022). ROSE: Robust online self-adjusting ensemble for continual learning on imbalanced drifting data streams. Machine Learning, 111(7), 2561–2599. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-022-06168-x

Status: ✅ Verified (full text read from Material/)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: ROSE is a strong reference for how modern adaptive ensembles handle drift + imbalance, and a useful comparator/design source for our Ch2 system chapter and the adaptation side of Ch3. It is not a delayed-label paper, but its background-ensemble + per-subspace-drift-detection pattern is exactly the kind of adaptation machinery our Ch2 service would run.

docs.title: Method (4 features)
docs.text:
1. Variable-size random feature subspaces per base classifier (normal distribution centered on μ·f, μ=0.7), giving diversity + noise robustness.
  2. ADWIN drift detection per subspace + background ensemble: on an ADWIN warning, a background ensemble is trained on the most recent per-class windows; after 1000 instances the top-k classifiers (by accuracy×Kappa) from the union replace the current ensemble.
  3. Sliding window per class (total budget 1000 instances, so 1000/num_classes each) — counters imbalance and, notably, latency of class arrival.
  4. Self-adjusting λ for bagging: λ = λ_min + log10(#majority/#instance class) × λ_min, λ_min=4; balances exposure of minority instances.

Complexity: O(2·k·λ·|S|) time; memory O((2·k·r·v·l·c) + (|w|·f)).

docs.title: Key numbers
docs.text:
Static class imbalance (Kappa, avg over 6 generators):

IR ROSE KUE ARF LB SRP 5 79.80 73.87 73.73 73.01 63.71 100 47.07 40.52 33.87 37.40 29.02 Avg 63.65 57.85 54.20 55.12 43.77 Rank 2.00 4.84 5.46 3.86 5.81
  • Drifting IR (Kappa): ROSE 59.95 (rank 2.23) vs KUE 53.24, ARF 49.08, LB 54.45.
  • Noise (Kappa, 0→40%): ROSE 59.95→36.54 (rank 1.70) — most robust.
  • Instance-level difficulty (Kappa avg): ROSE 71.47 (rank 2.72), SRP 65.02.
  • 24 real-world imbalanced streams: ROSE best on Kappa; SRP best on plain accuracy (metric matters!).
  • Ablations: buffer 50–500 stable; epochs 1→10 raises F1 0.965→0.983; K-means vs DBSCAN 0.973 vs 0.965.

docs.title: How it differs from Ch3 / our lemmas
docs.text:
• Immediate labels assumed throughout; no delay, no partial labels.
  • Drift handling is implicit+explicit but not the object of study — no detector-level delay/FP/FN metrics.
  • The per-class sliding window is motivated partly by "latency of class arrival" in real streams — an interesting hook connecting imbalance to label availability, worth citing in our selective-labeling discussion.
  • Strong methodological template: 30 ensembles, 24 real datasets, Friedman ranks, ablation study — a model for how we should present Ch1/Ch3 results.

docs.title: Recommended use
docs.text:
• Ch2: reference architecture for drift-triggered ensemble adaptation in a service.
  • Ch3 (adaptation side): a state-of-the-art adaptive baseline to include when we measure how delayed labels degrade adaptation (not just detection).
  • Methodology: emulate their experimental rigor (Friedman + ablation).

docs.title: STUDD: A Student–Teacher Method for Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection
docs.text:
Full citation: Cerqueira, V., Gomes, H. M., Bifet, A., & Torgo, L. (2023). STUDD: A student–teacher method for unsupervised concept drift detection. Machine Learning, 112(11), 4351–4378. (Online 21 Jun 2022.) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-022-06188-7

Status: ✅ Verified (Springer full text read)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: STUDD is the strongest candidate for the label-free early-warning stage (Stage 1) of our hybrid detector. It detects drift without any labels after deployment, and it explicitly documents the exact limitation (inability to catch posterior drift) that our Lemma 4 formalizes and that motivates the hybrid's supervised confirmation stage.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Teacher = the deployed classifier. Student = a model trained to mimic the teacher's predictions on the training set (model-compression style).
  • At run time, drift is detected by feeding the student's mimicking loss L(ŷ_T, ŷ_S) — the discrepancy between teacher and student predictions — into a standard detector (Page–Hinkley with δ=0.001).
  • On alarm, the classifier is retrained on the most recent window W.

docs.title: Experimental setup
docs.text:
• 19 benchmark streams (Electricity, Forest Covertype, Poker, Gas, Ozone, NOAA, Insects, etc.), truncated to 150k observations; W=2000 (500 for small sets).
  • Baselines: BL-st (static), BL-ret (periodic retrain); unsupervised OS/OF/FF (Žliobaitė-style output sliding/fixed, feature-fixed dos Reis et al.); supervised SS/DSS/WS/DWS (strong / delayed-strong / weak / delayed-weak).
  • Label-access parameters: l_access ∈ {1,10,25,50}%, l_delay ∈ {250..4000}.

docs.title: Key numbers
docs.text:
Metric Value Missed-detection ratio (MDR) ~19% (3/16 datasets; tied with DWS) Label efficiency best among non-baseline methods Predictive performance vs supervised often equivalent, or loses significantly vs unsupervised (OS/OF/FF) equivalent; ~25% prob of losing to FF Labeling cost vs all others wins significantly (Bayes sign test, ROPE 5%) Sensitivity to l_access STUDD relatively better as label availability drops; at l_access=50% it is worst

STUDD is conservative (few alarms) — good when false alarms / label acquisition are costly, which matches our Ch3 framing.

docs.title: How it differs from Ch3 / our lemmas
docs.text:
• Unsupervised only. It explicitly cannot detect real (posterior) drift that leaves P(X) unchanged — the identifiability ceiling (our Lemma 4). The authors say combining unsupervised detection with delayed/limited supervised feedback "may be worthwhile" — i.e., they name our hybrid direction as open work.
  • Its Page–Hinkley-on-mimicking-loss design is a candidate Stage-1 component, but there is no delayed confirmation, no tolerance-window protocol, no false-alarm-cost calibration for unconfirmed warnings.
  • It uses batch retraining (not streaming models), so it is not directly a Ch1-style detector benchmark.

docs.title: Recommended use
docs.text:
• Stage-1 baseline in Ch3 (label-free early warning), compared against the delayed-supervised baseline and the hybrid.
  • Cite when justifying the hybrid: STUDD's own discussion supports the need for supervised confirmation.

docs.title: When to Retrain: An Empirical Study of Retraining Policies for Streaming ML Under Concept Drift, Budget, and Latency Constraints
docs.text:
Full citation: Dasari, S. (2026). When to retrain: An empirical study of retraining policies for streaming ML under concept drift, budget, and latency constraints. arXiv:2608.19488. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19488

Status: ✅ Verified (arXiv record + full abstract; code public at github.com/sa1dasari/Study-of-Drift-Triggered-Retraining-Policies-Under-Budget-and-Latency-Constraints)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text:
This is the closest published answer to the teacher's Ch1 question — "take some models that are not streaming and beat them on real metrics" — posed at the level of retraining policy (clock-driven vs event-driven), not just learner type. It compares periodic retraining, error-threshold triggering, and ADWIN (statistical drift)-triggered retraining against a no-retrain baseline, under a unified system model that makes budgets and training-plus-deployment latency explicit.

Its headline result is a scope-defining caution for our thesis: the retraining policy is not the main lever — whether the deployed model learns incrementally per sample is. This forces our Ch1 claim to be stated about streaming learners, not about drift detectors bolted onto batch models.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Simulator-based controlled study; retraining consumes budget while a stale model keeps serving during training-plus-deployment latency (a queueing interaction).
  • Policies: periodic, error-threshold, ADWIN-triggered, and a no-retrain floor.
  • Grid: 3 drift regimes × 3 budget levels × up to 5 latency levels × 3 datasets × 2 learning modes (per-sample partial_fit incremental vs refit-only) → 3,933 runs; 54 paired comparisons for the incremental-mode analysis.
  • Learner: linear online learner; immediate labels (no delay regime).

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
1. Incremental learning dominates policy. With per-sample incremental updates, no retraining policy differed from the no-retrain baseline by a practically significant margin in any of the 54 paired comparisons — even at extreme latency.
  2. Without incremental updates, policy choice separates outcomes by 15–55 percentage points of post-drift accuracy, and simple periodic retraining significantly outperforms both reactive policies under abrupt and gradual drift.
  3. Reactive (drift-triggered / error-threshold) policies retain an advantage over periodic only under recurring drift.
  4. Systematic failure modes of reactive policies are documented, including a latency–budget queueing interaction that silently halves effective retraining budgets.

docs.title: How it differs from our project / Ch1 thesis
docs.text:
• Confirms our mechanism, redirects the claim. "Recovery is bounded because the model updates per sample" is the right statement; "recovery is bounded because a detector fires" is not — a detector firing at a batch refit cadence inherits all the clock's weaknesses (this paper: periodic beats reactive refits on abrupt and gradual drift).
  • Immediate labels only. No delayed/partial labels; leaves the Delay Tax (Ch3) untouched and supports our "reaction floor T ≥ τ + L_τ" framing as the extension.
  • Linear learner, three datasets. Narrower model/dataset coverage than our planned Ch1 sweep (trees/ensembles; real + synthetic with ground-truth drift).

docs.title: Recommended use
docs.text:
• Ch1 / Phase-1 thesis §1–3: cite as the empirical boundary of the "event-driven beats clock-driven" claim — the win requires a per-sample learner, and detectors alone (as refit triggers) do not beat a schedule except under recurring drift.
  • Ch1 protocol: adopt its "stale model serves during latency" simulator idea when justifying our scheduled-retrain baseline (the phase-noise argument) and when reporting throughput/latency.
  • Reproducibility: its public simulator is a candidate sanity-check harness before we build our own River-based one.

docs.title: A Survey on Semi-supervised Learning for Delayed Partially Labelled Data Streams
docs.text:
Full citation: Gomes, H. M., Grzenda, M., Mello, R., Read, J., Le Nguyen, M. H., & Bifet, A. (2022). A Survey on Semi-supervised Learning for Delayed Partially Labelled Data Streams. ACM Computing Surveys, 55(4), Article 75, pp. 1–42. https://doi.org/10.1145/3523055

Status: ✅ Verified (full text read via ACM DL)

docs.title: Why this paper matters for The Delay Tax
docs.text: This is the anchor survey for Ch3 and the single best "closest prior work" citation. It formalizes the exact setting our project studies (delayed + partially labelled streams), organizes the method landscape, and — crucially for us — includes an illustrative experiment showing what delayed labels do to drift detection.

docs.title: Core contribution
docs.text:
1. A unified problem setting. Defines a data stream as tuples {(x_k, ?)} (unlabelled) and {(·, y_k)} (labelled), a temporal-mapping function T(·), a verification latency V(x_k, y_k) = T(y_k) − T(x_k), and four label-arrival regimes:
  2. (i) Immediate + fully labelled (T(y)−T(x) = 1)
  3. (ii) Delayed + fully labelled (D random, bounded)
  4. (iii) Immediate + partially labelled (some labels never arrive)
  5. (iv) Delayed + partially labelled (both) — the regime we target.
  6. Taxonomy of SSL methods for streams: intrinsically SSL, self-training, learning by disagreement, representation learning, and unsupervised/SSL drift detection.
  7. Learning guarantees (SLT-based) for SSL, with the explicit caveat that a fixed JPD assumption breaks under drift.
  8. Evaluation review: test-then-train, prequential, continuous re-evaluation (Grzenda et al. 2020), Kappa+ / no-change baselines, and the need to report memory/time. They propose generating reduced partially-labelled streams by removing labels with probability p_u.

docs.title: Key numbers / empirical nugget (their small experiment)
docs.text:
Using AGRAWAL (100k instances, 3 abrupt drifts at 25k/50k/75k), a 10-learner SRP ensemble with ADWIN per learner, they compare no-delay vs 10,000-instance label delay:

Setting Effect No delay High detection rate immediately after each drift Delay = 10,000 Detections still occur but shifted by ~10,000 instances Prequential accuracy (delayed) Prolonged periods below 50% on a balanced binary problem

This is a direct empirical demonstration of our Lemma 1 (reaction floor): the detector cannot alarm before the delayed labels arrive. They do not prove a bound, do not isolate the detector's power loss vs label rate (our Lemma 2), and do not study batch-arrival autocorrelation (our Lemma 3).

docs.title: How it differs from what Ch3 proposes
docs.text:
• It is a survey; the experiment is illustrative, not a systematic detector benchmark under delay.
  • No formal bounds (no reaction-floor theorem, no 1/√p power law, no batch-correlation factor, no identifiability proof beyond citing Žliobaitė).
  • No hybrid detector architecture (label-free early warning + delayed confirmation) is built or evaluated.
  • Their stated open direction — "forget outdated labels once a drift has been detected" — is adjacent to our adaptation-side work.

docs.title: Formulas / bounds restated
docs.text:
• Verification latency: V(x_k, y_k) = T(y_k) − T(x_k).
  • They rely on Vapnik ERMP bounds with n = number of labelled instances: P(sup|R_emp − R| > ε) ≤ 2N(F,2n)exp(−2nε²); the key qualitative point for us: the effective sample size for any guarantee is the labelled count, which is the same intuition that drives our Lemma 2 (power loss ∝ 1/√p).

docs.title: Connections to our project
docs.text:
• Cite as the canonical formalization of the setting (our scope doc already does).
  • Their Table 1 (Žliobaitė's observability conditions) is the seed of our Lemma 4.
  • Their evaluation recommendations (report memory/time; continuous re-evaluation; Kappa+) feed directly into our Ch1 and Ch3 methodology.

docs.title: A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods
docs.text:
Full citation: Cerqueira, V., Gomes, H. M., Heyden, M., Pfahringer, B., & Bifet, A. (2026). A Framework for Evaluating and Benchmarking Concept Drift Detection Methods. Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26), V.2, pp. 8671–8682. https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3819070

Status: ✅ Verified (ACM DL full page fetched; open access, CC-BY-4.0)

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: This is the state-of-the-art answer to our Ch1 methodology problem: how to benchmark drift detectors fairly. It is the strongest candidate harness to reproduce for the "pin River version and reproduce one published baseline" pre-implementation task, and its metrics should be adopted in Ch3.

docs.title: Core contributions
docs.text:
1. Real-data drift injection via Monte Carlo. Instead of oversimplified synthetic generators, they inject controlled distributional changes into real-world datasets so drift position is known (supervised evaluation) while preserving real data complexity.
  2. Timing-aware evaluation protocol with new metrics:
  3. F1 detection score (combines precision/recall of alarms vs true drift events),
  4. normalized detection time (comparable across streams of different lengths).
  5. Leave-one-dataset-out hyperparameter optimization: tune on all-but-one dataset, test on the held-out one, to measure configuration robustness across heterogeneous stream dynamics.

docs.title: Experimental design
docs.text: Axis Value Detectors 14 widely used drift detection methods Datasets 7 real-world datasets Drift types class prior, label swap, feature permutation, feature filtering Transitions abrupt and gradual Metric emphasis F1-detection score, normalized detection time Availability all code and experiments public

docs.title: Key numbers
docs.text:
• KDD '26 acceptance rate 21% (1,157 of 5,395 submissions).
  • 0 citations / 315 downloads (as of Aug 2026 — brand new).
  • The paper's reference list is itself a useful Ch1 bibliography (DDM, EDDM, ADWIN, RDDM, HDDM, KSWIN, EWMA charts, Page 1954, Gama 2013, etc.).

docs.title: How it differs from Ch3 / our lemmas
docs.text:
• Immediate labels only. No delayed/partial/selective label regimes — which is exactly the gap Ch3 fills.
  • No formal bounds (no reaction floor, no power law).
  • It gives us the metric definitions (F1-detection, normalized delay) we should use to report our Lemma 1–4 experiments, and a baseline protocol (leave-one-dataset-out HP search) we should adopt for Ch1 and Ch3.

docs.title: Recommended use in the project
docs.text:
• Phase 0 baseline reproduction: reproduce a headline result from this paper with River/CapyMOA (e.g., ADWIN vs DDM vs KSWIN on one injected-drift real dataset) — a concrete, recent, citable published baseline.
  • Ch1: adopt their protocol (or explicitly justify deviations).
  • Ch3: extend their drift-injection framework with delay/label-coverage regimes; their normalized metrics make our delay curves comparable across streams.

docs.title: Batch-Incremental versus Instance-Incremental Learning in Dynamic and Evolving Data
docs.text:
Full citation: Read, J., Bifet, A., Pfahringer, B., & Holmes, G. (2012). Batch-incremental versus instance-incremental learning in dynamic and evolving data. In Advances in Intelligent Data Analysis XI (IDA 2012), LNCS 7619, pp. 313–323. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-34156-4_29

Status: ✅ Verified (Springer chapter page + abstract; 104 citations on Springer, Sep 2026). Full text not yet in vault — headline numbers to be extracted on full read.

docs.title: Why this paper matters
docs.text: The canonical, pre-Amekoe treatment of exactly our Ch1 axis: instance-incremental (streaming, one sample at a time) vs batch-incremental (gather examples, retrain on the accumulated batch) learning under concept drift. Written by the MOA/River core authors, it is the paper the field cites for "there is no blanket winner — the two paradigms have different advantages" — which is precisely the nuance our per-metric win card (thesis.md §1) is built on.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• First in-depth analysis comparing both paradigms, including how each adapts to concept drift, with an extensive empirical study over several versions of each approach (per abstract).
  • MOA-based classifiers; batch-incremental variants retrain on batches of accumulated/windowed data; instance-incremental variants update per example (detail in full text).

docs.title: Key findings (abstract-level; details to read)
docs.text:
• Both paradigms are dominant in the literature, but papers rarely justify the choice with evidence — this study supplies that evidence.
  • The results reveal respective advantages and disadvantages of each approach: no universal winner, consistent with the later, larger-scale studies (Chen 2019; Amekoe 2024) that report winner-by-algorithm, winner-by-drift-character interactions.

docs.title: How it differs from our project / Ch1 thesis
docs.text:
• No reactivity metrics. Comparison is framed around accuracy/adaptation behaviour, not recovery time, detection delay, or damage area — our metric family is not measured there.
  • Immediate labels assumed; no delay regime (Ch3 untouched).
  • 2012-era learner zoo (Hoeffding trees, ensembles) — our Ch1 adds the modern baselines (XGBoost scheduled-retrain, oracle-tuned) and per-metric statistics (rolling Kappa, Friedman + Nemenyi).

docs.title: Recommended use
docs.text:
• Ch1 / Phase-1 thesis §4 (Facts): the citation that "instance-incremental vs batch-incremental has been compared before and the result is context-dependent" — motivates why our claims must be per-metric and per-dataset, and why the win card structure (one claim per metric with dataset + number) is the honest presentation.
  • Do not cite it as "streaming beats batch" — it doesn't claim that.

docs.title: The assumption that gets dropped
docs.text:
Standard "batch" ML rests on an assumption so common it's usually invisible:

The dataset is finite, available all at once, and drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution that will not change.

Streaming ML drops all three parts of that. Data arrives continuously, you see each sample once, and the underlying distribution is allowed to change over time.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Batch learning (scikit-learn) Online / streaming learning (River) Data availability Whole dataset up front One sample at a time Passes over data Many (epochs) Exactly one Memory Grows with dataset size Constant / bounded Training fit(X, y) — from scratch learn_one(x, y) — incremental Prediction predict(X) on a matrix predict_one(x) on one sample Data representation NumPy array / DataFrame Python dict {"feature": value} Evaluation train/test split, cross-validation Prequential (test-then-train) Handling new data Retrain the whole model Model was never not-training Distribution changes Model silently rots Model detects and adapts

docs.title: The three hard constraints
docs.text:
Any algorithm that claims to be a streaming algorithm must respect these:

  1. Single pass — you cannot go back and look at sample #5 again. It's gone.
  2. Bounded memory — memory usage must not grow with the number of samples seen. A model that has processed 10 billion rows must occupy roughly the same space as one that has processed 10 thousand.
  3. Bounded time per sample — processing must keep up with arrival rate. If samples arrive faster than you can learn from them, you fall behind forever.

A useful test: if this ran for a year without restarting, would it still work? If the answer involves "well, memory would…", it isn't a streaming algorithm.

docs.title: Why anyone bothers
docs.text:
Two separate motivations, often confused:

(a) The engineering motivation — scale and latency. The data doesn't fit in RAM, or it arrives too fast, or you need the model updated now rather than after tonight's retraining job. Think clickstreams, sensor networks, network packets, financial ticks, log pipelines.

(b) The statistical motivation — the world changes. This one is more interesting and more researchable. Even if your data did fit in memory, a model trained on last year's data may be wrong about this year, because the process generating the data has changed. Batch learning has no mechanism to notice this. Streaming learning does. See 02 — Concept drift.

Motivation (b) is the better spine for a research project. (a) is an engineering benchmark; (b) is a scientific question.

docs.title: What "online" does not mean
docs.text:
Some clarifications worth having straight, because they come up in vivas:

  • Online ≠ real-time. Online means incremental updates. Real-time means latency guarantees. They usually co-occur but they're different properties.
  • Online ≠ mini-batch SGD. Training a neural net with mini-batches over multiple epochs is still batch learning — you're storing the dataset and revisiting it. Online learning sees each sample once.
  • partial_fit in scikit-learn is not the same thing. It supports incremental fitting, but the surrounding ecosystem (scalers, encoders, metrics, evaluation) still assumes batch. River makes the whole pipeline incremental — including the scaler, which maintains a running mean and variance and never sees a column.
  • Online learning ≠ the online learning of learning theory (regret bounds, adversarial settings). Related field, different emphasis. Worth one sentence in a related-work section, not more.

docs.title: The mental shift
docs.text:
In batch ML you ask: how accurate is my model? — a single number.

In streaming ML you ask: how does my model's accuracy behave over time? — a curve. Accuracy becomes a time series. Drops, recoveries, and how fast recovery happens are the interesting phenomena. Almost every good figure in this field is something plotted against "number of samples seen."

Next: 02 — Concept drift

docs.title: 02 — Concept drift (the actual research problem)
docs.text: If this project has a thesis, it lives here.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs. Formally it's estimating a joint distribution \(P(X, y)\), usually decomposed as \(P(y \mid X) \cdot P(X)\).

Concept drift is when that distribution changes between time \(t\) and time \(t+\Delta\):

\[P_t(X, y) \neq P_{t+\Delta}(X, y)\]

The world that produced your training data is not the world you're now predicting in.

docs.title: Two flavours — and the distinction matters
docs.text:
Real concept drift — \(P(y \mid X)\) changes. The relationship itself changed. The same input now warrants a different output. This genuinely breaks the model. Example: an email with a particular set of words used to be spam; spammers adapted and now legitimate marketing uses those words too.

Virtual drift (a.k.a. covariate shift / data drift) — \(P(X)\) changes but \(P(y \mid X)\) stays the same. The inputs you see have shifted, but the underlying rule is intact. Example: your user base expands into a new age bracket — different feature distribution, but the rule "high transaction velocity + new device = fraud" still holds.

Why it matters: virtual drift doesn't necessarily hurt accuracy; real drift does. Many "drift detectors" watch the input distribution and therefore fire on virtual drift — a false alarm from the model's point of view. Detectors that watch the error stream only fire on drift that actually costs you accuracy. This tension is itself a legitimate thing to investigate.

docs.title: Types, by shape over time
docs.text:
This is the taxonomy every paper uses. Assume the y-axis is "which concept is active":

SUDDEN (abrupt)         GRADUAL                 INCREMENTAL             RECURRING

 ────┐                   ──┐ ┌┐ ┌──┐             ──╲                 ──┐   ┌──┐   ┌──
     │                     └─┘└─┘  └───            ╲___                └───┘  └───┘
     └────────                                        ╲──

concept A flips        A and B interleave,      A morphs smoothly     A and B alternate
to concept B           B wins over time         into B                (e.g. seasonal)
instantly
  • Sudden / abrupt — instantaneous switch. Easiest to detect, most damaging on impact.
  • Gradual — during a transition window, samples come from A or B with shifting probability. Hard to detect: the error rises slowly and noisily.
  • Incremental — the concept deforms continuously through intermediate states.
  • Recurring — old concepts come back (day/night, weekday/weekend, seasons). Special because forgetting the old concept is actively wasteful — this motivates approaches that archive and restore old models rather than discarding them.

There's also blips / outliers — a one-off anomaly that is not drift. A good detector must not fire on these. This is precisely the stability–plasticity trade-off: react fast enough to catch real drift, but not so fast that noise triggers a reset.

docs.title: Three responses to drift
docs.text:
1. Blind adaptation (no detector). Just keep learning and let recent data outweigh old data — sliding windows, exponential decay / fading factors, or a learning rate that never goes to zero. Simple, always-on, but adapts slowly to sudden drift and permanently discards old-but-still-valid knowledge.

2. Informed adaptation (detector + reaction). Run an explicit drift detector. When it fires, do something drastic: reset the model, retrain on a recent buffer, swap in a background model that's been training in parallel. Reacts sharply, but is only as good as the detector — a false alarm throws away a perfectly good model.

3. Ensembles. Keep a pool of models, weight them by recent performance, drop the worst, add fresh ones. Drift handling is emergent rather than explicit. This is what Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) does, and it's the strongest general baseline. Internally it uses ADWIN per-tree — so it's arguably a hybrid of 2 and 3.

docs.title: How detectors work (the intuition)
docs.text:
Most detectors don't look at your features at all. They watch a 1-D stream of the model's errors (1 = wrong, 0 = right) and ask: has this stream's mean changed?

Detector Idea Notes DDM (Gama et al., 2004) Track error rate \(p\) and its std \(s\); warn at \(p + s > p_{min} + 2s_{min}\), alarm at \(3s\). Assumes error should decrease as learning proceeds. Weak on gradual drift. EDDM Like DDM but tracks the distance between errors. Designed to fix DDM's gradual-drift weakness. ADWIN (Bifet & Gavaldà, 2007) Keep an adaptive window; whenever two sub-windows have statistically different means, drop the older part. Rigorous guarantees, no window-size parameter, the de-facto standard. Page-Hinkley Sequential change detection (CUSUM family); accumulates deviation from the running mean. Classical statistics, sensitive to its threshold. KSWIN (Raab et al., 2020) Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between a sliding window and a reference sample. Non-parametric, distribution-based.

The trade-off is always the same: sensitivity vs. false alarms. Tune a detector to catch drift faster and it starts firing on noise. This trade-off curve is a perfectly good research object — you can measure it.

docs.title: Why this makes a good project
docs.text:
Because with synthetic streams you know the ground truth. You choose the drift position. That means you can compute things you can never compute on real data:

  • Detection delay — samples between true drift and the alarm.
  • False positives — alarms where no drift occurred.
  • Missed detections — drift that was never flagged.
  • Recovery time — samples until accuracy returns to pre-drift level.

Real datasets give you realism; synthetic streams give you measurable truth. A serious project uses both, and says why.

Next: 03 — The River library

docs.title: 03 — River: the library your teacher linked
docs.text: Docs: https://riverml.xyz/ · API overview: https://riverml.xyz/latest/api/overview/ Source: https://github.com/online-ml/river · Requires Python 3.11+

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
River is, in one line, "scikit-learn for data streams." It's the standard Python library for online machine learning. It was created in 2020 by merging two earlier projects — creme and scikit-multiflow — which is worth knowing because a lot of tutorials and papers still reference the older names.

Important framing for your report: River is your instrument, not your subject. The project is about streaming learning; River is how you run the experiments. Cite it (Montiel et al., JMLR 2021), don't make it the topic.

docs.title: The core API — four methods
docs.text:
Everything in River is built on a tiny interface:

model.learn_one(x, y)        # update the model with ONE labelled sample
model.predict_one(x)         # predict a label for ONE sample
model.predict_proba_one(x)   # predict class probabilities (classifiers)
metric.update(y, y_pred)     # update a running score — TRUE label first

The key detail: x is a Python dict, not a numpy array.

x = {"age": 31, "country": "IN", "amount": 240.5}

This is a deliberate design choice, not laziness. In a stream you handle one sample at a time, so vectorisation buys you nothing — and dicts let features appear, disappear, or be sparse without reshaping anything. It also means categorical features are just strings, no fixed-width one-hot encoding needed up front.

docs.title: The canonical loop
docs.text:
from river import compose, datasets, linear_model, metrics, preprocessing

model = preprocessing.StandardScaler() | linear_model.LogisticRegression()
metric = metrics.Accuracy()

for x, y in datasets.Phishing():
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)   # 1. TEST  (model hasn't seen this sample)
    metric.update(y, y_pred)        # 2. SCORE
    model.learn_one(x, y)           # 3. TRAIN (now it has)

print(metric)

Three things to notice:

  • The | operator builds a pipeline, same idea as sklearn's Pipeline.
  • StandardScaler also learns incrementally — it maintains a running mean and variance. It never sees a whole column. This is what "the whole pipeline is online" means in practice.
  • Predict-then-learn is not stylistic. It is the evaluation protocol. See 04 — Evaluation.

River also wraps this loop for you:

from river import evaluate
evaluate.progressive_val_score(dataset, model, metric)

Use the manual loop when you need per-step logging (which you will, for accuracy-over-time plots); use the wrapper for quick baselines.

docs.title: Drift detection API
docs.text:
from river import drift

detector = drift.ADWIN()

for i, val in enumerate(stream):
    detector.update(val)              # feed it a number — often the error (0/1)
    if detector.drift_detected:       # boolean property, checked after each update
        print(f"drift at index {i}")

That's the whole interface: update(value) then check .drift_detected. The same shape works for drift.DDM(), drift.PageHinkley(), drift.KSWIN(), drift.binary.DDM(), etc.

docs.title: Module map
docs.text:
Grouped by what you'd actually reach for. Full list at the API overview link above.

Getting data in - datasets — ready-made real streams: Phishing, Elec2, CreditCard, Bananas, SMSSpam, TrumpApproval, and more. - datasets.synth — synthetic generators, the important ones for research: ConceptDriftStream (injects drift at a position you choose), SEA, Agrawal, Hyperplane, RandomRBF, STAGGER, LED. - stream — helpers to iterate CSVs, SQL queries, arrays, and to shuffle/simulate delays.

Reacting to change - drift — ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, PageHinkley, KSWIN, HDDM_A, HDDM_W.

Models - tree — HoeffdingTreeClassifier (the classic VFDT), HoeffdingAdaptiveTreeClassifier (self-resetting subtrees under drift), regression variants. - forest — ARFClassifier / ARFRegressor (Adaptive Random Forest), the strong baseline. - ensemble — bagging/boosting variants: ADWINBaggingClassifier, SRPClassifier (Streaming Random Patches), LeveragingBaggingClassifier. - linear_model — LogisticRegression, LinearRegression, PAClassifier. - naive_bayes — GaussianNB, MultinomialNB. Cheap, surprisingly strong baseline. - neighbors — KNNClassifier over a sliding window. - neural_net — small MLPs. (Also see the separate deep-river project for PyTorch.)

Data handling - preprocessing — running scalers, encoders. - feature_extraction — aggregations, TF-IDF, target encoding. - feature_selection, imblearn (class imbalance), compose (pipelines, unions).

Other tasks - anomaly — HalfSpaceTrees, OneClassSVM. - cluster — KMeans, DBSTREAM, CluStream. - time_series — SNARIMAX, HoltWinters. - reco — recommender models. bandit — multi-armed bandits. active — active learning.

Measuring - metrics — incrementally-updated Accuracy, F1, ROCAUC, MAE, Rolling(...) windowed wrappers, ClassificationReport. - evaluate — progressive_val_score. - stats — running mean, variance, quantiles, entropy. - optim — SGD variants, learning-rate schedules. - base — the abstract interfaces everything inherits from. Read this if you want to write your own estimator, which is a legitimate way to add novelty.

docs.title: The one algorithm to understand deeply
docs.text:
Hoeffding Tree / VFDT (Domingos & Hulten, 2000) is the foundational streaming algorithm and the one most likely to be asked about.

The problem: a normal decision tree picks a split by scanning the entire dataset. You can't do that in a stream.

The insight: you don't need the whole dataset — you need enough samples to be statistically confident that the currently-best attribute is genuinely best. The Hoeffding bound tells you how many that is. It states that after \(n\) independent observations of a variable with range \(R\), the true mean is within \(\epsilon\) of the observed mean with probability \(1 - \delta\), where

\[\epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 \ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\]

So: accumulate statistics at a leaf; when the gap between the best and second-best split attribute exceeds \(\epsilon\), you can split now and never look back. The tree is built in one pass, in bounded memory, with a probabilistic guarantee that it matches what a batch tree would have chosen.

Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT) adds ADWIN to each internal node: when a subtree's error stream shifts, it grows a replacement subtree in the background and swaps it in. That's informed adaptation (02) built into the model.

docs.title: Practical gotchas
docs.text:
• metric.update(y_true, y_pred) — ground truth first. Easy to silently reverse.
  • learn_one returns None in current versions (older tutorials chain .learn_one(...) expecting self — that pattern is dead).
  • Dict keys are the feature names. Inconsistent keys between samples are allowed, which is powerful but means typos fail silently rather than crashing.
  • Everything is pure Python + some Cython — it is slow per-sample compared to a vectorised batch fit. That's expected and is itself worth measuring honestly.
  • Set random seeds on synthetic generators (seed=) or your experiments aren't reproducible.

Next: 04 — Evaluation

docs.title: 04 — How you evaluate a streaming model
