docs.text: This is where students most often go wrong, and where a careful project scores marks.

docs.title: The problem with train/test split
docs.text:
A train/test split assumes the data is exchangeable — that it doesn't matter which rows land in which half. In a stream that's false twice over:

  1. There is no "end" of the data to hold out from.
  2. Order is meaningful. If the concept drifts, a random split leaks future information into training. Your model gets to see post-drift samples while "training on the past," and the reported accuracy is fiction.

Random shuffling a temporal stream is the streaming-ML equivalent of using future prices to predict past ones. If you do it, your numbers are meaningless.

docs.title: Prequential evaluation (test-then-train)
docs.text:
The standard protocol, also called progressive validation or interleaved test-then-train:

For each arriving sample: predict first, score the prediction, then learn from it.

for x, y in stream:
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)   # model has NEVER seen this sample
    metric.update(y, y_pred)        # so this score is honest
    model.learn_one(x, y)           # now let it learn

Every sample is used for both testing and training, in that order — so no data is wasted and no data leaks. The measured accuracy is genuinely out-of-sample at every step.

docs.title: Cumulative vs. rolling metrics — pick deliberately
docs.text:
Cumulative (metrics.Accuracy()) averages over everything seen so far. It converges and becomes sluggish: after 100,000 samples, one bad stretch barely moves it. It hides drift.

Rolling (metrics.Rolling(metrics.Accuracy(), window_size=1000)) averages over the last w samples only. It reveals dips and recoveries.

cumulative accuracy          rolling accuracy (w=1000)

1.0 ┤                        1.0 ┤    ╭──────╮      ╭────
    │  ─────────────╲___         │────╯      ╲     ╱
0.5 ┤                            0.5 ┤            ╲___╱
    └──────────────────          └────────────────────────
         ↑ drift                       ↑ drift
    barely visible               clearly visible + recovery

Use rolling metrics for your plots. Report cumulative for headline single numbers. Saying why you did both is the kind of thing that earns credit.

docs.title: Metrics for the model
docs.text:
Standard classification/regression metrics apply, but note:

  • Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance, which is common in streaming applications (fraud, intrusion detection). Report F1 / precision / recall / ROC-AUC as well.
  • The accuracy-over-time curve is a result in itself, not just a picture. Its dip depth and recovery slope are what you're actually comparing.
  • Memory (model._memory_usage or sys.getsizeof / pympler) and wall-clock time per sample are first-class results in this field, not afterthoughts. Streaming ML's whole claim is bounded resources — measure it.

docs.title: Metrics for the drift detector
docs.text:
Different question, different metrics. These require known ground-truth drift points, which is why synthetic streams are non-negotiable for this part.

Metric Definition Good value Detection delay samples between true drift and first alarm low False positives (FP) alarms with no drift nearby low Missed detections (FN) drift points with no alarm within a tolerance window low MTFA mean time between false alarms high MTD mean time to detection low Recovery time samples until rolling accuracy returns to pre-drift level low

You need a tolerance window — a drift at index 5000 with an alarm at 5040 is a successful detection with delay 40; an alarm at 9000 is a false positive plus a missed detection. Define the window explicitly and justify it; papers vary, and being explicit about it is a mark of rigour.

The central finding to expect: no detector wins on all three of delay, FP, and FN. Sensitivity trades against false alarms. Showing that trade-off with real numbers is a legitimate result.

docs.title: Experimental hygiene (what separates a project from a demo)
docs.text:
• Multiple seeds. Synthetic streams are random. Run ≥10 seeds and report mean ± standard deviation, never a single run.
  • Fixed budget. Same stream length, same drift positions, same seeds across all compared methods. Otherwise you're comparing noise.
  • Statistical testing. For comparing many models over many streams, the standard is the Friedman test + Nemenyi post-hoc, visualised as a critical difference diagram. This is the accepted convention in the streaming-ML literature and using it signals you read the actual papers (Demšar, 2006).
  • A null baseline. Include something trivial — majority-class, or a model that never adapts. If your clever method doesn't clearly beat "do nothing," that's an important finding and you should report it rather than hide it.
  • Report the losses. If the adaptive model is slower or heavier, say so. A results section where the proposed method wins on every axis reads as unconvincing, not impressive.

Next: 05 — Project directions

docs.title: The trap to avoid first
docs.text:
"I applied River to dataset X and got 92% accuracy."

That is a tutorial, not research. It has no question, so it can have no finding. Nothing about it could have come out the other way.

A research project needs a question whose answer you don't know in advance and can measure. The template:

Under condition C, does method A outperform method B on measure M — and why?

Every option below fits that template.

docs.title: Option A — Drift detector benchmark under controlled drift
docs.text:
Question. How do ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley and KSWIN compare on detection delay, false-alarm rate and missed detections, across sudden / gradual / incremental / recurring drift, and how does that change with noise level and drift magnitude?

Method. datasets.synth.ConceptDriftStream — you set the drift position, so you have ground truth. Sweep drift type × noise × detector × seed. Report mean ± std.

  • Rigour: ★★★★★ — real ground truth, real numbers
  • Effort: ★★☆☆☆ — cheap to run, laptop-scale
  • Novelty: ★★☆☆☆ — this comparison exists in the literature; your angle has to be the specific conditions you sweep
  • Risk: low. Guaranteed to produce results.

docs.title: Option B — Does adaptation actually pay off?
docs.text:
Question. Do drift-aware models (Hoeffding Adaptive Tree, ARF, ADWIN-Bagging) actually recover better than static ones (Naive Bayes, plain Hoeffding Tree) — and what does adaptation cost in time and memory?

Method. Same streams, adaptive vs static models. Measure the accuracy-over-time curve: dip depth and recovery time after each injected drift, plus throughput and memory.

Why it's good. Produces the single best figure in this whole area — the "V" where a static model drops and never recovers while the adaptive one climbs back.

  • Rigour: ★★★★☆ · Effort: ★★☆☆☆ · Novelty: ★★☆☆☆ · Risk: low

docs.title: Option C — A + B combined ⭐ recommended
docs.text:
One coherent story in two acts:

Act 1: How well can we detect drift? (Option A) Act 2: Does detecting it actually help? (Option B)

Why this is the right pick. It's a complete narrative rather than a lone experiment. Both halves share the same infrastructure — one stream generator, one experiment runner — so the second act is nearly free once the first works. Every result is measurable against ground truth, it runs on a laptop, and it validates on real datasets (Elec2, Phishing) at the end for credibility. It cannot fail to produce results, which matters when there's a deadline.

  • Rigour: ★★★★★ · Effort: ★★★☆☆ · Novelty: ★★★☆☆ · Risk: low

docs.title: Option D — Online vs. batch: the real trade-off
docs.text:
Question. Against a batch model (scikit-learn) periodically retrained on a sliding window, how does an online model compare on accuracy, memory, latency, and total compute — and where is the crossover point?

Method. Same data, two regimes. Sweep the retraining interval for the batch side. Plot accuracy against cost.

Strength. The practical/engineering question a lot of people actually care about, and the resource measurements are concrete. Weakness. Easy to make an unfair comparison. You must be scrupulous about the batch model's retraining budget, or a reviewer will (correctly) dismiss it.

  • Rigour: ★★★☆☆ · Effort: ★★★☆☆ · Novelty: ★★☆☆☆ · Risk: medium

docs.title: Option E — Applied: streaming fraud / intrusion detection
docs.text:
Question. How do streaming models perform on a severely imbalanced real stream, and do streaming resampling methods (river.imblearn) help?

Data. datasets.CreditCard (0.17% fraud), or a network intrusion dataset (NSL-KDD, CICIDS2017) fed through river.stream.iter_csv.

Strength. Concrete application, easy to motivate, imbalance is a genuinely open problem in streams. Weakness. Ground-truth drift points are unknown in real data, so you can't measure detection delay — you lose the cleanest metrics from A. Also risks becoming a benchmark run rather than a question.

  • Rigour: ★★★☆☆ · Effort: ★★★☆☆ · Novelty: ★★★☆☆ · Risk: medium

docs.title: Option F — Build something: a hybrid or an ensemble strategy
docs.text:
Question. Can a meta-detector (e.g. requiring 2 of 3 detectors to agree before resetting) beat any single detector on the delay/false-alarm trade-off?

Method. Implement it against river.base interfaces, benchmark it with Option A's harness.

Strength. Highest novelty — you produce an artefact, not just a comparison. Weakness. Highest risk. It might simply not work, and you need Option A's infrastructure built first anyway.

  • Rigour: ★★★★☆ · Effort: ★★★★★ · Novelty: ★★★★★ · Risk: high

Sensible move: treat F as a stretch chapter on top of C. If it works, it's your headline contribution. If it doesn't, C is already a complete project and the failed attempt is an honest, reportable negative result.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Rigour Effort Novelty Risk A — detector benchmark ★★★★★ ★★ ★★ low B — adaptation payoff ★★★★ ★★ ★★ low C — A + B ⭐ ★★★★★ ★★★ ★★★ low D — online vs batch ★★★ ★★★ ★★ medium E — imbalanced application ★★★ ★★★ ★★★ medium F — novel method ★★★★ ★★★★★ ★★★★★ high

Recommendation: C, with F as an optional stretch chapter.

Next: 06 — Literature & landscape

docs.title: 06 — Literature and landscape
docs.text: Reading list and context. Citations are from memory — verify every one on Google Scholar before it goes in your bibliography.

docs.title: Read these first (surveys)
docs.text:
Start here. Surveys give you the vocabulary, the taxonomy, and a map of who did what.

  • Gama, Žliobaitė, Bifet, Pechenizkiy & Bouchachia (2014). A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation. ACM Computing Surveys. → The reference. The drift taxonomy in 02 is essentially from here. If you read one paper, read this one.

  • Lu, Liu, Dong, Gu, Gama & Zhang (2019). Learning under Concept Drift: A Review. IEEE TKDE. → More recent, more detector-focused. Good complement to Gama 2014.

  • Bifet, Gavaldà, Holmes & Pfahringer (2018). Machine Learning for Data Streams, with Practical Examples in MOA. MIT Press. → Textbook by the people who built the field. Available free online.

docs.title: Foundational algorithms
docs.text:
• Domingos & Hulten (2000). Mining High-Speed Data Streams. KDD. → VFDT / Hoeffding Tree. The origin of streaming decision trees. Understand the Hoeffding bound argument (see 03).

  • Hulten, Spencer & Domingos (2001). Mining Time-Changing Data Streams. KDD. → CVFDT — VFDT extended to handle drift.

  • Bifet & Gavaldà (2007). Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing. SDM. → ADWIN. The most-used drift detector; has actual theoretical guarantees. Essential if you pick Option A or C.

  • Bifet & Gavaldà (2009). Adaptive Learning from Evolving Data Streams. IDA. → Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT).

  • Gama, Medas, Castillo & Rodrigues (2004). Learning with Drift Detection. SBIA. → DDM, the first widely-used detector. Simple enough to reimplement yourself.

  • Baena-García et al. (2006). Early Drift Detection Method. → EDDM.

  • Page (1954). Continuous Inspection Schemes. Biometrika. → The origin of Page-Hinkley / CUSUM. Nice to cite — shows the field's roots in 1950s sequential analysis, not 2010s ML.

  • Raab, Heusinger & Schleif (2020). Reactive Soft Prototype Computing for Concept Drift Streams. Neurocomputing. → KSWIN.

docs.title: Ensembles (the strong baselines)
docs.text:
• Gomes et al. (2017). Adaptive Random Forests for Evolving Data Stream Classification. Machine Learning. → ARF. Your main baseline for Option B/C.
  • Gomes, Read & Bifet (2019). Streaming Random Patches for Evolving Data Stream Classification. ICDM. → SRP.
  • Bifet, Holmes & Pfahringer (2010). Leveraging Bagging for Evolving Data Streams. ECML-PKDD.
  • Oza & Russell (2001). Online Bagging and Boosting. → the Poisson(1) trick that makes bagging work in a stream.

docs.title: Tools and evaluation
docs.text:
• Montiel, Halford, Mastelini, et al. (2021). River: Machine Learning for Streaming Data in Python. JMLR 22(110). → Cite this for River itself. Non-negotiable.
  • Bifet, Holmes, Kirkby & Pfahringer (2010). MOA: Massive Online Analysis. JMLR. → The Java framework. Still the reference implementation for most algorithms.
  • Montiel, Read, Bifet & Abdessalem (2018). Scikit-Multiflow. JMLR. → River's predecessor. Cite when explaining River's lineage.
  • Gama, Sebastião & Rodrigues (2013). On Evaluating Stream Learning Algorithms. Machine Learning. → Read this for your methodology chapter. Justifies prequential evaluation and fading factors. Cite it when you explain why you didn't use a train/test split.
  • Demšar (2006). Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets. JMLR. → Friedman + Nemenyi, the convention for comparing many methods. Cite it when you do your statistical testing.

docs.title: Related but distinct — one paragraph each, no more
docs.text:
Mentioning these shows breadth; going deep on them derails the project.

  • Continual / lifelong learning (deep learning). Same underlying worry — catastrophic forgetting — different community, different methods (EWC, replay buffers). Streaming ML cares about bounded memory and single-pass; continual learning usually doesn't.
  • Transfer learning / domain adaptation. Handles distribution shift between two fixed domains, not a continuous stream.
  • Online learning theory. Regret bounds, adversarial settings, online convex optimisation. Theoretically adjacent, practically separate.
  • Time-series forecasting. Also sequential, but the task is extrapolating a signal, not classifying incoming samples under a shifting concept.

docs.title: The tool landscape
docs.text: Tool Language Notes River Python What you're using. Merger of creme + scikit-multiflow. MOA Java The original, from Waikato (the WEKA group). Most complete algorithm set; most papers benchmark here. scikit-multiflow Python Deprecated — merged into River. Many tutorials still use it; don't. deep-river Python River + PyTorch, for online neural nets. Apache Flink / Spark Streaming JVM Production stream processing, not ML research frameworks. Mention as deployment context.

docs.title: Standard benchmark datasets
docs.text:
Knowing these by name is useful — they appear in nearly every paper.

Real, with genuine drift - Elec2 / Electricity — Australian electricity prices, 45k samples. The most-used real drift benchmark. Caveat: known to have autocorrelation issues that inflate naive-classifier results — worth mentioning, it shows you read critically. - Airlines, Covertype, Poker Hand, KDDCup99, CreditCard (severe imbalance). - River ships several: datasets.Phishing, Elec2, CreditCard, SMSSpam, Bananas.

Synthetic (ground-truth drift — your main tool) - SEA — sudden drift via a shifting threshold. The classic. - Agrawal — 10 predefined functions; switching function = drift. - Hyperplane — a rotating hyperplane; the standard incremental drift generator. - RandomRBF — drifting cluster centroids. - STAGGER — small, abrupt, very interpretable. - LED — 7-segment display digits with noise.

All available under river.datasets.synth, and composable with synth.ConceptDriftStream to place drift exactly where you want it.

Next: 07 — Open questions

docs.title: 07 — Open questions (decide these before planning)
docs.text: Things that change what the project is. Not implementation details.

docs.title: 1. Which direction? ⭐ the big one
docs.text:
See 05 — Project directions. Current recommendation: Option C (detector benchmark + does-adaptation-pay-off), with Option F (a hybrid meta-detector) as an optional stretch chapter.

Nothing else can be settled until this is.

  • [ ] Decided: ______________________

docs.title: 2. What does your teacher actually want?
docs.text:
The word "research-based" is doing a lot of unspecified work. Worth asking directly, because the answer changes the shape of everything:

  • Is the deliverable a paper/report, a working system, or both?
  • Expected length? Is there a required format (IEEE two-column is common)?
  • Is a literature review a required chapter, or just background?
  • Is novelty required, or is a rigorous reproduction/comparison acceptable? → This single answer decides whether Option F is mandatory or optional.
  • Individual or group? Deadline? Any interim milestones?

  • Is River required, or just a suggestion? (It's a good choice either way — but if MOA is acceptable too, that's worth knowing, since more algorithms live there.)

  • [ ] Asked

  • [ ] Answers recorded here: ______________________

docs.title: 3. Synthetic only, real only, or both?
docs.text:
Recommendation: both, and say why. Synthetic streams give ground-truth drift positions (so detection delay is computable); real datasets give external validity. Using only synthetic invites "but does this matter in practice?"; using only real makes half the interesting metrics impossible.

  • [ ] Decided: ______________________

docs.title: 4. Scope guard — what are you explicitly NOT doing?
docs.text:
Writing this down early prevents scope creep later. Candidates to rule out:

  • Regression and clustering (stick to classification?)
  • Deep learning / deep-river
  • Distributed or production deployment (Kafka, Flink)
  • Unsupervised drift detection (no labels available)

  • The delayed/partial-labels problem — realistic, but a whole project on its own

  • [ ] Out of scope: ______________________

docs.title: 5. Do you need a "system," or just experiments?
docs.text:
Some teachers want something that runs — a live dashboard, a demo where a stream plays and you watch accuracy dip and recover as drift hits. That's a genuinely compelling demo and not much extra work on top of Option C, since the data is already being logged per-step.

  • [ ] Needed? ______________________

docs.title: 6. Practical constraints
docs.text:
• Machine: RAM, CPU cores? (Option C is laptop-scale; wide sweeps × 10 seeds are where it adds up.)
  • Time budget: weeks available?
  • Comfortable with Python, pandas, matplotlib? Any of these needing learning time?
  • Version control / backups sorted?

docs.title: Once 1–4 are answered
docs.text: Then we plan: environment setup, experiment harness design, the run matrix, and the report skeleton. Not before — planning against an undecided question wastes the plan.

docs.title: The problem with the old scope
docs.text:
The detector benchmark from 05 is good work, but it's 6–8 weeks, not a year. Stretching it to fill twelve months would mean adding more detectors and more datasets — more rows in a table, not more insight. Examiners notice that. A bigger table is not a bigger contribution.

So we need a bigger question, not more runs of the same one.

docs.title: The move: make it a systems question
docs.text:
Here's the thing nobody told you yet. Look at how concept drift research is almost always evaluated:

  • A CSV is replayed in a single Python process
  • Labels arrive instantly and always — learn_one(x, y) gets y in the same tick as x
  • No network, no queue, no concurrency, no backpressure
  • Success is measured almost entirely as accuracy
  • Nothing is said about versioning, rollback, audit, or reproducibility

Now compare that to how a model actually runs in production. Every single one of those assumptions is false. That gap is your project. And it's a gap that exists precisely because the field is populated by ML researchers, not infrastructure people. You're walking in with the exact background that's missing.

Thesis spine: Streaming ML works in simulation. Does it work in production? Build the system, find where it breaks, fix one thing properly.

That's a year. It's genuinely novel. And roughly 70% of it is systems engineering, which is your day job.

docs.title: The specific gap worth attacking: delayed labels
docs.text:
This is the sharpest version of the problem, and worth understanding fully because it's likely your core contribution.

In every paper: sample x arrives, and its true label y arrives with it. The model predicts, is immediately told whether it was right, and learns.

In reality: you approve a transaction now. You find out it was fraudulent 30–90 days later, when the chargeback lands. You show an ad now. You learn whether it converted next week. You flag a login as suspicious now. You find out when the user complains, or never.

Follow the consequence, because it's not obvious and it's nasty:

A drift detector works by watching the model's error stream. If labels are 30 days late, the error stream is 30 days late. So you detect drift 30 days after it happened — and you've been silently wrong for a month.

It gets worse. The standard evaluation protocol itself breaks: prequential evaluation (04) assumes you can score each prediction as it happens. Under delayed labels you cannot even measure your own accuracy in real time, let alone react to it. The instrument the entire field uses to measure success doesn't work in the setting the field claims to serve.

That's a real research gap. And the way out is interesting:

  • Unsupervised drift detection — watch the input distribution P(X) instead of the error stream. No labels needed, so no delay. But it fires on harmless changes too (virtual drift, 02).
  • Hybrid — use the label-free signal for an early warning, then confirm with the delayed supervised signal when it eventually arrives.

Designing, building, and evaluating that hybrid is a legitimate contribution. It's also — conveniently — a queueing and state-management problem, which is your turf.

docs.title: Secondary gap: operating a model that never stops training
docs.text:
A batch model is an artifact. model_v3.pkl sits in blob storage. It's immutable, versioned, hashable, rollback-able. Standard deployment.

A streaming model has no artifact. It's a mutating in-memory process. So every operational practice you rely on quietly breaks:

You normally do With a streaming model Roll back to the last good version Roll back to what? There are no versions. Pin a build for reproducibility State depends on every event ever seen, in order A/B test v2 against v1 Both keep changing while you test Audit "why was I denied in March?" That model state no longer exists Restart a pod You just lost all learned state Scale to 3 replicas Three models now diverge — which one is the model?

That last row is worth sitting with. Horizontally scaling a stateful learner is an open problem. Nobody has a clean answer. You're allowed to just measure how bad the divergence gets — that alone is a publishable observation.

This chapter is nearly pure infra, and it's underexplored because ML researchers don't run production systems.

docs.title: The year, in phases
docs.text: Assume this runs alongside coursework — call it 10–15 hours/week, not full time. Deliberate slack is built in.

docs.title: Phase 0 — Orientation (Weeks 1–4)
docs.text: Understand the field well enough to know what's already done. - Deep literature survey (see research/perplexity-prompts.md) - Get River running; reproduce a published baseline number - Deliverable: annotated bibliography + a working hello-world stream - Checkpoint: can you explain concept drift to a classmate in 5 minutes?

docs.title: Phase 1 — The offline baseline (Weeks 5–12)
docs.text: The original Option C, now correctly sized as one chapter, not the project. - Detector benchmark under controlled synthetic drift - Adaptive vs static models: dip depth, recovery time, memory, throughput - Deliverable: a reusable experiment harness + your first real results - Why it matters: this is your control condition. Everything later is measured against "what the literature says happens." You need the idealised numbers before you can show reality is worse.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Build the real system (Weeks 13–24)
docs.text: The infrastructure spine. Your home turf, and the part that makes this a major project rather than a notebook. - Event source (Kafka / Redpanda / Redis Streams — your call) - A model service exposing POST /predict and consuming a learning stream - Metrics → Prometheus, dashboards → Grafana - Drift detection running as a live monitor, not an offline script - Load generation so you can push it until something breaks - Deliverable: a running system, containerised, reproducible - Chapter: "an architecture for continual learning in production"

docs.title: Phase 3 — Break it, measure it (Weeks 25–32)
docs.text: Now the research gets interesting, because you can ask questions nobody has data on. - What does drift adaptation cost — p50/p99 prediction latency, throughput ceiling? - What happens when a model reset coincides with peak load? - How do replicas diverge when you scale out? How fast? - What happens under backpressure — do you drop learning or drop serving? - Restart/recovery: how expensive is checkpointing model state? - Deliverable: the "reality tax" chapter — the operational cost the literature never reports

docs.title: Phase 4 — The delayed-label contribution (Weeks 33–44)
docs.text: The core novel work. - Simulate realistic label delay (fixed, variable, partial, never-arriving) - Show that standard detectors degrade badly — quantify it - Build the hybrid: unsupervised early-warning + delayed supervised confirmation - Evaluate against the Phase 1 baselines - Deliverable: your actual contribution - Fallback: if the hybrid doesn't beat the baselines, that's still a result. "We quantified how much delayed labels break existing methods, and show why the obvious fix is insufficient" is a perfectly good chapter. You cannot fail this phase, which is exactly why it's the one to bet on.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Write up (Weeks 45–52)
docs.text:
• Full report, figures, statistical testing
  • Clean the repo, write a proper README, make it reproducible
  • Prepare the demo (a live drift-and-recovery dashboard is a genuinely good viva prop)

docs.title: What this gets you
docs.text:
Three chapters that each stand alone, in increasing order of novelty:

  1. Baseline — "here's what the literature says happens" (safe, guaranteed)
  2. System — "here's what happens when you actually deploy it" (novel, infra-heavy)
  3. Contribution — "here's a gap, and here's my attempt at it" (the research)

If Phase 4 goes badly, you still have 1 and 2 and a complete project. If Phase 2 runs long, Phase 3 can shrink. The failure modes are all survivable, which is what you want when you've never done this before.

docs.title: Scope guards — write these down and defend them
docs.text:
Things it will be tempting to add. Don't.

  • ❌ Deep learning / online neural nets — different field, huge time sink
  • ❌ Regression, clustering, recommendation — classification only
  • ❌ Distributed training (parameter servers, federated learning) — a PhD, not this
  • ❌ Building your own streaming framework — use River
  • ❌ Multi-cloud / k8s production-grade deploy — docker-compose is sufficient and nobody will mark you down for it
  • ❌ More than ~3 real datasets

The single most common way student projects fail is scope creep, not difficulty.

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text:
• [ ] Does your teacher require novelty, or is rigorous comparison enough?
  • [ ] Report only, or report + working system? (This scope assumes both)
  • [ ] Is there a required format (IEEE two-column?) and length?
  • [ ] Interim milestones / review presentations during the year?
  • [ ] Individual or group?

See research/perplexity-prompts.md for the literature survey prompts. Phase 0 starts there — you need to confirm the gap is real before betting a year on it.

docs.title: Literature Survey: Online Learning and Concept Drift Adaptation
1.1 Origins
docs.text:
Online learning predates modern stream mining. Its roots include stochastic approximation, the perceptron, adaptive filters, sequential Bayesian inference, and incremental statistics. The modern data-stream-mining field emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s because databases and sensor systems began producing data that were effectively unbounded, arrived continuously, and could not be stored or repeatedly scanned.

The central constraints are:

  • Each example may be observed only once.
  • The stream may be too large to store.
  • Predictions must be available while learning continues.
  • Computation and memory per instance should be bounded.
  • The data-generating process may be non-stationary.

Domingos and Hulten’s VFDT paper is generally regarded as a foundational stream-classification work: it showed that a decision tree could be learned in one pass, with constant memory per leaf, using the Hoeffding bound to approximate the tree that would have been learned from a much larger batch. The MOA framework later consolidated stream generators, online classifiers, ensembles, drift detectors, and evaluation protocols into a common research platform. oamonitor.ireland.openaire

docs.title: 1.2 Important distinctions
docs.text:
Let a stream be

\[ S=\{(x_t,y_t)\}_{t=1}^{\infty}, \]

where \(x_t\) is observed at time \(t\), and \(y_t\) may arrive immediately or after a delay.

Term Meaning Typical constraint Batch learning Train on a fixed dataset, usually with multiple passes and random access Data are assumed to be available before training Incremental learning Update an existing model with new observations or mini-batches May support repeated passes over stored data Online learning Update sequentially, usually one example at a time, while making predictions continuously Often single-pass and bounded-memory Stream mining Online/incremental learning under potentially unbounded arrival, resource, and non-stationarity constraints Emphasizes throughput, memory, latency, and adaptation Continual learning Learning sequential tasks or experiences while controlling forgetting Usually broader than classical stream mining Test-then-train Predict on \(x_t\), receive \(y_t\), evaluate, then update Standard prequential protocol

“Online” and “incremental” are therefore not exact synonyms. A system that periodically retrains on a growing database is incremental but not necessarily online. Conversely, an online algorithm may use mini-batches or replay buffers and still be considered stream-oriented if it processes data sequentially.

docs.title: 1.3 Concept drift and related shifts
docs.text:
A concept is often represented by the joint distribution \(P_t(X,Y)\), or, in supervised prediction, by the conditional relationship \(P_t(Y\mid X)\). Concept drift occurs when the data-generating process changes over time:

\[ P_t(X,Y)\neq P_{t+\Delta}(X,Y). \]

The practically important decomposition is:

\[ P(X,Y)=P(X)P(Y\mid X). \]

This gives several cases:

  • Real concept drift: \(P(Y\mid X)\) changes. The relationship being learned changes, so predictive performance can deteriorate even if the input distribution is stable.
  • Virtual drift / covariate shift: \(P(X)\) changes while \(P(Y\mid X)\) remains approximately stable. The model may remain valid, although regions of the feature space may become more or less important.
  • Label shift: \(P(Y)\) changes while \(P(X\mid Y)\) is approximately stable.
  • Prior-probability or class-ratio drift: Often used informally for changes in \(P(Y)\).
  • Feature or sensor drift: Changes in measurement properties, calibration, missingness, or feature semantics.
  • Novel-class drift: New target classes appear that were absent during initial training.

The literature does not use these labels perfectly consistently. Some papers call any change in \(P(X,Y)\) “concept drift,” whereas others reserve the term for changes in \(P(Y\mid X)\). Gama et al.’s survey remains the standard conceptual reference, defining drift primarily around changes in the relation between inputs and targets. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih

docs.title: 1.4 Formal drift types
docs.text:
The widely used four-way taxonomy concerns the temporal transition between concepts rather than only the statistical distance between distributions.

Drift type Formal intuition Operational consequence Sudden / abrupt A transition from \(C_a\) to \(C_b\) occurs over a very short interval Old model becomes obsolete quickly Gradual Examples from \(C_a\) and \(C_b\) coexist during a transition, with the probability of \(C_b\) increasing Detection is difficult because both concepts are temporarily present Incremental The target concept moves through a sequence of small intermediate concepts Short-term change may be almost invisible Recurring / reappearing A previous concept returns after an interval; recurrence may be periodic or irregular Reusing historical models can be beneficial

Bose et al.’s Characterizing Concept Drift is the work most commonly associated with formalizing this four-category characterization, including transition duration and the distinction between recurring concepts and genuinely new concepts. The earlier literature used related but less standardized terminology: abrupt and gradual change were already common, while incremental and recurring drift became more systematically distinguished in later taxonomies. arxiv

Two additional dimensions are important:

  • Magnitude/severity: How different \(C_a\) and \(C_b\) are.
  • Duration: How long the transition lasts.
  • Frequency: How often drift occurs.
  • Predictability: Whether drift is known, scheduled, seasonal, or unexpected.
  • Location: Whether all classes/features are affected or only a subregion.
  • Blip drift: A short-lived excursion followed by a return to the previous concept.

A recurring concept is not necessarily gradual. A stream may switch abruptly between two previously seen regimes, or transition gradually between them.

docs.title: VFDT / Hoeffding Tree
docs.text:
Domingos, P., and Hulten, G. (2000). “Mining High-Speed Data Streams.” Proceedings of the 6th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, pp. 71–80.

VFDT incrementally grows a decision tree using sufficient statistics at leaves. It applies the Hoeffding bound to decide when the observed difference between the best and second-best split attributes is statistically large enough to justify a split. The algorithm provides a probabilistic guarantee that, after enough examples, its selected split is close to the split selected by an ideal batch learner. The paper reports constant-time-per-example behavior and very high throughput. oamonitor.ireland.openaire

Influence: Very high; canonical, hundreds-to-thousands citation tier.

Important limitations are that standard VFDT is effectively stationary: once a split is made, it is not naturally revised when the distribution changes. It can also become biased by stale sufficient statistics, delayed labels, class imbalance, and high-cardinality attributes.

docs.title: CVFDT
docs.text:
Hulten, G., Spencer, L., and Domingos, P. (2001). “Mining Time-Changing Data Streams.” Proceedings of the 7th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, pp. 97–106.

CVFDT extends VFDT to changing streams. It maintains statistics over a sliding window, grows alternative subtrees when an existing subtree becomes questionable, and replaces the old subtree when the alternative becomes more accurate. Its goal is to approximate repeatedly rebuilding VFDT on a moving window while retaining near-constant processing cost. bibbase

Influence: Very high; canonical, hundreds-to-thousands citation tier.

docs.title: Important successors
docs.text:
• Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT): Adds ADWIN-based monitoring at tree nodes and replaces unreliable subtrees with alternatives. It is more local and adaptive than a single global detector.
  • Hoeffding Option Tree: Represents multiple possible paths and can improve predictive flexibility at additional memory and computation cost.
  • Hoeffding Adaptive Tree with Naive Bayes leaves: Often strong on streams where local class boundaries are approximately linear.
  • Extremely Fast Decision Tree: Reduces the number of examples needed before splitting and improves efficiency in some settings, but has less broad adoption than VFDT/HAT. ar5iv.labs.arxiv
  • Very Fast Decision Tree variants: Add numeric-attribute handling, improved split criteria, memory management, and better treatment of imbalanced or evolving streams.
  • Adaptive model trees and neural stream learners: More recent systems increasingly combine adaptive trees with linear models, neural networks, replay, or continual-learning mechanisms.

The major design pattern introduced by CVFDT—maintaining an incumbent model and testing candidate replacements—reappears in adaptive ensembles, drift-triggered retraining, and model repositories.

docs.title: Online Bagging and Boosting
docs.text:
Oza, N., and Russell, S. (2001). “Online Bagging and Boosting.” Proceedings of the 2nd International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, pp. 105–112.

Oza and Russell derive online approximations to bootstrap bagging and boosting. Each arriving example is assigned a Poisson-distributed multiplicity for each base learner, allowing a batch-style ensemble to be simulated in one pass. proceedings.mlr

Influence: High; foundational ensemble paper.

docs.title: Leveraging Bagging
docs.text:
Bifet, A., Holmes, G., and Pfahringer, B. (2010). “Leveraging Bagging for Evolving Data Streams.” In Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases, ECML PKDD 2010.

Leveraging Bagging strengthens online bagging using larger Poisson multiplicities, output codes, and randomization mechanisms. The method was designed particularly for noisy and drifting streams.

Influence: High within stream mining; hundreds citation tier.

docs.title: Adaptive Random Forest
docs.text:
Gomes, H. M., Bifet, A., Read, J., Barddal, J. P., Enembreck, F., Pfahringer, B., Holmes, G., and Abdessalem, T. (2017). “Adaptive Random Forests for Evolving Data Stream Classification.” Machine Learning, 106, 1469–1495.

Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) combines online random forests, random feature subspaces, Poisson resampling, background trees, and drift/warning detectors. A warning signal can initiate a background tree, while a confirmed drift can replace the incumbent tree. ARF is designed to diversify errors and adapt locally rather than rebuild the entire forest. link.springer

Influence: Very high for modern stream classification; hundreds citation tier and a frequent baseline.

docs.title: Streaming Random Patches
docs.text:
Gomes, H. M., et al. (2019/2021). “Learning from Evolving Data Streams through Ensembles of Random Patches.” Knowledge and Information Systems.

Streaming Random Patches (SRP) combines online bagging with random subspaces and random instance-feature patches. It often provides a strong accuracy–diversity–adaptation trade-off and is now a standard benchmark model in River, MOA-derived systems, and CapyMOA. dl.acm

Influence: High and growing; tens-to-hundreds citation tier.

docs.title: Current practical ranking
docs.text:
There is no universally accepted “state-of-the-art” classifier for all streams. The strongest repeatedly competitive classical baselines are typically:

  1. ARF, especially when drift detection and background learners are configured properly.
  2. SRP, often competitive with or better than ARF on heterogeneous streams.
  3. Leveraging Bagging and OzaBag/OzaBoost, particularly when computational simplicity matters.
  4. HAT, when a single adaptive tree is preferred for interpretability or memory constraints.
  5. Adaptive linear, neural, and continual-learning models, when the feature space is high-dimensional, temporal, or representation learning is necessary.

The field has moved since the 2017–2020 wave in four directions:

  • From proposing another detector or ensemble to measuring compute, memory, energy, and latency.
  • From purely supervised, immediately labeled streams toward delayed-label, semi-supervised, and label-free monitoring.
  • From small synthetic streams and Elec2 toward more realistic temporal, transactional, sensor, and industrial data.
  • From single-model adaptation toward model repositories, replay, meta-learning, online continual learning, and adaptive representations.

However, most post-2020 methods do not yet have the same independent replication base as VFDT, ADWIN, ARF, or MOA. Claims of state-of-the-art performance are often benchmark-dependent.

docs.title: 2.3 Drift detectors
docs.text:
Most classical detectors monitor a sequence of binary prediction outcomes:

\[ e_t=\mathbf{1}[\hat y_t\neq y_t]. \]

This means they detect changes in error behavior, not necessarily changes in the input distribution. A detector can miss covariate drift that does not affect accuracy, and it can signal because of noise, class imbalance, or a temporary difficult region.

Detector Mechanism Assumptions and strengths Main weaknesses DDM Monitors online error rate and its estimated standard deviation; signals when the current error is sufficiently larger than the historical minimum Very simple and cheap; designed for abrupt degradation Sensitive to noise, class imbalance, early unstable estimates, and gradual drift EDDM Monitors the distance between consecutive errors rather than error rate Better than DDM for gradual drift and changes occurring after a long period of high accuracy Still error-stream dependent; can be unstable with sparse errors or noisy labels ADWIN Maintains an adaptive window and repeatedly tests whether older and newer subwindows have significantly different means Nonparametric-ish adaptive memory; automatically shrinks after change and expands during stability Computational overhead; sensitivity depends on confidence, compression, and error distribution; may detect performance fluctuations rather than semantic drift Page-Hinkley CUSUM-like cumulative test of deviations from a running mean Cheap and useful for persistent mean shifts Primarily suited to sustained changes; parameter-sensitive; not inherently robust to autocorrelation HDDM-A Uses Hoeffding bounds on differences between historical and recent error means Statistical guarantee under bounded independent observations Independence assumptions are often violated; can be slow or conservative HDDM-W Exponentially weighted moving averages plus Hoeffding-style tests More responsive to recent observations and often useful for gradual drift Fading parameter and threshold influence false alarms and delay KSWIN Compares recent and reference portions of an error window using a two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test Can detect distributional changes in the monitored sequence; often strong on abrupt changes Sensitive to window size, dependence, continuous-value assumptions, and repeated testing; can be expensive FHDDM Uses a sliding window and Hoeffding bounds to compare the maximum observed correct-prediction rate with the recent rate Fast and designed to reduce false alarms relative to simple error-rate schemes Requires labeled predictions and can be less effective when drift is gradual or errors are sparse

DDM was introduced by Gama, Medas, Castillo, and Rodrigues (2004); EDDM by Baena-García et al. (2006); ADWIN by Bifet and Gavalda (2007); HDDM by Frías-Blanco et al. (2015); KSWIN by Raab, Heusinger, and Schleif (2020); and FHDDM by Pesaranghader and Viktor (2016). The exact detector configuration matters at least as much as the detector name.

docs.title: 2.4 Label-free and unsupervised detection
docs.text:
When labels are delayed or unavailable, the system cannot directly monitor \(e_t\). Label-free methods instead compare the current input distribution with a reference distribution.

Common families include:

  • Univariate statistical tests: Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Mann–Whitney, chi-square, population-stability index, and Jensen–Shannon divergence.
  • Multivariate two-sample tests: Maximum Mean Discrepancy, energy distance, classifier-based two-sample tests, and kernel change-point detection.
  • Density and likelihood monitoring: Compare current likelihoods, reconstruction errors, or density estimates with a reference period.
  • Representation-space monitoring: Embed observations using an encoder and test drift in the latent space.
  • Prediction-distribution monitoring: Track changes in \(P(\hat Y)\), confidence, entropy, calibration, or disagreement among an ensemble.
  • Model-based detectors: Train a discriminator to distinguish reference from current examples.
  • Change-point methods: Bayesian online change-point detection, Page-Hinkley-like tests on features, and sequential likelihood-ratio tests.

The crucial limitation is that input drift is not equivalent to harmful predictive drift. A statistically significant change in \(P(X)\) may be irrelevant to \(P(Y\mid X)\); conversely, real concept drift may occur with little detectable change in \(P(X)\). Recent surveys explicitly distinguish “label-free at monitoring time” from fully unsupervised learning because many systems still require a labeled reference set or a pretrained model. arxiv

docs.title: 2.5 Comparative evidence
docs.text:
Comparative studies generally reach three conclusions:

  1. No detector dominates across drift types. Detector rankings change with drift speed, severity, noise, class imbalance, base learner, and threshold settings.
  2. Synthetic benchmarks favor detectors whose assumptions match the generator. A detector designed for error-rate shifts can look excellent when the generator directly changes class boundaries.
  3. Detection accuracy is not enough. False alarms, detection delay, computational cost, recovery time, and downstream predictive accuracy must be reported.

A 2014 comparative study evaluated DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, STEPD, DoF, ADWIN, Paired Learners, and ECDD under abrupt and gradual changes, with noise and irrelevant attributes. A later benchmark of DDM, EDDM, HDDM-A, and HDDM-W found HDDM-W to offer a strong overall trade-off, especially for abrupt and gradual drift, but weaker performance on incremental drift. A 2024 controlled energy-and-accuracy study reported KSWIN as accuracy-oriented but more energy-intensive, HDDM-W and ADWIN as balanced, and DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, and HDDM-A as computationally cheap but often practically weak in that experimental setting. 2024.sci-hub

These findings are useful but not definitive. Detector comparisons are often single-study or small-family results, while the robust conclusion—“detector choice is data- and drift-dependent”—is well replicated.

docs.title: 3.1 Prequential evaluation
docs.text:
The standard protocol is test-then-train, also called predictive sequential or prequential evaluation:

  1. Receive \(x_t\).
  2. Predict \(\hat y_t\) using the current model.
  3. Receive \(y_t\).
  4. Record the loss \(L(\hat y_t,y_t)\).
  5. Update the model with \((x_t,y_t)\).

The cumulative prequential error is

\[ \hat L_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}L(\hat y_t,y_t). \]

For drifting streams, recent-window or fading-factor error is usually more informative:

\[ \hat L_t^{(\alpha)} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha^{t-i}L_i} {\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha^{t-i}}, \qquad 0<\alpha<1. \]

Dawid introduced the broader prequential perspective in statistical theory. For stream learning, Gomes et al. argue that prequential error with forgetting mechanisms is reliable: under stationary data and consistent algorithms, holdout, ordinary prequential, sliding-window prequential, and fading-factor estimates converge to the Bayes error. cs.ubc

docs.title: 3.2 Metrics
docs.text:
A serious survey or experiment should report more than mean accuracy:

  • Prequential accuracy and error.
  • Balanced accuracy, macro-F1, geometric mean, or Matthews correlation for imbalance.
  • Kappa and Kappa-plus, especially when temporal persistence creates a strong no-change baseline.
  • Prequential AUC or log loss when probabilistic predictions matter.
  • Detection delay, false-positive rate, missed-drift rate, and warning-to-drift interval.
  • Recovery time after drift.
  • Memory, throughput, CPU time, energy, and model size.
  • Statistical uncertainty across seeds and stream orderings.

docs.title: 3.3 Problems with standard practice
docs.text:
The main criticisms are methodological:

  • Temporal leakage: Random train/test splits destroy the temporal structure and may expose future regimes during training.
  • Unreported ordering: Some “real” datasets are shuffled, partially sorted, or distributed in ways that change the drift pattern.
  • One-pass claims with multiple passes: Hyperparameter tuning or repeated evaluation can violate the intended stream constraint.
  • Immediate-label assumption: Many applications have delayed, missing, selective, or noisy labels.
  • Single metric reporting: Accuracy may reward a trivial persistence predictor.
  • Detector-adaptation confounding: A detector can improve a classifier’s accuracy while producing poor drift timestamps, or vice versa.
  • Weak statistical testing: Many papers compare many algorithms on a few streams without confidence intervals, paired tests, or correction for multiple comparisons.
  • Synthetic simplicity: Standard generators often change only one controlled factor and do not reproduce real temporal dependence, missingness, or heterogeneous drift.
  • Configuration sensitivity: Results depend heavily on window sizes, confidence levels, grace periods, ensemble size, and random seeds.

docs.title: Synthetic generators
docs.text:
Common generators include:

  • SEA concepts: Abrupt threshold changes with controllable noise.
  • Hyperplane: Gradual or abrupt movement of a separating hyperplane.
  • Random RBF: Moving class centroids and varying drift speed.
  • LED: Irrelevant features and noise.
  • AGRAWAL: Rule-based concepts and controlled changes.
  • STAGGER: Small categorical concept space.
  • Sine and mixed generators: Boundary movement and feature/class changes.
  • Random tree and rotating-hyperplane generators: More complex evolving decision surfaces.

Generators are valuable because drift location, severity, speed, and recurrence can be known exactly. They are insufficient as the sole evidence because algorithms may be tuned to their simple mechanisms.

docs.title: Real datasets
docs.text:
Frequently used real streams include:

  • Electricity / Elec2.
  • Forest Covertype.
  • Poker-Hand.
  • Airlines.
  • NOAA weather.
  • Electricity pricing and demand.
  • Sensor, network intrusion, fraud, click, and industrial monitoring streams.
  • Image and text streams in newer continual-learning work.

docs.title: The Elec2 problem
docs.text:
The Electricity dataset is widely used but should not be treated as a neutral benchmark. The data are from the Australian New South Wales electricity market; the common version contains 27,552 complete records sampled from a larger set, with observations every 30 minutes and a binary label related to price movement. Documentation and preprocessing histories are inconsistent across implementations. search.r-project

More importantly, the sequence exhibits strong temporal dependence. A classifier that predicts the previous label or “no change” can be surprisingly competitive. Bifet and colleagues’ benchmarking critique argues that ordinary accuracy can overstate learning ability on Electricity and proposes temporally aware baselines and Kappa-plus-like measures. A later discussion also emphasizes that poorly documented “real-world” datasets can harm reproducibility and make apparent algorithmic improvements difficult to interpret. users.ics.aalto

Therefore, a defensible study should:

  • State the exact Elec2 file, preprocessing, ordering, missing-value treatment, and label definition.
  • Include a previous-label or no-change baseline.
  • Report balanced and temporal-aware metrics.
  • Avoid presenting Elec2 as evidence of general superiority.
  • Include multiple real streams with different dependence structures.

docs.title: 4. Tooling and research practice
docs.text:
Framework Language and status Strengths Limitations Research role MOA Java; mature reference platform Large collection of stream learners, generators, detectors, ensembles, and evaluators; historically dominant in academic stream mining Java integration overhead; less convenient for modern Python ML and deep learning The most established academic benchmark platform scikit-multiflow Python; largely legacy compared with River Accessible scikit-learn-like API, stream generators, multi-output learning, detectors Development and ecosystem momentum have shifted toward River and newer systems; slower in some benchmarks Important historical Python baseline River Python; actively used and broadly accessible Clean one-instance API, preprocessing, metrics, drift detectors, linear models, trees, ensembles, anomaly detection, and practical deployment support Pure-Python implementations can be slower than Java/C++; not every MOA algorithm is available Best general-purpose Python choice for prototyping and reproducible applied research CapyMOA Python interface over efficient MOA components, with integrations for PyTorch and scikit-learn Combines Python usability with MOA performance; supports classification, regression, clustering, anomaly detection, drift detection, and online continual learning Newer; smaller independent adoption and citation base; some evidence is currently preprint or project-reported Promising research platform for efficient Python experiments creme Python; predecessor to River Introduced practical online-learning APIs Superseded by River Historical rather than new-project choice Vowpal Wabbit C++ with Python bindings Highly efficient online linear learning and contextual prediction Narrower algorithmic scope; less focused on drift benchmarks Strong for large sparse linear streams scikit-learn partial-fit Python Familiar models and ecosystem Not a full stream-mining framework; weak support for drift-specific evaluation and adaptation Useful component inside custom pipelines PyTorch/JAX continual-learning stacks Python Representation learning, deep models, replay, adapters, and custom research Require substantial engineering for strict online constraints and fair evaluation Increasingly important for high-dimensional streams

MOA’s foundational paper is Bifet, Holmes, Kirkby, and Pfahringer (2010), “MOA: Massive Online Analysis,” Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11, 1601–1604. It remains the most influential stream-mining software citation. semanticscholar

Montiel et al. (2018), “scikit-multiflow: A Multi-output Streaming Framework,” Journal of Machine Learning Research, 19, 1–5, provided a Python framework for stream learning, generators, evaluators, and multi-output tasks. jmlr

Montiel et al. (2021), “River: Machine Learning for Streaming Data in Python,” arXiv:2012.04740, describes River as the merger of creme and scikit-multiflow, with a redesigned architecture for dynamic streams and continual learning. arxiv

Gomes et al. (2025), “CapyMOA: Efficient Machine Learning for Data Streams in Python,” arXiv:2502.07432, presents CapyMOA as a Python layer integrating MOA, scikit-learn, PyTorch, and stream-learning components. Its reported SRP benchmark was close to MOA and substantially faster than the Python alternatives tested, although these results are from the authors’ benchmark rather than a broad independent replication. arxiv

docs.title: Recommended tooling strategy
docs.text:
For a one-year Master’s project:

  • Use River for rapid prototyping, custom detectors, delayed-label experiments, and deployment-oriented pipelines.
  • Use MOA or CapyMOA for comparison against canonical literature and efficient large-scale experiments.
  • Reimplement or cross-check the key baselines in at least two frameworks when possible.
  • Record exact versions, random seeds, parameters, stream order, label delays, and resource measurements.
  • Benchmark ARF, SRP, Leveraging Bagging, HAT, a non-adaptive Hoeffding Tree, and at least one online linear model.
  • Treat scikit-multiflow mainly as a compatibility or historical baseline rather than the primary new platform.

The community most consistently benchmarks on MOA-compatible algorithms and datasets. River is more common in Python-centric applied work, while CapyMOA is a promising bridge between the two ecosystems. Adoption of CapyMOA should not yet be described as equivalent to MOA’s long-established maturity.

docs.title: 5.1 What is well established
docs.text:
Strongly replicated findings

  • Single-pass Hoeffding-style trees are effective, interpretable, and computationally attractive baselines.
  • Ensembles generally outperform isolated trees on heterogeneous and drifting streams.
  • ARF, SRP, and Leveraging Bagging are strong classical baselines.
  • Prequential evaluation is more appropriate than random train/test splitting for temporally ordered streams.
  • No drift detector is uniformly best.
  • Detection performance depends on drift type, noise, class imbalance, window parameters, and the base learner.
  • Realistic evaluation must include resource usage and delayed-label conditions.

Less settled findings

  • Whether detector-triggered adaptation consistently beats passive adaptation.
  • Whether explicit drift detection is necessary for strong ensembles.
  • Whether deep continual-learning models outperform well-tuned adaptive trees under strict one-pass and bounded-memory constraints.
  • Whether label-free input-distribution drift predicts degradation in task performance.
  • Which detector is best under gradual, recurring, multivariate, or high-dimensional drift.
  • Whether recent neural and meta-learning methods generalize beyond their authors’ datasets.

docs.title: 5.2 Main disagreements
docs.text:
1. Active versus passive adaptation: Active detectors can save computation and provide alerts, but false alarms and missed detections can damage the learner. Passive forgetting, sliding windows, fading factors, or continuously adaptive ensembles often perform competitively without explicit drift decisions.

  2. Error drift versus input drift: Error-based detectors are directly connected to predictive degradation but require labels. Input-based detectors work earlier in deployment but may detect harmless covariate shift.

  3. Synthetic versus real benchmarks: Synthetic streams provide ground-truth drift times and controlled comparisons; real streams provide realism but often have undocumented preprocessing, unknown drift locations, and confounded temporal dependence.

  4. Accuracy versus efficiency: KSWIN-like and multivariate detectors may improve detection in some settings while consuming considerably more time or energy. The best detector depends on the application’s cost model, not solely predictive accuracy. ieeexplore.ieee

docs.title: 5.3 Proposed research gap
docs.text:
A defensible Master’s project could focus on:

Resource-aware adaptation under delayed or unavailable labels, comparing error-based, input-distribution, and hybrid drift detectors with ARF/SRP/HAT across controlled and real temporal streams.

A strong experimental design would measure:

  • Predictive performance.
  • Detection delay and false alarms.
  • Recovery time.
  • Memory and throughput.
  • Energy or CPU cost.
  • Robustness to label delay, noise, class imbalance, recurrence, and temporal dependence.

This would address a genuine gap between classical detector benchmarks—which usually assume immediate labels—and deployment-oriented drift monitoring—which often lacks ground-truth labels.
