  20. Raab, C., Heusinger, M., and Schleif, F.-M. (2020). “Reactive Soft Prototype Computing for Concept Drift Streams.” Related work introduced and popularized KSWIN-style two-window Kolmogorov–Smirnov monitoring in stream-learning implementations. arxiv

  21. Rabanser, S., Günnemann, S., and Lipton, Z. C. (2019). “Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32.

  22. Žliobaitė, I. (2010). “Learning under Concept Drift: An Overview.” Technical report and widely cited conceptual survey.

  23. van der Aalst, W. M. P., et al. (2013). “Drift Characterization and Detection in Process Mining.” Related process-mining work contributed formal language for gradual, incremental, and recurring changes.

docs.title: Delayed labels
docs.text:
The problem is not solved, but it is also not untouched. There is a recognizable research thread spanning roughly 2008–2026, including a dedicated 2022 survey and a 2026 experimental survey focused specifically on drift detection with delayed and partial labels. However, the literature is fragmented: delayed labels, verification latency, partial labels, extreme verification latency, semi-supervised streams, active learning, and positive–unlabelled learning are usually studied separately rather than as one unified deployment problem.

The strongest conclusion is that there is still a substantial research gap in detection, adaptation, evaluation, and benchmarking under realistic label-observation mechanisms—especially when latency is stochastic, labels are selection-biased, some labels never arrive, and the data-generating process itself drifts.

docs.title: Overall volume and maturity
docs.text:
The literature falls into several partially overlapping lines:

Line of work Approximate development Main concern Delayed-label stream classification 2008–present Updating classifiers when labels arrive after the instance Detecting drift without current labels 2010–present Inferring change from \(X\), predictions, uncertainty, or representations Delayed-label evaluation 2016–present Measuring performance without immediate test-then-train feedback Semi-supervised streams 2009–present Exploiting unlabeled examples during drift Stream-based active learning with latency 2021–2022 onward Querying labels whose utility changes before the answer arrives Extreme or infinite verification latency 2023–2025 onward Learning and adapting when labels are very rare or never available Dedicated delayed/partial drift surveys 2026 Consolidating detector methods and experiments

The most important synthesis is Gomes, Grzenda, Mello, Read, Le Nguyen, and Bifet, “A Survey on Semi-supervised Learning for Delayed Partially Labelled Data Streams,” ACM Computing Surveys, 2022. It defines a unified setting containing both unlabeled observations and delayed or permanently unavailable labels, reviews semi-supervised and active-learning methods, discusses learning guarantees, and proposes changes to benchmarking practice. dl.acm

A second important synthesis is Alencar, Cassales, Gomes, Prazeres, Rios, Bifet, and Rios, “Concept drift detection in delayed and partially labeled data streams: An experimental survey,” Digital Signal Processing, vol. 182, 2026, article 106325. This is particularly relevant to your proposed gap because it organizes drift detectors under delayed and partially labeled conditions and experimentally examines detector performance as label availability decreases. sciencedirect

So the area is active, but the volume is modest compared with ordinary concept-drift research. There is a large literature on concept drift assuming immediate labels; a much smaller literature studies the consequences of violating that assumption.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
The following terms are substantially overlapping but not perfectly interchangeable:

  • Immediate labeling or immediate-label setting: the label is available immediately after prediction, usually before the next instance is processed.
  • Delayed labeling or delayed labelling: a label arrives after a finite delay.
  • Label delay: the time or number of instances between feature arrival and label arrival.
  • Label latency: a newer, broader term for the same delay; often defined as \(d=t_Y-t_X\).
  • Verification latency: probably the most established term in concept-drift and active-learning papers. It emphasizes that the label is obtained only after an external verification process.
  • Delayed supervised information: common in fraud-detection work, where investigator feedback or chargeback information arrives later.
  • Partially labeled data streams or partially labelled data streams: only a subset of observations receives labels.
  • Delayed partially labeled data streams: the unified term used by Gomes et al. for streams that combine finite delays with labels that may never arrive.
  • Weakly supervised streams: labels are incomplete, noisy, coarse, or indirect; this can include but is not limited to delayed labels.
  • Infinite verification latency: a label is effectively never received.
  • Extreme verification latency (EVL): recent papers use this for very long or indefinite delays, particularly when labels are unavailable for extended periods. AiGAS-dEVL explicitly uses this terminology for streams where labels are delayed or may remain unavailable indefinitely. arxiv
  • Delayed feedback: broader than delayed labels; it can include rewards, outcomes, user responses, fraud confirmations, or other feedback signals.
  • Delayed supervision: another broad term, often used in continual learning and online learning.
  • Delayed ground truth or delayed outcomes: common in applied papers, especially healthcare, finance, and forecasting.
  • Missing labels, label scarcity, and label sparsity: usually refer to partial availability, although they do not necessarily imply a time-based delay.
  • Selective labeling, verification bias, or selective labels: labels are observed conditional on an action, such as reviewing only transactions that were flagged.
  • Positive–unlabelled learning (PU learning): a related but distinct setting in which positive examples are observed and the remaining examples are unlabeled; the unlabeled set is not automatically equivalent to delayed or missing labels.

Historically, Kuncheva and Sánchez used “label delay,” while Marrs and colleagues used “verification latency”; later papers use both terms. The terminology inconsistency is real and can hide relevant work. The 2022 survey is useful partly because it tries to distinguish these settings formally. link.springer

docs.title: What happens to supervised detectors?
docs.text:
Classical detectors such as DDM, EDDM, Page-Hinkley, CUSUM, ADWIN, and accuracy-based ensemble detectors usually monitor a loss or error sequence:

\[ e_t = \mathbb{1}[\hat y_t \ne y_t]. \]

With verification latency, \(e_t\) cannot be computed at time \(t\). It becomes available only when the corresponding label arrives. Therefore:

  1. The detector cannot react earlier than the label-observation process allows.
  2. The errors it receives correspond to historical predictions, not necessarily the current model or current concept.
  3. Labels may arrive out of order.
  4. A long delay can produce stale alarms.
  5. Batch or bursty label arrivals can produce artificial bursts in the error stream.
  6. Partial labeling reduces the effective sample size and changes the missingness mechanism.

The theoretical issue was analyzed by Žliobaitė, “Change with Delayed Labeling: When is it Detectable?” IEEE ICDM Workshops, 2010. The paper characterizes which types of changes can be detected without observing new labels and proposes monitoring classifier outputs as a computationally practical alternative. It shows that some changes are identifiable from unlabeled inputs or prediction behavior, while other changes are fundamentally indistinguishable without labels. ieeexplore.ieee

This last point is crucial: a detector using only \(X\) cannot generally detect a pure conditional drift such as

\[ P_t(Y\mid X)\ne P_{t+\Delta}(Y\mid X) \]

when \(P_t(X)\) remains unchanged. Conversely, input-distribution drift can occur without any degradation in predictive accuracy.

docs.title: Has degradation been quantified?
docs.text:
Only partially and inconsistently.

There are many papers showing that delayed labels harm adaptation or active learning, but relatively few provide a clean detector-level curve of:

  • detection delay versus label latency;
  • false-alarm rate versus label coverage;
  • missed-drift rate versus partial-label mechanism;
  • performance under constant versus stochastic latency;
  • performance under missing-not-at-random labels.

The 2026 experimental survey appears to be the first recent work aimed directly at organizing and experimentally comparing concept-drift detection under delayed and partially labeled streams. Its existence is itself evidence that this evaluation problem was not previously standardized. sciencedirect

Earlier studies establish the mechanisms of degradation, but often study classifiers or active-learning systems rather than isolating the detector. For example, Plasse and Adams, “Handling Delayed Labels in Temporally Evolving Data Streams,” IEEE Big Data, 2016, provides a taxonomy of delay mechanisms and discusses how delayed labels affect stream learning. computer

In fraud detection, Dal Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi, and Bontempi, “Credit Card Fraud Detection and Concept-Drift Adaptation with Delayed Supervised Information,” IEEE IJCNN, 2015, separates immediate investigator feedback from delayed labels and finds that training separate models on the two information sources and aggregating their outputs is better than treating them identically. semanticscholar

That is relevant evidence, but it is not a general detector benchmark. It is an application-specific adaptation strategy.

docs.title: Label-free detectors
docs.text:
Label-free detectors can be grouped into four broad families:

Family What it monitors Main advantage Main limitation Input-distribution tests Changes in \(P(X)\) Works immediately Misses pure posterior drift Representation or embedding tests Changes in learned feature distributions More useful for high-dimensional data Depends on representation stability Prediction-distribution tests Changes in \(P(\hat Y)\), confidence, or output histograms Uses model information without ground truth Can confuse prior shift, uncertainty, and model bias Model/uncertainty monitors Confidence, entropy, disagreement, reconstruction error, residual proxies May provide early warning before labels Proxy can change without actual error increase

Examples include statistical tests, window-based divergence measures, clustering, density monitoring, reconstruction-error monitoring, classifier disagreement, and prediction-uncertainty methods.

Shen, Ming, Li, Gao, and Zhang, “Unsupervised Concept Drift Detectors: A Survey,” Springer, 2023, surveys unsupervised detectors and classifies them separately from supervised error-based methods. link.springer

Hinder, Vaquet, and Hammer, “One or Two Things We Know about Concept Drift—A Survey on Monitoring Evolving Environments,” 2023, focuses specifically on unsupervised data streams and drift localization. The authors note that much of the prior survey literature assumes supervision, despite the importance of unsupervised monitoring for anomaly detection and engineering systems. arxiv

A later benchmark, “A Benchmark and Survey of Fully Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection,” International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 2024, evaluates fully unsupervised detectors on real-world streams and reports that performance depends strongly on the metric and data set; no detector dominates universally. d-nb

Recent representation-based examples include DriftLens, which detects distributional changes in deep-model embeddings without requiring labels, and prediction-uncertainty approaches such as PUDD, which use changes in uncertainty rather than error rate as an early-warning signal. arxiv

docs.title: Comparison with supervised detectors
docs.text:
There is no accepted universal ranking, because the methods detect different phenomena:

  • A supervised detector is usually more semantically aligned with real performance degradation, but its earliest possible alarm is bounded by label latency.
  • An input-based detector can alarm immediately, but it may detect harmless covariate shift.
  • An output or uncertainty detector may provide a useful compromise, but its relationship to true error depends on calibration and class balance.
  • In high-dimensional data, simple distribution tests may have low power unless applied to a suitable representation.
  • Under selective labeling, supervised detectors can be biased because the observed errors are not representative of the stream.

Thus, comparing “detection delay” alone is misleading. A label-free detector may alarm earlier but with more false positives or with respect to a different definition of drift.

docs.title: Hybrid early warning and confirmation
docs.text:
There are several partial examples, but not yet a mature, generally accepted framework.

The clearest early work is Žliobaitė’s prediction-output monitoring: use a classifier trained on older labeled data, monitor its predictions on current unlabeled observations, and use later labels to confirm or refine the alarm. research.tue

Fraud-detection systems also use a practical hybrid pattern:

  • immediate investigator feedback;
  • delayed outcome labels;
  • unsupervised or anomaly-based signals for unlabeled transactions;
  • separate models or memory windows for immediate and delayed information.

Dal Pozzolo et al. found that separating immediate feedback from delayed labels was beneficial in a real fraud setting. semanticscholar

The 2022 active-learning work by Mello et al., “Stream-Based Active Learning with Verification Latency in Non-stationary Environments,” 2022 proposes PRopagate, which estimates the utility of a query despite unknown label delay and predicts requested but unavailable labels. It also proposes a drift-dependent labeling-budget strategy and reports improvements over existing active-learning methods. arxiv

The related Mello et al., “Stream-based Active Learning for Sliding Windows under the Influence of Verification Latency,” Machine Learning, 2021 proposes Forgetting and Simulating. It simulates the learner’s future state when a queried label will arrive, rather than estimating utility using the present state. Experiments report improvements under both constant and variable latency. dl.acm

These are hybrid in spirit, but they primarily address label acquisition and adaptation, not a standardized two-stage detector of the form:

  1. label-free alarm;
  2. delayed supervised confirmation;
  3. calibrated action under confirmation uncertainty.

That architecture remains a promising research direction.

docs.title: Why ordinary prequential evaluation fails
docs.text:
Standard test-then-train evaluation assumes:

  1. observe \(x_t\);
  2. predict \(\hat y_t\);
  3. immediately observe \(y_t\);
  4. score the prediction;
  5. train on \((x_t,y_t)\).

Under delay, the actual sequence is more like:

  1. observe \(x_t\);
  2. predict \(\hat y_t\);
  3. continue processing many future instances;
  4. receive labels for older instances, possibly out of order;
  5. update the model using only the labels that have arrived.

If a model is updated with \(y_{t-k}\) at time \(t\), the learner’s state is different from that under ordinary prequential evaluation. Directly replaying the data with immediate labels therefore gives optimistic results.

docs.title: Main evaluation proposals
docs.text:
The main dedicated evaluation proposal is Grzenda, Gomes, and Bifet, “Delayed Labelling Evaluation for Data Streams,” Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 34, 1237–1266, 2020. It introduces continuous re-evaluation. link.springer

The method:

  • makes an initial prediction when \(x_i\) arrives;
  • stores the instance while its label is pending;
  • periodically predicts again as the model evolves;
  • evaluates predictions in time bins between instance arrival and label arrival;
  • computes performance both immediately after arrival and just before the label becomes available;
  • supports fixed and variable delays.

This is more informative than scoring only the first prediction because it measures whether the system can refine a decision while waiting for ground truth. The authors provide an open-source implementation for MOA. github

A related paper is Grzenda, Gomes, and Bifet, “Performance Measures for Evolving Predictions under Delayed Labelling Classification,” IEEE IJCNN, 2020. It formalizes binned performance measures for evolving predictions and treats the final pre-label prediction as a distinct evaluation point. dl.acm

Other approaches include:

  • replaying the stream with fixed artificial delays;
  • delaying model updates but scoring at the original prediction time;
  • evaluating labels only when they arrive;
  • using chronological train/validation/test periods;
  • reporting performance against the age of available supervision;
  • comparing immediate-label and delayed-label versions of the same stream;
  • separate evaluation of initial predictions and revised predictions.

docs.title: Is there an accepted benchmark?
docs.text:
No. There is no universally accepted benchmark or protocol.

The field has useful ingredients:

  • MOA and related stream-learning frameworks;
  • synthetic generators with injected fixed or stochastic delays;
  • real temporal data such as flight delays, electricity, fraud, and software-defect streams;
  • continuous re-evaluation;
  • fully unsupervised drift benchmarks;
  • semi-supervised streaming protocols.

But papers still differ in:

  • whether delay is measured in time or instance count;
  • whether labels arrive in order;
  • whether latency is constant, random, heavy-tailed, or feature-dependent;
  • whether missing labels are missing completely at random;
  • whether the model may use unlabeled instances for representation learning;
  • whether pseudo-labels count as training data;
  • whether drift detectors are evaluated for statistical alarm quality or downstream accuracy;
  • whether performance is measured when predictions are made or when labels arrive.

The 2022 survey explicitly reviews current benchmarking practices and proposes adaptations, which suggests that protocol consensus remains incomplete. dl.acm

A proper benchmark should specify at least:

\[ \mathcal{O}_t = \{x_t,\; \text{labels revealed by }t,\; \text{query responses by }t\}. \]

It should then define the learner’s information set at every time \(t\), rather than merely attaching a delay to a conventional labeled data set.

docs.title: Semi-supervised streaming
docs.text:
Semi-supervised stream learning is the closest neighboring field. It uses unlabeled \(x_t\) for clustering, density estimation, representation learning, pseudo-labeling, or model regularization, while updating from the labels that eventually arrive.

Important earlier work includes:

  • Abdulsalam, Skillicorn, and Martin, work on intermittent labeling and streaming random forests, 2010, where labeled and unlabeled blocks alternate and the system decides whether enough labeled data exists to update or trust the model. link.springer
  • Masud et al., “Classification and Novel Class Detection in Concept-Drifting Data Streams under Time Constraints,” IEEE TKDE, 2011, which detects novel classes before their labels become available. dl.acm
  • Larranaga et al., “Classifying Evolving Data Streams with Partially Labeled Data,” 2011, which uses unlabeled data for drift detection and an EM-based classifier. The method monitors feature, conditional, and dual drift. oa.upm
  • COMPOSE: A Semisupervised Learning Framework for Initially Labeled Nonstationary Streaming Data, IEEE TNNLS, 2013, which uses unlabeled data in initially labeled nonstationary streams. dl.acm
  • Mello et al., “Online Reliable Semi-Supervised Learning on Evolving Data Streams,” Information Sciences, 2020, which addresses reliability of semi-supervised updates under evolving distributions. dl.acm

Semi-supervised learning contributes mechanisms for exploiting \(X\) before labels arrive, but it does not automatically solve selective-label bias or guarantee that pseudo-labels remain reliable after drift.

docs.title: Active learning on streams
docs.text:
Active learning addresses partial labeling by deciding which instances should be sent to an oracle. It contributes:

  • query-budget allocation;
  • uncertainty and diversity sampling;
  • drift-triggered queries;
  • sampling-bias correction;
  • label-value estimation;
  • explicit treatment of oracle delay.

The important limitation is that many active-learning algorithms assume a queried label is immediately available. The 2021 and 2022 verification-latency papers show that this assumption can make utility estimates stale or even cause active-learning strategies to fail. arxiv

The 2023 survey “Active Learning for Data Streams: A Survey,” Machine Learning, 2023 reviews online active-learning methods and identifies annotation cost, stream evolution, and delayed responses as continuing challenges. dl.acm

Active learning is particularly relevant to your biased-label scenario, because “only flagged cases are reviewed” is not merely label scarcity: it is an endogenous observation policy. The selection mechanism must be modeled, logged, or corrected.

docs.title: Self-training and pseudo-labeling
docs.text:
Self-training can increase the effective training rate by assigning labels to high-confidence unlabeled examples. In a drifting stream it is useful for:

  • pretraining representations before ground truth arrives;
  • maintaining a model during long label gaps;
  • expanding class coverage;
  • providing an early estimate of current class proportions.

But error propagation is especially dangerous under drift. A wrong pseudo-label can become part of the detector’s reference distribution and cause confirmation bias. Strong confidence calibration, temporal consistency, disagreement-based filtering, and delayed correction are needed.

The literature contains many semi-supervised stream algorithms, but comparatively little work systematically evaluates pseudo-labeling under the combination of:

  • concept drift;
  • verification latency;
  • selection-biased labels;
  • class imbalance;
  • non-random missingness.

docs.title: Positive–unlabelled learning
docs.text:
PU learning is transferable, but only under specific assumptions.

The useful analogy is:

  • confirmed positive = observed positive;
  • unlabeled = not-yet-confirmed or never-confirmed cases.

However, the analogy breaks when:

  • negatives are also eventually observed;
  • labels arrive after a known delay;
  • confirmation probability changes over time;
  • the probability of being labeled depends on the model’s prediction;
  • the positive class itself drifts;
  • labels arrive through delayed events rather than random sampling.

There is older work specifically titled “Positive Unlabeled Learning for Data Stream Classification,” SDM, 2009, which already recognized that concept drift makes traditional PU methods inadequate. personal.ntu.edu

PU methods can contribute:

  • class-prior estimation;
  • correction for positive-selection bias;
  • risk estimators using positive and unlabeled data;
  • delayed-positive modeling;
  • propensity-weighted learning.

The key research opportunity is to combine PU risk estimation with explicit temporal processes for label arrival. In other words, treat label availability as a stochastic observation process:

\[ P(R_t=1\mid X_t,Y_t,A_t,t), \]

where \(R_t\) indicates that the true label is observed and \(A_t\) may represent the system’s action, such as flagging or manual review.

docs.title: The central unsolved problem
docs.text:
The missing general solution is a learner that jointly models:

\[ P_t(X,Y,R,L), \]

where:

  • \(X\) is the incoming data;
  • \(Y\) is the true target;
  • \(R\) indicates whether the label is observed;
  • \(L\) is the random label-arrival time;
  • all of these may change under concept drift.

Most existing papers simplify this substantially:

  • fixed delay;
  • labels eventually arrive;
  • labels arrive independently of the prediction;
  • labels arrive in order;
  • missing labels are random;
  • the drift type is known or synthetically injected;
  • one particular classifier or detector is evaluated.

That is why the problem remains open despite many individual papers.

docs.title: 1. Identifiability
docs.text: A label-free detector cannot distinguish every type of concept drift. Pure changes in \(P(Y\mid X)\) can be invisible when \(P(X)\) does not change. Future work needs explicit guarantees stating which drift classes are identifiable under which observation assumptions.

docs.title: 2. Joint drift and label-process modeling
docs.text:
Most work treats latency as an experimental nuisance rather than a drifting process. In real systems, review capacity, fraud-reporting behavior, medical follow-up, and chargeback timing may all change over time.

The arrival process itself can drift:

\[ P(L_t \mid X_t,Y_t,t) \ne P(L_{t+\Delta}\mid X_{t+\Delta},Y_{t+\Delta},t+\Delta). \]

This can create apparent concept drift or conceal real drift.

docs.title: 3. Selection bias and verification bias
docs.text:
“Only flagged cases are labeled” is a missing-not-at-random problem. A detector trained on reviewed cases may estimate the performance of the review policy rather than the performance of the deployed model on the full population.

This remains insufficiently integrated into stream concept-drift benchmarks.

docs.title: 4. Detector calibration under delayed errors
docs.text:
A detector should know whether its alarm probability is calibrated when:

  • errors arrive in bursts;
  • errors correspond to old model versions;
  • only a subset of errors is observed;
  • the delay distribution is heavy-tailed;
  • the stream is strongly imbalanced.

Existing detectors generally do not expose these assumptions.

docs.title: 5. Early warning versus actionable drift
docs.text:
An early warning is not necessarily useful. A label-free detector may identify a change in \(P(X)\) that does not affect decisions, generating expensive or harmful retraining.

Future systems should optimize a cost-sensitive objective involving:

  • time-to-action;
  • false alarms;
  • missed drifts;
  • retraining cost;
  • delayed confirmation;
  • downstream business loss.

docs.title: 6. Confirmation protocols
docs.text:
There is no standard protocol for combining:

  1. an unsupervised warning;
  2. a temporary safe response;
  3. delayed labels;
  4. confirmation or rejection of the warning;
  5. retrospective correction.

This is perhaps the clearest opportunity for a focused thesis or research program.

docs.title: 7. Evaluation with multiple predictions per sample
docs.text:
Continuous re-evaluation is a strong start, but open issues remain:

  • How frequently should a pending sample be re-predicted?
  • Should predictions be weighted by time, exposure, or business cost?
  • How should predictions be scored when features also evolve after initial arrival?
  • How should several model versions be credited for one eventual outcome?
  • How should delayed labels arriving out of order be handled?

docs.title: 8. Realistic benchmarks
docs.text:
The field needs benchmark generators and real data sets with explicit metadata for:

  • label-arrival timestamps;
  • missing-label indicators;
  • review or intervention actions;
  • model scores that triggered review;
  • delayed outcome processes;
  • drift annotations;
  • label-order violations;
  • class imbalance;
  • recurrent and gradual drift.

Current practice often creates a synthetic delay by shifting labels by \(k\) instances. That is useful for controlled experiments but does not reproduce fraud, healthcare, or moderation workflows.

docs.title: 9. Learning from label absence
docs.text:
A missing label is not always uninformative. In fraud, no chargeback after a sufficiently long period may be weak negative evidence. In healthcare, lack of follow-up may encode access, severity, or demographic bias.

The literature needs models that distinguish:

  • not labeled yet;
  • unlikely ever to be labeled;
  • labeled negative;
  • censored outcome;
  • label suppressed by a review policy.

docs.title: 10. Safety of pseudo-label adaptation
docs.text: A model that self-trains during a long label blackout may adapt quickly—or reinforce its own mistakes. Drift-aware confidence thresholds, ensemble disagreement, abstention, and later label-based correction remain open design problems.

docs.title: Recent activity: active or dormant?
docs.text:
The area is active but fragmented, not dormant.

Evidence of recent activity includes:

  • the 2022 dedicated survey on delayed partially labeled streams; dl.acm
  • 2021–2022 work on active learning with verification latency; arxiv
  • 2023 surveys of unsupervised drift detection and stream active learning; link.springer
  • the 2024 benchmark of fully unsupervised drift detection; d-nb
  • 2024–2025 work on extreme verification latency and label-free adaptation, including AiGAS-dEVL; arxiv
  • the 2026 experimental survey dedicated to delayed and partially labeled drift detection. sciencedirect

At the same time, the publication pattern suggests that the field has not yet converged on a canonical problem formulation, benchmark, or dominant algorithm. The newest papers often introduce a method for one specific combination of delay, drift, data type, and application rather than resolving the general problem.

docs.title: Bottom-line assessment
docs.text:
You would not be entering an empty field, but you would also not be duplicating a solved problem.

A defensible research contribution would need to go beyond “apply ADWIN without labels” or “use pseudo-labeling under delay.” The strongest gap is:

A unified, benchmarked framework for concept-drift detection and adaptation when labels arrive through a delayed, partial, and selection-biased observation process, with label-free early warnings and delayed supervised confirmation.

A particularly strong project could contribute:

  1. a formal observation model for delayed and selectively observed labels;
  2. a taxonomy of immediate, finite-delay, stochastic-delay, partial, and infinite-latency settings;
  3. a hybrid detector combining input/representation/uncertainty signals with delayed error confirmation;
  4. detection-delay, false-alarm, missed-drift, and downstream-cost metrics;
  5. synthetic generators plus at least one real temporal benchmark;
  6. ablations separating covariate drift, posterior drift, label-process drift, and review-policy drift.

The literature already supplies the foundations—Žliobaitė’s detectability analysis, Plasse and Adams’s delay taxonomy, Grzenda et al.’s continuous re-evaluation, the Gomes et al. survey, active-learning-with-latency methods, and recent unsupervised-detector benchmarks—but no widely accepted framework currently combines all of these pieces.

docs.title: Exp-01 — DeepRiver rolling deep classifier vs frozen batch on SEA
docs.text:
Series: Ch1 / thesis pilot ("streaming vs non-streaming on real metrics"), first atomic experiment.

Aim → libs → method → calculations → results → conclusions as requested; §5–6 were pre-registered placeholders and are now filled from the first run (experiments/exp01/results.json).

Status: ✅ Run on 2026-09-09 (seed 42, RTX 3050 Laptop GPU). Code: experiments/scripts/exp01_deepriver_vs_frozen_sea.py; data artifact: experiments/exp01/results.json; figure: figures/exp01-rolling-kappa-deepriver-vs-frozen.png.

Metric correction (E01, 2026-11-12)

The damage-area numbers on this page use the legacy τ→recovery integral, which truncated the streaming arm. The corrected 11-seed result is damage_ref 74.8 vs 515.0 samples·κ (≈6.9×) and damage_full 321.4 vs 3,472.9 (≈10.8×). The legacy 294×/24× are retired. See E01 — Metric v2 correction.

Formatting note: math is written in Unicode (τ, κ₀, Δκ, ≈, ≥) so it renders identically in Obsidian, GitHub, and the mkdocs site — no LaTeX pipeline required.

docs.title: 1. Aim
docs.text:
First empirical check of the thesis (see thesis.md §1) using a deep streaming learner:

Can a DeepRiver rolling classifier — a bounded-memory model that retrains on a recent window of data — beat a frozen batch model (trained once, never updated) on a drifting stream, when measured prequentially?

This is deliberately the weakest form of the claim: no scheduled-retrain batch, no delay, no oracle tuning, no statistics. If DeepRiver cannot show the expected recovery behaviour here, the bigger experiments are pointless. Small and atomic by design: one synthetic stream, one injected drift, two models, three metrics.

docs.title: Hypotheses (pre-registered)
docs.text:
• H1 — Recovery: after the drift at τ, DeepRiver's rolling Kappa re-enters its pre-drift band within a bounded number of samples; the frozen RF's does not recover before the stream ends.
  • H2 — Steady state (expected loss): before τ, frozen RF (trained on the whole warm-up) has higher Kappa than the online net. This is expected and not the claim — it is the honest control half of the picture.
  • Falsification: if DeepRiver does not recover within a generous window (pre-registered: rolling Kappa back to ≥ 0.95 · κ₀ within 5,000 samples of τ), the pilot is inconclusive and the result is recorded as such rather than tuned away silently.

docs.title: 2. Libraries
docs.text:
Focus: DeepRiver (deep learning on data streams, River + PyTorch).

Package Role Notes deep-river 0.3.4 streaming deep models (RollingClassifier) the subject of the experiment river 0.25.0 metrics (Accuracy, CohenKappa, Rolling), prequential loop pinned by deep-river (<0.26); see notes/03-river-library.md torch 2.5.1 neural net backend CUDA build; run on the RTX 3050 (Laptop) GPU scikit-learn 1.9.0 frozen batch baseline (RandomForestClassifier) the opponent numpy stream generation, numerics pytest not used by us required at import time by deep-river 0.3.4 (its utils.estimator_checks imports it) — packaging bug, so it's a project dep

Environment: repo-root uv project, Python 3.12 (deep-river's torch <2.6 has no cp313 wheels, so the repo pins >=3.12,<3.13). Run: uv run experiments/scripts/exp01_deepriver_vs_frozen_sea.py — the script auto-selects CUDA if present (--device cuda|cpu to force). Exact versions in pyproject.toml / uv.lock.

docs.title: 3a. Stream (SEA, one abrupt drift)
docs.text:
• Generator: SEA concepts — 3 numerical features drawn once, continuously, from U(0, 10)³; only features 0+1 matter (x₀ + x₁ vs a threshold); binary labels.
  • Length: 60,000 samples. Label rule: x₀ + x₁ > 8 (SEA concept 0) for t < 30,000, then x₀ + x₁ > 9 (SEA concept 1) → abrupt drift at τ = 30,000.
  • noise = 0.1 (10% label noise, so the problem is non-trivial); balanced classes by construction; fixed seed 42 (single seed for Exp-01; the ≥10-seed sweep is a later, separate experiment).
  • Implementation note: river 0.25's synth.SEA reseeds its RNG per generator, so concatenating two variants replays identical feature vectors under the new label rule (train-set memorisation confound). The script therefore draws one uninterrupted feature stream and switches only the label rule at τ — identical semantics to the intended SEA abrupt drift.

docs.title: 3b. Models
docs.text:
Role Model Warm-up Update rule Streaming DeepRiver RollingClassifier over a small RNN head (RNN 3 → 16 hidden → Linear → 2 logits; Adam, lr 1e-3, cross-entropy; one optimiser step per sample) learns from sample 1 onwards per sample: predict → score → learn_one on a rolling window of 500 (bounded memory; old samples fall out → drift adaptivity) Frozen batch sklearn RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100) fit once on first 12,000 samples (20%) never updated after warm-up
  • Architecture note: the spec'd "MLP 2 → 16 → 2" cannot be expressed in DeepRiver's RollingClassifier — its feature-incremental layer handling requires the module's first layer to take n_features units, and it feeds the net a temporal window. The RNN head is the architecture DeepRiver documents for rolling models; capacity (16 hidden) and lr are unchanged.
  • DeepRiver 0.3.4 bug worked around in the script: _learn runs the forward before module.train(), so a predict-first (eval-mode) cuDNN RNN backward crashes; the wrapper forces train mode before learn_one.
  • Window size and learning rate are the two tuning knobs; pre-registered defaults (window_size = 500, lr = 1e-3) may be swept in a follow-up, not silently fitted to make H1 pass.

docs.title: 3c. Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
Standard prequential (test-then-train) loop over the post-warm-up region (t ∈ [12,000, 60,000)) for both models, on identical samples:

for x, y in stream[12k:60k]:
    y_pred = model.predict_one(x)     # frozen RF: predict only, no learning
    metric.update(y, y_pred)
    if model is streaming:
        model.learn_one(x, y)         # DeepRiver: windowed update

Metrics recorded per sample: accuracy, Cohen Kappa, rolling Cohen Kappa (w = 1,000). Runtime (seconds) and peak process RSS measured around the whole loop.

docs.title: 4. Calculations
docs.text:
Let κ(t) be rolling Cohen Kappa at sample t (window w = 1,000).

  • Pre-drift baseline: κ₀ = mean of κ(t) over the 1,000 samples immediately before τ (i.e. t ∈ [29,000, 30,000)).
  • Dip depth: Δκ = κ₀ − min κ(t) over t ∈ [τ, τ + 5,000).
  • Recovery time: the smallest r such that κ(t) ≥ 0.95 · κ₀ for 500 consecutive samples within [τ, τ + 5,000]; reported as samples from τ. Frozen model: "never" if the stream ends before the band is re-entered.
  • Damage area (the thesis's money metric, thesis.md §3): area = Σ (κ₀ − κ(t)) summed over t = τ … t_recover, in units of samples × Kappa; frozen area measured to stream end when it never recovers.
  • Full-run metrics: prequential accuracy and Cohen Kappa over the whole post-warm-up region (cumulative).
  • Cost: wall-clock seconds, samples/second, and memory (max RSS − baseline RSS).

docs.title: 5. Results
docs.text: Measured, seed 42, first run. Full per-sample series and metrics: experiments/exp01/results.json. Pre-registered expectations are in italics after each table; deviations are stated, not tuned away.

docs.title: 5a. Full-run metrics (post-warm-up, cumulative, n = 48,000)
docs.text:
Model Accuracy Cohen Kappa Runtime (s) Samples/s Peak RSS (MB) DeepRiver rolling 0.885 0.757 99.1 (CUDA) 484 1074 Frozen RF 0.856 0.689 0.17 (fit only) — —

Expectation was frozen RF winning cumulative accuracy/Kappa (H2). Deviated: DeepRiver wins both — its pre-drift steady state is not below the frozen RF (κ_dr ≈ 0.755 vs κ_fr ≈ 0.759), and it keeps that level after the drift while the frozen model drops. The per-metric win is therefore even cleaner than pre-registered. Runtime is for the DeepRiver loop on the RTX 3050 (CUDA); the same 48k loop takes ~1,089 s (44 samples/s) on CPU, so GPU is effectively required at this window size. RSS is peak process RSS (both models + CUDA context in one process), not a per-model delta.

Figure 1 — rolling Cohen Kappa (w = 1,000), drift at τ = 30,000 marked. The blue (DeepRiver) dip is shallow and self-healing; the red (frozen RF) dip is deeper and never heals before the stream ends.

docs.title: 5b. Drift-window metrics (τ = 30,000)
docs.text:
Model κ₀ Min κ Dip depth Δκ Recovery time (samples from τ) Damage area (samples·κ) DeepRiver rolling 0.755 0.703 0.052 835 (bounded) 31 Frozen RF 0.759 0.592 0.167 never (≥ 5,000) 3,307

Expectation (H1): DeepRiver dips then recovers within a few thousand samples; frozen RF dips and stays depressed. Confirmed — DeepRiver is back inside its pre-drift band (≥ 0.95 · κ₀ for 500 consecutive samples) 835 samples after τ, within the pre-registered 5,000-sample budget; the frozen RF never re-enters the band in the window and is still depressed at stream end. Damage area differs by two orders of magnitude (31 vs 3,307 samples·κ) — the recovery-time and damage-area columns are the win card, as pre-registered.

docs.title: 5c. Headline verdict
docs.text:
• H1 (bounded recovery): pass — DeepRiver re-enters its pre-drift band 835 samples after τ; frozen RF does not recover before the stream ends.
  • H2 (batch wins steady state): refuted — DeepRiver matches frozen RF pre-drift (κ 0.755 vs 0.759) and wins cumulative Kappa 0.757 vs 0.689. The honest-control half of the pre-registration did not materialise; the streaming model is not penalised in steady state on this problem.

docs.title: 6. Conclusions
docs.text:
Written after the run (seed 42, single replicate — see caveats below).

  • First DeepRiver-backed data point for thesis.md §6b: a streaming deep learner (RollingClassifier, window 500) shows bounded recovery (835 samples) on an abrupt drift where a frozen batch model never recovers within the stream. The win is per-metric (recovery time 835 vs never, damage area 31 vs 3,307 samples·κ), and — beyond the pre-registration — DeepRiver also wins cumulative accuracy/Kappa because its steady state matches the frozen RF pre-drift instead of trailing it.
  • Interpretation against the literature (literature_review/index.md §1): consistent with Read 2012 / Chen 2019 in that there is no universal winner — context matters — and with Dasari 2026's "the learner matters more than the trigger": the rolling window's continuous refit was what recovered, no detector needed. The deep net did not pay a steady-state tax on this simple problem, which is the part most likely to change on harder streams.
  • Falsification path honoured: the pre-registered recovery budget was 0.95 · κ₀ within 5,000 samples; H1 passed at 835. The result was not tuned — window (500), lr (1e-3) and architecture (16 hidden) are the pre-registered defaults; the two model changes from spec (single continuous stream; RNN head) were forced by river/DeepRiver mechanics and are documented in §3a–3b.
  • Caveats, recorded honestly:
  • Single seed, single replicate — the ≥10-seed sweep (with the confidence interval on recovery time) is the follow-up; this pilot is existence evidence, not statistics.
  • Cost is real: 484 samples/s on an RTX 3050 (1,089 s / 44 samples/s on CPU) for a 2.3k-parameter net — per-sample windowed refits are the slow path, and the cost column stands even though it is unfavourable. At this scale the GPU is not optional.
  • Peak RSS 1,074 MB includes the CUDA context; the pure model footprint is far smaller. A CPU-only measurement belongs to the cost-focused experiment.
  • Next knobs, as separate atomic experiments: seed sweep; harder drift (SEA concept 3 threshold 9.5, or a real stream); window-size/lr sweep; DeepRiver per-sample Classifier vs this rolling one (the windowed-refit vs per-sample-SGD question the literature flags); a scheduled-retrain batch baseline.

docs.title: 7. Cross-references
docs.text:
• Thesis + expected-result sketches: thesis.md (§6a–6c, §6f falsifiers).
  • Ch1 protocol (models/datasets/statistics): streaming-vs-batch-metrics.md.
  • Literature (direct comparisons, scope-defining evidence): Phase0:Research/literature_review/index.md §1 subgroup.
  • Scope guard note: the old notes/08-scope.md excludes deep learning — this experiment series is a deliberate, teacher-relevant extension of it.

docs.title: Exp-02 — seed sweep: is the 835-sample recovery reproducible?
docs.text:
Series: Ch1 / thesis pilot ("streaming vs non-streaming on real metrics"), second atomic experiment — the first statistical one.

Aim → libs → method → calculations → results → conclusions as in Exp-01. Every number below is read from experiments/exp02/results.json; every figure is re-rendered from that file.

Status: ✅ Run on 2026-09-12 — 11 seeds, RTX 3050 Laptop GPU, 1,127 s total (≈102 s/seed). Code: experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py; data artifact: experiments/exp02/results.json; figures: figures/exp02-*.png (a nine-figure suite — one story per figure — embedded through §5–§6).

Metric correction (E01, 2026-11-12)

The damage-area numbers on this page use the legacy τ→recovery integral. On 8/11 seeds recovery collapsed to τ, so the streaming integral was truncated and 294×/24× are upper bounds. The corrected metric gives damage_ref 74.8 vs 515.0 samples·κ (≈6.9×) and damage_full 321.4 vs 3,472.9 (≈10.8×); on the clean panel the worst streaming seed is 0.74× the best frozen seed. The frozen-never-recovers result (0/11) is unchanged. See E01 — Metric v2 correction.

Formatting note: math is written in Unicode (τ, κ₀, Δκ, ≈, ≥) so it renders identically in Obsidian, GitHub, and the mkdocs site — no LaTeX pipeline required.

docs.title: 1. Aim
docs.text:
Exp-01 produced one number on one seed: DeepRiver recovered from the drift in 835 samples. A synthetic stream is random (feature draws + 10% label noise), so a single replica cannot distinguish a property of the model from a property of that one draw — per the project's own rule (thesis F8, Demšar 2006), single runs are noise.

This experiment reruns exactly the Exp-01 replica — same stream construction, same two models, same warm-up, same prequential loop, same metric definitions — and changes one thing: the RNG seed.

Question: is Exp-01's 835-sample recovery reproducible across seeds, or was it an artefact of seed 42?

docs.title: Hypotheses (pre-registered)
docs.text:
• H1 — robustness of recovery: the streaming model re-enters its pre-drift band within the 5,000-sample budget on every seed; the frozen model fails to recover on every seed.
  • H2 — steady state (honest control): the frozen model's pre-drift baseline is at least as good as the streaming model's, i.e. batch wins while the concept is stationary (Exp-01's H2, now with n = 11 to be judged against).
  • Acceptance bar (fixed in the global results registry before the run): recovery time is reported as a distribution (mean ± SD) over ≥ 10 seeds, not one number.
  • Falsification: if streaming recovery is not bounded and inside budget on the large majority of seeds, or if the frozen model recovers on any seed, then Exp-01's claim is a seed artefact and does not generalise.

docs.title: 2. Libraries
docs.text:
Identical stack and versions to Exp-01 (deliberately — this is a sweep of one experiment, not a new one).

Package Role Notes deep-river 0.3.4 streaming deep models (RollingClassifier) the subject of the experiment river 0.25.0 metrics (Accuracy, CohenKappa, Rolling), prequential loop pinned by deep-river (<0.26) torch 2.5.1 neural net backend CUDA build; RTX 3050 (Laptop) scikit-learn 1.9.0 frozen batch baseline (RandomForestClassifier) the opponent numpy stream generation, numerics pytest not used by us required at import time by deep-river 0.3.4 (packaging bug)

Python 3.12, repo-root uv project. Run: uv run experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py --require-cuda (--figure-only re-renders the whole suite from the committed artifact without a rerun; --figures-dir overrides where the PNGs land).

docs.title: 3a. Stream (SEA, one abrupt drift) — identical to Exp-01, seeded per replica
docs.text:
• One continuous SEA feature draw, x ~ U(0, 10)³, drawn once per seed; only features 0+1 matter (x₀ + x₁ vs a threshold); binary labels; noise = 0.1; 60,000 samples; label rule x₀ + x₁ > 8 (concept 0) before τ = 30,000, then x₀ + x₁ > 9 (concept 1) — an abrupt drift.
  • The single-seed memorisation confound fixed in Exp-01 §3a is fixed here too: one uninterrupted feature stream, only the label rule switching at τ.
  • Seeds: 42 (Exp-01's, included as a reproducibility cross-check) plus 0–9 — 11 replicas in total. Each replica draws its own stream and its own model inits.

docs.title: 3b. Models — identical to Exp-01
docs.text:
Role Model Warm-up Update rule Streaming DeepRiver RollingClassifier over an RNN head (RNN 3 → 16 hidden → Linear → 2; Adam, lr 1e-3, cross-entropy; one optimiser step per sample) learns from sample 1 per sample: predict → score → learn_one on a rolling window of 500 Frozen batch sklearn RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=seed) fit once on first 12,000 samples (20%) never updated after warm-up

Same two documented deep-river 0.3.4 workarounds as Exp-01 (train-mode forced before learn_one; the RNN head rather than a flattened MLP, which RollingClassifier's feature-incremental handling cannot express).

docs.title: 3c. Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
Standard prequential (test-then-train) loop over the post-warm-up region (t ∈ [12,000, 60,000)) for both models, on identical samples, exactly as Exp-01 §3c (predict_one → metric.update → learn_one; the frozen model predicts only). Per-seed metrics recorded as in Exp-01; the rolling-Kappa series is not retained in this artifact (the experiment's outputs are the drift metrics, and the figure is re-rendered from them).

Determinism. torch.manual_seed(seed) and np.random.seed(seed) are set per replica before anything stochastic is built; the frozen RF is seeded with the same seed. cuDNN RNN backward is not guaranteed bit-deterministic in general, so exact reproduction is checked, not assumed (§5c).

docs.title: 3d. What "recovery = 0" means
docs.text: Recovery is defined (Exp-01 §4) as the first sample from which rolling Kappa stays ≥ 0.95 · κ₀ for 500 consecutive samples, measured from τ. A seed where the model never leaves its pre-drift band therefore satisfies the rule immediately at τ and is recorded as recovery = 0. This floor is the single most important caveat in the results below: 0 means "no excursion to recover from", not "instant recovery".

docs.title: 4. Calculations
docs.text:
Identical definitions to Exp-01 §4 (so the two experiments are comparable sample-for-sample), plus the distribution statistics this experiment exists to produce:

  • κ₀ — mean rolling Kappa over the 1,000 samples before τ.
  • Dip depth Δκ — κ₀ − min rolling Kappa over [τ, τ + 5,000).
  • Recovery time — smallest r with κ ≥ 0.95 · κ₀ for 500 consecutive samples within [τ, τ + 5,000); reported as samples from τ, null if the budget expires.
  • Damage area — Σ max(κ₀ − κ(t), 0) from τ to recovery (to stream end if never), in samples·κ.
  • Distribution — mean, SD, median, min, max over seeds; separate counts of never (budget expired) and of the metric floor (recovery = 0).

Note on the summary statistic: the recovery distribution is heavy-tailed and floored at 0 (8 of 11 seeds fall on the floor), so the mean is not a robust centre — the median and the counts are reported alongside it. This is flagged rather than hidden.

docs.title: 5. Results
docs.text: Measured 2026-09-12, 11 seeds, full 60k stream. Full per-seed detail: experiments/exp02/results.json.

docs.title: 5a. Headline — the distribution Exp-01 could not produce
docs.text:
Metric (11 seeds) Streaming (DeepRiver rolling) Frozen (RF) Pre-drift baseline κ₀ 0.751 ± 0.017 0.767 ± 0.018 Minimum rolling Kappa after τ 0.706 ± 0.015 0.594 ± 0.013 Dip depth Δκ 0.045 ± 0.015 0.173 ± 0.018 Recovery time (samples from τ) median 0, mean 319 ± 765 (0 / 174 / 835 / 2,497) never, 11/11 Damage area (samples·κ) 13 ± 31 (median ≈ 0.001, max 103) 3,710 ± 592 (min 2,439, max 4,368) Full-run accuracy 0.8830 ± 0.0021 0.8539 ± 0.0017 Full-run Cohen Kappa 0.7530 ± 0.0044 0.6850 ± 0.0035 Worst-case / best-case damage worst streaming 103 best frozen 2,439 — still 24× larger

Figure 1 — left: recovery time per seed. Eight of eleven seeds sit on the metric floor (0 = never left the pre-drift band); where an early excursion does occur, recovery is 174 / 835 / 2,497 samples — all inside the pre-registered 5,000 budget. Right: damage area per seed on a log axis; the 5 seeds with exactly zero measured damage are drawn as hatched stubs at the axis floor. The damage gap is the stable result; the recovery number is not.

Figure 2 — the same damage numbers as a distribution rather than a per-seed race: one dot per seed with the median marked. Every frozen seed sits within a factor of two of every other frozen seed; every streaming seed is two orders of magnitude below them. The medians (≈ 0.001 vs 3,822 samples·κ) are the honest centre of this comparison.

Figure 3 — how hard the drift hit each model, paired by seed. The frozen dip (red) is deeper than the streaming dip (blue) on all 11 seeds — 0.173 against 0.045 on the mean, ≈ 3.8× — with no seed where the ordering flips.

docs.title: 5b. Per seed
docs.text:
Seed Streaming recovery Streaming Δκ Streaming damage Frozen damage 42 (Exp-01) 835 0.052 31.2 3,307 0 0 0.027 0.001 3,708 1 0 0.027 0.0 3,267 2 0 0.042 0.019 3,224 3 0 0.071 0.0 4,368 4 0 0.033 0.0 3,822 5 0 0.054 0.016 4,151 6 174 0.037 4.6 2,439 7 0 0.053 0.0 4,223 8 0 0.035 0.0 4,121 9 2,497 0.066 103.1 4,180

Figure 4 — the recovery column of the table above, on its own. Eight seeds sit on the floor; the three that do not (42, 6, 9) recover in 174 / 835 / 2,497 samples. The mean (319) is dragged up by seed 9 and the SD (765) exceeds it, which is why the median (0) and this plot are reported alongside the distribution.

docs.title: 5c. Reproducibility cross-check vs Exp-01
docs.text: Seed 42, re-run through this script, produced 835 samples — exactly Exp-01's committed value (delta 0), with the same κ₀ (0.755), dip depth (0.052) and damage area (31.2 vs Exp-01's 31.2). The pipeline is therefore reproducible end-to-end on this machine and configuration: Exp-02 is a genuine sweep of Exp-01, not a different experiment wearing its name.

docs.title: 5d. Acceptance bar
docs.text: Pre-registered condition Required Measured Verdict Seeds ≥ 10 11 PASS Recovery reported as a distribution mean ± SD mean 319 ± 765, median 0, range 0–2,497 PASS (with a heavy-tail caveat, §6) Streaming recovers on every seed every seed 11/11 (of which 8 never left the band) PASS Frozen never recovers on every seed every seed 11/11 PASS

docs.title: 5e. Beyond the drift window — the full run
docs.text:
The streaming model also wins the ordinary, drift-agnostic scoreboard on every seed. The thesis does not require this (and pre-registered the opposite as an honest control), so it is reported as a bonus rather than a claim:

Figure 5 — full-run Cohen Kappa, one point per seed. Streaming is above frozen on all 11 seeds; the shaded band is the gap. 0.7530 ± 0.0044 against 0.6850 ± 0.0035.

Figure 6 — the same picture for accuracy: 0.8830 ± 0.0021 against 0.8539 ± 0.0017, streaming ahead on all 11 seeds.

docs.title: 6a. The claim generalises; the number does not
docs.text:
Exp-01's 835 was a property of seed 42, not of the method. Across 11 seeds the recovery time is 0 on eight seeds and 174 / 835 / 2,497 on the other three — a heavy-tailed spread whose mean (319) and SD (765) are not a useful summary on their own.

What is stable, and therefore what Exp-01's claim actually rests on:

  • The frozen model never recovers — 11/11 seeds, no exceptions. This is the thesis's structural prediction and it has no counterexample in the sweep.
  • The damage gap is large and stable. Streaming pays 13 ± 31 samples·κ against 3,710 ± 592 — about 294× smaller on the mean, and even the worst streaming seed (103) is 24× smaller than the best frozen seed (2,439). The comparison does not depend on picking a favourable seed.
  • The streaming dip is consistently shallow. Δκ = 0.045 ± 0.015 versus 0.173 ± 0.018 for the frozen model — the frozen model's dip is ~3.8× deeper on every seed, and its rolling Kappa bottoms out near 0.59 while streaming stays near 0.71.
  • The streaming model also wins the full run: 0.883 accuracy / 0.753 Kappa versus 0.854 / 0.685 (§5e).

Figure 7 — the damage column of Figure 1 on its own, so the gap is readable without a squint: frozen bars sit in a narrow 2,439–4,368 band, streaming bars in 0–103.

Figure 8 — each model's own baseline (hollow marker) and its worst rolling Kappa after τ (filled marker), paired by seed. The frozen model starts slightly higher than streaming and falls 0.173 on average; the streaming model falls 0.045 and stays close to its own band, which is why so many of its "recovery times" are 0.

docs.title: 6b. H2 is now (mildly) supported, unlike in Exp-01
docs.text: Exp-01's single seed showed the two models essentially level before the drift (κ₀ 0.755 vs 0.759) and recorded H2 — "batch wins steady state" — as refuted. Over 11 seeds the frozen model does start ahead: κ₀ = 0.767 ± 0.018 versus 0.751 ± 0.017. So the honest control half of the pre-registration holds after all: a frozen batch model is slightly better while the concept is stationary, and it still loses the full run because it collapses permanently at τ. The refined statement is that streaming pays a small steady-state tax and more than earns it back on drift.

docs.title: 6c. A real methodological finding: the recovery metric under-reports late dips
docs.text:
Comparing dip depth against recovery time exposes a flaw in the metric as defined:

Dip depth Recovery recorded Seeds that breached the band early (42, 6, 9) 0.052 / 0.037 / 0.066 835 / 174 / 2,497 Seeds that breached the band later than τ+500 (2, 3, 5, 7) 0.042 / 0.071 / 0.054 / 0.053 0 — scored as "never left the band" Seeds that never breached (0, 1, 4, 8) ≤ 0.035 0

Seven of eleven seeds did leave the pre-drift band at some point after τ, but only three are credited with a recovery time, because the rule looks for the first sustained in-band run starting at τ: a model that stays in band for the first 500 samples and dips afterwards is scored 0. Recovery time is therefore not monotone in dip depth (seed 3 has a deeper dip than seed 9 yet scores 0), and it silently conflates "never dipped" with "dipped late and healed".

The practical consequence for the project: damage area and dip depth are the trustworthy drift-window metrics; recovery time is only meaningful conditional on an early excursion. A future revision should measure recovery from the first band-exit rather than from τ. This is recorded rather than patched, because changing the definition now would break comparability with Exp-01's committed numbers.

Figure 9 — the flaw in one picture. Each seed is placed by how deep its dip was and what recovery time was recorded. Green = an early excursion whose recovery is credited; orange X = a seed that did leave its band but was scored 0 because the excursion began after τ + 500; hollow blue = genuinely never left the band. Four of the eleven seeds are orange, which is why the mean recovery time is not a property of the model.

docs.title: 6d. Caveats, recorded honestly
docs.text:
• One stream family (SEA), one drift type (abrupt), one drift position (τ at 50%), two models — no scheduled-retrain baseline, no drift detector, no label delay. Each of those is a separate experiment (§7).
  • Cost is real and unchanged from Exp-01: ~102 s per seed, 454–490 samples/s on the RTX 3050, peak process RSS 1,108 MB. The sweep is GPU-bound in practice; the per-sample windowed refit is the slow path.
  • cuDNN RNN backward is not bit-deterministic in general; the seed-42 cross-check matched exactly here (§5c), but that is an observed result, not a guarantee.
  • Script fix along the way: the --limit dev slice originally pinned τ to the end of the slice, leaving no post-drift region (every metric n/a). It now scales the full run's geometry (τ at 50%, warm-up at 20%) so a smoke test actually measures a drift.

docs.title: 7. Cross-references
docs.text:
• Thesis + expected-result sketches: thesis.md (§6b, §6f falsifiers, F8 statistics).
  • Exp-01 (the single-seed pilot this experiment sweeps): exp01-deepriver-vs-frozen-sea.md.
  • Ch1 protocol (models/datasets/statistics): streaming-vs-batch-metrics.md §5.
  • Global verdict registry: ../Reports/Results.md.
  • Data artifact: experiments/exp02/results.json · code: experiments/scripts/exp02_seed_sweep_sea.py.

Next, in order: Exp-03 baseline ladder (scheduled-retrain + oracle-tuned batch) · Exp-04 real streams (Elec2, Phishing, Covertype, Airlines, CreditCard) · Exp-05 the Delay Tax (label-delay sweep) · and the recovery-metric revision in §6c.

docs.title: Streaming vs Batch: Real Metrics Where Online Learning Wins (and Where It Doesn't)
docs.text:
Purpose: Evidence dossier + experimental protocol for the teacher's plan — "take some models that are not streaming and beat them on real metrics." Produced for the Delay Tax major project.

Status: ✅ Evidence verified (citations below); protocol to be run in Ch1.

docs.title: 1. The metrics that prove streaming learning works
docs.text: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation is the accepted protocol: for each sample, predict_one(x) → metric.update(y, y_pred) → learn_one(x, y) (Gama, Sebastião & Rodrigues, 2013, Machine Learning 90:317–346). All metrics below are computed inside that loop.

docs.title: Predictive quality metrics (per sample, over the stream)
docs.text: Metric What it proves River class Prequential Accuracy overall correctness on the live stream metrics.Accuracy Kappa (Cohen) chance-corrected agreement — the headline metric; robust to class imbalance metrics.CohenKappa Rolling/windowed Kappa recency-biased view — shows recovery after drift metrics.RollingCohenKappa AUC-ROC / AUC-PR ranking quality; PR for rare classes (fraud) metrics.ROCAUC, metrics.PrecisionRecallAUC F1 / Recall / Precision per-class utility (e.g., recall of the fraud class) metrics.F1, metrics.Recall

docs.title: Drift-response metrics (what batch models structurally can't report)
docs.text:
Metric What it proves Detection delay (samples from drift onset to alarm) speed of adaptation False-alarm rate / mean time to false alarm (MTFA) alarm cost Missed-detection ratio (MDR) reliability Recovery time (samples from drift onset until rolling Kappa returns to pre-drift level) the money metric — batch models never recover until the next scheduled retrain

Metric definitions follow Cerqueira et al., KDD '26 (F1-detection score, normalized detection time; DOI 10.1145/3770855.3819070 — already noted in literature_review/papers/kdd2026-drift-benchmark.md).

docs.title: Resource metrics (the three streaming constraints from notes/01)
docs.text: Metric Constraint Memory footprint (bytes / model) bounded memory Throughput (samples/sec), latency per sample bounded time Number of passes over the data single pass

docs.title: Label-efficiency metric
docs.text: Metric What it proves Performance vs. fraction of labels used (l_access sweep) streaming keeps working when labels are scarce (STUDD's headline)

docs.title: 2. Evidence that streaming learning works — with numbers
docs.text:
Verified from the vault's literature index (✅ in literature_review/index.md):

  • ROSE (Cano & Krawczyk, 2022, Machine Learning 111:2561–2599): streaming self-adjusting ensemble, Kappa 63.65 vs next-best 57.85 across 24 imbalanced real datasets, 30 ensembles compared. Streaming wins on real, imbalanced, drifting data.
  • ARF (Gomes et al., 2017, Machine Learning 106:1469–1495): adaptive operators + resampling cope with abrupt, gradual, and recurring drift "without complex optimizations" — the flagship streaming learner.
  • HAT (Bifet & Gavaldà, 2009): ADWIN-per-node drift handling; superior adaptability on Adult and Poker-Hand (the origin of "adaptive beats static").
  • STUDD (Cerqueira et al., 2023, Machine Learning 112:4351–4378): label-free early warning; best label efficiency among non-baseline methods on 19 benchmark streams; MDR ~19%. Batch retraining starves without labels; streaming detectors don't.
  • KDD '26 drift benchmark (Cerqueira et al., 2026): 14 detectors × 7 real datasets; gives us the protocol and metrics to make our comparisons rigorous.
  • Botacin & Gomes (2024, Computers & Security 147): delayed labels (the Delay Tax) raise user exposure ~50% and cut detection up to 75% — the production cost that adaptive streaming systems mitigate.
  • Gomes et al. (2022, ACM Computing Surveys 55(4):75): a 10,000-instance label delay on AGRAWAL shifts detections by ~10,000 instances and keeps prequential accuracy below 50% — the reaction-floor effect our project formalizes.

docs.title: 3. Non-streaming models we can beat (and the honest caveat)
The counter-evidence first (do not cherry-pick)
docs.text:
Amekoe et al. 2024 (arXiv:2409.10111) — the most direct batch-vs-streaming study: - No-delay synthetic benchmark (5 streams, 1M samples, Optuna-tuned): retrained XGBoost r_XGBoost Avg AUC-ROC 92.81 vs ARF 91.02; batch wins, slightly. - Real fraud data (6.5M IBANs, 0.1% fraud, delayed labels): propagate_XGBoost AUCPR 23.41 vs ARF 14.23; batch wins clearly under delay + extreme imbalance. - ARF runtime ~2.2× r_XGBoost (3,702 s vs 1,689 s).

Implication for our claims: we cannot promise "streaming beats tuned, frequently-retrained batch" — the literature says otherwise under delay and rare-class conditions. That is fine: it is exactly why our project's gap (delay-aware adaptation) exists. Our defensible wins are below.

docs.title: Batch models we beat, and on what metric
docs.text: Batch model (non-streaming) Setting we beat it in Metric where we win Frozen RF / XGBoost / LR / SVM / DT (train once on warm-up window, deploy, never update) Any drifting stream Accuracy/Kappa after drift onset; recovery time; AUC Scheduled-retrain batch (refit every k samples, no drift detection) Between retrain points, and drift occurring right after a retrain Rolling Kappa dip depth + recovery time; detection delay Batch models needing all labels before retraining Label-scarce streams Label efficiency (STUDD-style l_access sweep) Any batch model on unbounded streams Memory Bounded-memory footprint (batch stores data; streaming doesn't)

docs.title: Why these wins are structural, not cherry-picked
docs.text:
• A frozen model has no mechanism to react to drift; a streaming model with a detector has a bounded reaction time. This is the Delay Tax's Lemma 1 (reaction floor) in reverse: streaming's floor is T ≥ τ + L_τ; a frozen batch model's "recovery" is undefined (never).
  • A scheduled retrain reacts on a fixed clock, not on evidence; streaming reacts to detected change, so it recovers faster and spends less compute when nothing changes.

docs.title: 4. Protocol to prove it (Ch1 experiments)
docs.text:
1. Pin the stack: Python ≥3.11, pin River version (per notes/03-river-library.md), scikit-learn for batch baselines.
  2. Datasets: real streams — Elec2, Phishing, Forest Covertype, Airlines, CreditCard fraud (report Elec2 Kappa+ caveats); synthetic with known drift timing — SEA, Agrawal, Hyperplane, RandomRBF, STAGGER, LED (for ground-truth detection-delay/recovery measurement).
  3. Streaming models: Hoeffding Tree, HAT, ARF, SRP, Leveraging Bagging, kNN(+ADWIN), online LR.
  4. Batch baselines: (a) frozen — fit on first 20–30%, predict-only afterwards; (b) scheduled — refit every k on a sliding window, no drift detection; (c) oracle-tuned (XGBoost/EBM with Optuna) — reported as the honest upper bound (Amekoe-style).
  5. Seeds & statistics: ≥10 seeds on synthetic; real ordered streams use bootstrap windows; Friedman + Nemenyi across datasets; Wilcoxon signed-rank pairwise; report effect sizes (per notes/04-evaluation.md).
  6. Outputs: per-metric tables; accuracy-over-time / rolling-Kappa-over-time curves with drift onsets marked (Amekoe Fig. 1 style); recovery-time and detection-delay tables; memory/throughput columns. The "win card": one claim per metric, with the number and the dataset it came from.

docs.title: 5. Expected claims (the win card, preview)
docs.text:
• Streaming models recover rolling Kappa to pre-drift level within a bounded number of samples on every synthetic drift; frozen batch models never do before the stream ends.
  • On real streams with drift, HAT/ARF rolling Kappa ≥ frozen RF/XGBoost on the post-drift window (supported by ROSE 63.65 vs 57.85 Kappa and HAT's ADWIN results).
  • Streaming matches scheduled-retrain batch accuracy while using 1 pass and bounded memory; and with drift detectors, reacts between retrain points where batch cannot.
  • Under label scarcity, streaming + detectors hold performance where batch retraining starves (STUDD label-efficiency result).

docs.title: 6. Risks / what could sink the claim (and mitigations)
docs.text:
• Amekoe-style tuned batch beats streaming on delay/rare-class → our headline is frozen and scheduled batch, reported alongside oracle-tuned batch as an upper bound; never overclaim.
  • ARF is compute-expensive → use HT/HAT/LB as the cheap streaming proof; report ARF as the accuracy ceiling with its cost stated.
  • Elec2 Kappa+ collapse → prefer rolling Cohen Kappa + AUC-PR; treat Elec2 as secondary.
  • Synthetic-only results → real datasets carry the headline; synthetic only provides ground-truth drift timing for delay/recovery metrics.
  • Teacher requires novelty → the note is evidence for Ch1 (baseline chapter); the novelty stays in Ch3 (delay tax). The comparison harness itself is a deliverable.

docs.title: Conclusion — groundwork update
docs.text:
What we're proving: streaming learning beats non-streaming models on real, drifting, label-scarce data.

  • Models — streaming: Hoeffding Tree, HAT, ARF, SRP, Leveraging Bagging, kNN(+ADWIN), online LR (River). Batch to beat: frozen (RF/XGBoost/LR/SVM/DT, train-once) and scheduled-retrain (refit every k, no drift detector); oracle-tuned XGBoost/EBM reported as honest upper bound.
  • Metrics: prequential accuracy, Cohen Kappa, rolling Kappa, AUC-ROC/PR, F1/recall, detection delay, MTFA, MDR, recovery time, memory, throughput, label efficiency.
  • How: prequential test-then-train loop; ≥10 seeds, Friedman + Nemenyi, Wilcoxon; real datasets (Elec2, Phishing, Covertype, Airlines, CreditCard) + synthetic with known drift (SEA, Agrawal, Hyperplane, RBF, STAGGER, LED); win card = one claim per metric, with dataset + number.
  • Where we win: frozen batch → decisively after drift; scheduled batch → recovery time + compute between retrains. Caveat: tuned frequent-retrain batch beats streaming under delay + rare classes — that is the Delay Tax gap (Ch3).
